name: Jensen Huang
domain: building and leading a company for decades, strategy and creating new markets, accelerated computing and AI, flat organisations and management, resilience and suffering, first-principles decision making, and advice to founders and students
sourcesLabel: interviews, fireside chats, commencement speeches and keynotes

sources.title: How Jensen Huang reasons from first principles and bets on accelerated computing and AI for decades
sources.originalTitle: What NVIDIA's Jensen Huang Believes
sources.summary: Jensen explains how Nvidia went from a parallel-plus-sequential computing insight, through gaming, CUDA and AlexNet, to reinventing the computing stack. He covers staying committed for a decade on core beliefs, physical AI, energy efficiency, and advice to students to use AI.

principles.text: Reason from first principles; if the principles and assumptions don't change, don't change your core beliefs.
principles.quote: you reason from first principles and at some point you have to believe something and if those principles don't change and the assumptions don't change uh then you there's no reason to change your core beliefs

principles.text: Build the large market first so its R&D budget funds the technology, creating a flywheel.
principles.quote: having it being a large Market is important because the technology is complicated and if we had a large Market our R&D budget could be large we could create new technology and that flywheel between technology and market and greater technology

principles.text: Take the optimist's view of creating something new: if you don't build it, they can't come.
principles.quote: if you build it they might not come and and that's that's always the the cynic perspective however The Optimist perspective would say but if you don't build it they can't come

principles.text: Invest in your own belief even when investors and others doubt it, even for tens of billions over a decade.
principles.quote: you have to believe in your future you have to invest in yourself and and um uh we believ this so deeply uh that that we we invested you know tens of billions of dollars uh before before it really happened

principles.text: Keep architectures flexible, because no idea in computing stays dominant forever; bet on the richness of innovation.
principles.quote: we want to create an architecture that let inventors and innovators and software programmers and AI researchers swim in the soup and come up with some Amazing Ideas

principles.text: Ask how AI can make you better at your own job; learn to prompt it and get an AI tutor.
principles.quote: if I were a student today irrespective whether it's for uh for math or for science or chemistry or biology or doesn't matter what field of science I'm going to go into or what profession I am I'm going to ask myself how can I use AI to do my job better

sources.title: How Jensen Huang built Nvidia: first principles, accelerated computing and an only-in-America story
sources.originalTitle: Jensen Huang on Vision, Risk, and the GPU | Only In America
sources.summary: Jensen tells his immigrant path and Nvidia's founding thesis: general-purpose CPUs can't be the only computing platform, so he solved the chicken-and-egg adoption problem via 3D gaming. He also covers suffering for belief, returning to first principles, and advice to young people.

principles.text: When uncertain or things move fast, go back to first principles and core values.
principles.quote: When I'm uncertain about the future, when things are moving too fast, you always go back to first principles. What are my core values? What makes me great today? What do I aspire for?

principles.text: Nvidia was founded on the first-principles conviction that a CPU cannot be the only computing platform.
principles.quote: we were just determined that on first principle basis, the general-purpose computer cannot possibly be the only computing platform.

principles.text: Solve the chicken-and-egg adoption problem by finding a high-volume first application that needs the new architecture.
principles.quote: how do we find an application that would, on the one hand, need this architecture, on the other hand, be sufficiently high volume to cause this architecture to proliferate?

principles.text: Keep finding new problems that fit your architecture, one after another, until a breakthrough like deep learning arrives.
principles.quote: we just kept finding one problem after another.

principles.text: Building something nobody believes in means suffering without external feedback; belief and grit carry you.
principles.quote: We suffered our way here. You know, we suffered every single step of the way we suffered our way here, because nobody believed in it.

principles.text: Technology change is the opportunity for greatness; status quo rarely lets you make a difference.
principles.quote: During technology change, during world change is the only opportunity for greatness. Status quo, you know, it's really hard to make a difference.

sources.title: Jensen Huang on Rogan: surviving Nvidia's near-death, fear as fuel, and why AI won't end jobs
sources.originalTitle: Joe Rogan Experience #2422 - Jensen Huang
sources.summary: Jensen tells Nvidia's origin story: an impossible 1993 mission, three wrong technology bets, Sega's $5M lifeline, and an untested chip tape-out. He explains leading through vulnerability, first-principles reassessment and fear of failure, and why AI, energy and jobs will change gradually.

principles.text: Fear of failure drives him more than the desire to succeed.
principles.quote: I have a greater drive from not wanting to fail than the drive of wanting to succeed.

principles.text: Vulnerable leaders can pivot; leaders who must always be right cannot.
principles.quote: the more vulnerable we are as a leader the more able other people are able to tell you you know that Jensen that's not exactly right

principles.text: Reason from first principles and reassess continuously, even though it breeds anxiety.
principles.quote: I just have to make sure that I stay alert, that I reason about things from first principles all the time. Always break things down to first principles.

principles.text: Crisis teaches you to strip waste and do only what is essential.
principles.quote: We learned how to remove all waste in the company and work from first principles and doing only the things that are essential.

principles.text: Narrow focus on one audience, plus an ecosystem, turns technology into a platform.
principles.quote: instead of building a 3D graphics chip for every 3D graphics application, we decided to build a 3D graphics chip for one application. We bet the farm on video games.

principles.text: Success involves long suffering, and sharing that honestly helps others.
principles.quote: there's long periods of suffering and loneliness and uncertainty and fear and embarrassment and humiliation.

sources.title: Jensen Huang at Stanford GSB: creating markets, first principles, flat orgs, core beliefs
sources.originalTitle: Jensen Huang, Founder and CEO of NVIDIA
sources.summary: Jensen recounts founding NVIDIA, the OpenGL pivot that saved it, and creating markets alongside technology. He explains first-principles thinking, early indicators of future success, his flat organization with about 50 direct reports, and how he steadied the company through an 80% stock drop.

principles.text: Create the market while you create the technology; for new computing the two can't be separated.
principles.quote: we had to create technology, create markets. The idea that a company would create technology, create markets, defines NVIDIA today.

principles.text: Treat unfamiliar problems as learnable, then rebuild from first principles instead of copying.
principles.quote: my first thought is always, how hard can it be? And it's probably just a textbook away. You're probably one archive paper away from figuring this out.

principles.text: Use early indicators of future success, not lagging results, to keep conviction in far-off bets.
principles.quote: gross margins. That's not a KPI, that's a result. You're looking for something that's an early indicators of future positive result

principles.text: Choose work by its importance and whether it would happen without you, not by market size.
principles.quote: We find inspiration not from the size of a market, but from the importance of the work.

principles.text: In a crisis, gut-check your core beliefs; change nothing unless the underlying facts changed.
principles.quote: if those things change, you've gotta change everything. But if none of those things change, you change nothing, keep on going

principles.text: Design the organization from first principles and let information flow freely rather than hoarding it.
principles.quote: I don't believe in a culture, an environment, where the information that you possess is the reason why you have power.

sources.title: Jensen Huang on extreme co-design, shaping belief, speed-of-light thinking and resilience (Lex Fridman #494)
sources.originalTitle: Jensen Huang: NVIDIA - The $4 Trillion Company & the AI Revolution | Lex Fridman Podcast #494
sources.summary: Jensen explains why Nvidia moved from chips to rack and AI-factory scale design, and how he builds a company around the output. He covers betting CUDA on GeForce, pre-shaping belief before big announcements, first-principles "speed of light" thinking, and handling suffering by decomposing problems. He also gives career advice on AI and jobs.

principles.text: Design the company's structure around the output it must produce, not a copied org chart.
principles.quote: the goal of au of a company is to be the machinery, the mechanism, the system that produces the output and that output is the product that we like to create.

principles.text: Run a flat org: large direct staff, no one-on-ones, problems attacked in the open by everyone.
principles.quote: My direct staff is 60 people. You know, I don't have one-on-ones with them because it's impossible.

principles.text: Install base is the most important property of a computing platform, so seed it even at great cost.
principles.quote: install base defines an architecture not everything else is secondary.

principles.text: Shape belief with everyone daily so the big announcement feels obvious, not shocking.
principles.quote: I'm trying to shape their belief system such that when I come the day I say, "Hey, let's buy Melanox." It's completely obvious to everybody that we absolutely should.

principles.text: Break pressure into parts, tell someone who can act, forget setbacks, and keep moving.
principles.quote: I decompose the problem. I reason about the problem and I I share the load with it.

principles.text: Jobs have purposes that outlast the tasks AI automates; learn to use AI.
principles.quote: the purpose of your job and the tasks and the tools that you use to do your job are related, not the same.

sources.title: Jensen Huang at Caltech 2024: first principles, setbacks, and a craft
sources.originalTitle: Jensen Huang’s Speech At CalTech｜黃仁勳加州理工演講【中英文對照】
sources.summary: Jensen tells the Caltech class of 2024 how NVIDIA bet on deep learning from first principles, and how repeated setbacks pushed it into robotics. He argues that resilience, tolerance for suffering, a chosen craft and strict prioritisation matter more than raw intelligence.

principles.text: Reason from first principles, form a belief about the future, then act on it even when the payoff is unknown.
principles.quote: A new computing model has emerged, and a new industry has emerged, all because we reasoned from first principles, formed our belief about the future, and we acted on them.

principles.text: If you want to learn how far a technology scales, you have to build it; you can't wait for customers to prove it.
principles.quote: This is one of those, if you build it, will they come? Our logic is if we don't build it, they can't come.

principles.text: When a company believes something, it should act on it, investing heavily into the unknown for years.
principles.quote: when the company believes something, we should go act on it.

principles.text: Treat setbacks as opportunities; they build agility and corporate character.
principles.quote: One setback after another, we shook it off and skated to the next opportunity. Each time, we gained skills and strengthened our character.

principles.text: Create a market with no customers and you also have no competitors.
principles.quote: where there are no customers, there are also no competitors, and nobody cares about you.

principles.text: Endurance, long-term focus and handling setbacks are his superpowers, more than intelligence.
principles.quote: My ability to endure pain and suffering, my ability to work on something for a very, very long period of time, my ability to handle setbacks and see the opportunity just around the corner I consider to be my superpowers

sources.title: Jensen Huang on AI doomerism, open vs closed models, and going as far up the stack as needed, as low as possible
sources.originalTitle: Jensen Huang: The Doomer Hoax, Superintelligence is Here, and The Future of AI (ft. President Trump)
sources.summary: Jensen rebuts AI doom predictions by pointing to failed forecasts, argues regulation should solve real problems via engineering root-cause, and explains why Nvidia runs every model and builds only what customers need. He also covers open models, supply chain foresight, and long-horizon thinking.

principles.text: Regulation should solve actual problems; root-cause incidents from an engineering perspective and institutionalize the fix.
principles.quote: regulation should solve actual problems. And so the question is what actual problems have we enjoyed,

principles.text: Safety and leadership are false choices; you can innovate, execute fast and lead safely at once.
principles.quote: You're you're able to innovate quickly. You're able to execute quickly and and uh America's able to lead and to do it safely.

principles.text: Go up the stack only as far as needed, as low as possible, then let a thousand flowers bloom.
principles.quote: Our strategy is go up as far as we need to and as low as possible.

principles.text: Build out of customer need and help everyone succeed, not to disrupt or take a slice.
principles.quote: So I do everything out of need. I'm not trying to disrupt I mean we don't wake up in the morning try to disrupt anybody.

principles.text: Think in decades: a CEO must plan the next decade and the one after, so a few years is just a click.
principles.quote: I think in decades as well you know I've been around a long time and you know for Nvidia I've got to think about what happens next decade and decade after that.

principles.text: The AI race is won by who exploits the technology best, not who invents it.
principles.quote: the race is really about who exploits the technology best.

sources.title: Jensen Huang on Nvidia's moat: do as much as needed, as little as possible, and earn trust yearly
sources.originalTitle: Jensen Huang – Will Nvidia’s moat persist?
sources.summary: Jensen explains Nvidia's moat as ecosystem, install base and programmable co-design, not scarce supply. He covers shaping the supply chain by educating CEOs, refusing to pick winners or auction GPUs, owning misses like Anthropic, and defending selling to China.

principles.text: Do as much as needed, as little as possible: do only what nobody else would, and partner for the rest.
principles.quote: We should do as much as needed as little as possible.

principles.text: Shape the supply chain by educating partners until they reason about the future the way you do.
principles.quote: I need to make sure that the entire supply chain upstream and downstream the ecosystem understands what is coming at us, why it's coming, when it's coming, how big is it going to be

principles.text: Don't pick winners. Humility from near-death: Nvidia was once the least likely of 60 graphics companies to survive.
principles.quote: Nvidia's graphics architecture was precisely wrong. It's not a little bit wrong.

principles.text: Be dependable: quote a price and keep it, even when demand spikes. Trust compounds over decades.
principles.quote: You set your price and then people decide to buy it or not.

principles.text: Programmability plus extreme co-design beats Moore's law; 10x leaps come from changing algorithms and the whole stack.
principles.quote: the only way to really get 10x leaps, 100x leaps, is to fundamentally change the algorithm and how it's computed every single year.

principles.text: Own your misses plainly, then fix them and don't repeat them.
principles.quote: I'm not going to make that same mistake again.

sources.title: Jensen Huang on AI alarmism: jobs, safety as engineering, open models, and the five-layer cake
sources.originalTitle: Jensen Huang Thinks A.I. Alarmism Has Gone Too Far | The Ezra Klein Show
sources.outlet: The Ezra Klein Show and 2 more
sources.summary: Jensen argues AI is a revolution best understood as software and engineering, not myth. He separates a job's purpose from its tasks, says safety is part of accelerating AI, and backs open models and diffusion across every industry. He also rejects doomer narratives as harmful.

principles.text: Every job has a purpose and tasks. AI automates tasks, not the purpose, so jobs change rather than vanish.
principles.quote: for everybody's job, there's the purpose of the job and then there's the task you do as the job.

principles.text: Human ambition is the missing input in job-loss forecasts; he expects net job creation and new industries.
principles.quote: I believe the power of ambition is the greatest force in fact and is missing in everybody's calculation

principles.text: Treat AI as an engineering problem: root-cause failures, fix the process. If you can't control it, don't ship it.
principles.quote: if they believe they're out of control, then the right answer is don't ship products until they're in control.

principles.text: Safety, alignment and evaluation are part of accelerating the technology, not a brake on it.
principles.quote: AI needs to accelerate to be safe.

principles.text: Alarmism isn't a social good. Be scientific and evidence-based, because scaring people harms society.
principles.quote: Don't think for a second just because you're an alarmist that you're doing a social good.

principles.text: Responsible optimist: carry the worries yourself and give others the optimism. The hard problems are the builder's.
principles.quote: it turns out that's not society's problem. That's my problem.

sources.title: Jensen Huang on All-In: pick insanely hard problems, expect suffering, sell the system not the chip
sources.originalTitle: Jensen Huang: Nvidia's Future, Physical AI, Rise of the Agent, Inference Explosion, AI PR Crisis
sources.summary: At GTC, Jensen explains how Nvidia chooses what to build (only insanely hard, never-done things that tap its superpowers), why it became an AI factory company, and why agents drive an inference explosion. He also covers open vs proprietary models, physical AI, and advice to students: be expert at using AI.

principles.text: Pursue only what is insanely hard, never done before, and tied to your company's superpowers; if it's easy, back away.
principles.quote: Is this something that has never been done before that's insanely hard to do and that somehow taps into the special superpowers of our company?

principles.text: Great things come with pain and suffering, so you had better enjoy the hard work.
principles.quote: There are no great things that are invented because it was just easy to do and just like first try, here we are.

principles.text: Defining strategy and vision and shaping the future is the CEO's job, informed by great people across the company.
principles.quote: In a final analysis, that's the job of the CEO.

principles.text: Define what you make by the customer's problem, not the component: customers want full systems, not chips.
principles.quote: it's not about building the chip, it's about building the system. And that system's really hard to build.

principles.text: Vertically optimize, horizontally innovate, and let partners choose how much of the stack to buy; solve the problem rather than force a solution.
principles.quote: We open this we we vertical optimization, we horizontally innovate, and we let everybody decide.

principles.text: Judge a factory by cost per token and throughput, not sticker price; falling behind the technology pace makes even free chips too expensive.
principles.quote: even when the chips are free, it's not cheap enough.

sources.title: Jensen Huang at SIEPR 2024: accelerated computing, resilience through suffering, and a flat 55-report org
sources.originalTitle: Keynote by NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang at 2024 SIEPR Economic Summit
sources.outlet: Stanford Institute for Economic Policy Research (SIEPR)
sources.summary: Jensen explains how 30 years of accelerated computing drove marginal compute cost toward zero and enabled AI. He also covers competing on total cost of ownership, why resilience beats high expectations, and how he runs a flat company with 55 direct reports and no private information.

principles.text: Drive the marginal cost of a resource toward zero and entirely new ways of working become possible.
principles.quote: if we could reduce the marginal cost of computing down to approximately zero we might use it to do something insanely amazing large language models

principles.text: Make the alternative irrelevant by winning on total cost of operations, not chip price.
principles.quote: our TCO is so good that even when the competitor's chips are free it's not cheap enough and that that is our goal to add so much value that the alternative um is not about cost

principles.text: Be open with competitors and customers: show them your roadmap so they can see why you are good.
principles.quote: if you don't make an attempt at uh uh explaining why you're good at something they'll never get a chance to to buy your your products

principles.text: Resilience, not high expectations, drives success, and it is built through suffering and setbacks.
principles.quote: people with very high expectations have very low resilience and unfortunately resilience matters in success I don't know how to teach it to you except for I hope suffering happens to you

principles.text: Greatness comes from character, and character is formed by people who have suffered, not just smart ones.
principles.quote: greatness is not intelligence as you know greatness comes from character and character isn't isn't formed out of smart people it's formed out of people who suffered

principles.text: Run a flat organisation: no secret information, no private one-on-ones, so information flows fast and people are empowered by what they do.
principles.quote: there's not one piece of information that I that I somehow secretly tell eaff that I don't tell the rest of the company

sources.title: Jensen Huang at Columbia: choosing hard problems, accelerated computing, and the flywheel
sources.originalTitle: NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang Reveals Keys to AI, Leadership
sources.summary: Jensen explains how NVIDIA invented accelerated computing, found the narrow middle between general and specialized chips, and built a platform flywheel. He shares his rule for choosing work (hard, destined, loved), why suffering wins, and what a CEO must own: character, strategy, craft.

principles.text: Choose something insanely hard that no one has done; the one willing to suffer longest wins.
principles.quote: the reason why you choose something insanely hard to do by the way so that you have lots of time to go learn it

principles.text: Pick work you are destined for and love, because the pain and suffering will be great.
principles.quote: you should choose something that somehow you're destined to do

principles.text: Avoid commodity markets and chasing rivals' share; great people want to do what has never been done.
principles.quote: we naturally selected ourselves out of commodity markets

principles.text: Don't duplicate what partners already do well; spend time on what nobody has done.
principles.quote: let's not squander my time to go repeat what they've already done let's go squander my time on something that nobody has done

principles.text: Define the mission around the problem, not the product, and it can last forever.
principles.quote: make sure that your mission is not build trains but enable Transportation

principles.text: A CEO must lead with character and be chief strategy officer; strategy is action, not rhetoric.
principles.quote: the most important thing for a CEO is strategic thinking there's just no alternative

sources.title: Jensen Huang on Acquired: betting the company on simulation, platforms, and the zero-billion-dollar market
sources.originalTitle: NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang
sources.summary: Jensen recounts how Nvidia survived 1997 by emulating a perfect chip before tape-out, and how first-principles reasoning from AlexNet led to CUDA and the data center. He explains Nvidia's org as a computing stack, positioning near opportunities, and why entrepreneurs must trick themselves with "how hard can it be."

principles.text: Pushing chips in means pulling future risk forward: simulate and prefetch everything before betting the farm.
principles.quote: when you bet the farm you're saying I'm going to take everything in the future all the risky things and going to pull it in advance and that is probably the lesson

principles.text: Constraint breeds excellence: with your back against the wall, do it right once instead of repeatedly.
principles.quote: why tape out a chip seven times if you could tape it out one time right and so the most efficient the most coste effective the most competitive um uh speed is technology right

principles.text: When a new technology leapfrogs the old, go back to first principles and ask why it works and whether it scales.
principles.quote: you have to take a step back and ask yourself but why and fundamentally is is it scalable and if it's scalable what other problems can it solve

principles.text: Design the company's organisation as the architecture of what you build; information flows to everyone at once, and the mission is the boss.
principles.quote: your organization should be the architecture of the Machinery of building the product right that's what a company is

principles.text: Position the company near future opportunities, even if unsure of exact what and when, so you can catch the apple when it falls.
principles.quote: our job as CEO is to look around corners and and anticipate where will opportunity be someday and even if I'm not exactly sure what and when how do I position the company to be near it

principles.text: Target zero-billion-dollar markets; by the time the market emerges, few competitors remain, and the ecosystem you build becomes a network, not a moat.
principles.quote: we prefer to position ourselves in a way that serves a need that usually hasn't emerged

sources.title: Jensen Huang at Stripe Sessions: suffering, 60 direct reports, zero-billion-dollar markets, CUDA
sources.originalTitle: A conversation with NVIDIA’s Jensen Huang
sources.summary: Jensen explains why greatness requires pain and suffering, why he runs 60 direct reports with no one-on-ones, and how he bets on zero-billion-dollar markets by reasoning in words, not spreadsheets. He recounts the decade-long CUDA struggle, and argues AI is a new industrial revolution that produces tokens.

principles.text: Great things are never easy, so expect suffering; loving the company doesn't mean being happy every day.
principles.quote: I don't love every day of my job I don't think every day brings me joy nor does Joy have to be the definition of a good day and every day I'm not happy every year I'm not happy about the company um but I love the company every single second

principles.text: Flatten the org: 60 direct reports, no one-on-ones, and share information and feedback with everyone at once.
principles.quote: I believe that when you give everybody equal access to information it empowers people

principles.text: Give feedback publicly so everyone learns from other people's mistakes.
principles.quote: learning from mistakes other people's mistakes is the best way to learn why learn from your own mistakes you know why learn from your own embarrassment you got to learn from other people's embarrassment

principles.text: Be a market maker, not a market taker. Aim at zero-billion-dollar markets and skip the focus on share.
principles.quote: I'd rather be a market maker Market Creator than a market taker you know to create something new that never existed before versus thinking about share

principles.text: Reason in words, not spreadsheets. Hard things take long, which filters out less committed competitors.
principles.quote: I hate spreadsheets because you can make spreadsheets do whatever you want you can make any chart you want out of a spreadsheet you just got to type in some numbers

principles.text: Separate determination from stubbornness by gut-checking your first principles daily, and find small revenue to buy time.
principles.quote: you gut check it right constantly and and to the extent that that's number one gut check you have to first of all you really have to be careful to distill down the first principles

sources.title: CMU 2026 Commencement: Jensen Huang on resilience, the AI reset, and putting your heart in the work
sources.originalTitle: 2026 CMU Commencement Keynote Speaker: Jensen Huang
sources.summary: Jensen tells his immigrant origin story and the near-death Sega episode at Nvidia, framing failure as character-building and the CEO role as responsibility. He then argues AI is a full reset of computing and a once-in-a-generation infrastructure buildout, and that everyone should engage with it optimistically and responsibly.

principles.text: Being CEO is responsibility for keeping the company alive, not power.
principles.quote: I learned early that being CEO is not about power, but the responsibility that comes with keeping the company alive.

principles.text: Honesty and humility can be met with generosity, even in business.
principles.quote: And that honesty and humility can be met with generosity and kindness, even in business.

principles.text: Failure is not the opposite of success; it builds humility, character and resilience.
principles.quote: we learn never to see failure as the opposite of success. Each failure is just another learning moment, a humility moment, a character-strengthening moment.

principles.text: Desperation can force invention; a crisis reset produced methods Nvidia still uses.
principles.quote: We used the money to reset the company. And out of desperation, we invented new ways of designing chips and computers that we still use today.

principles.text: Optimism helps you start hard things; reality shows they're harder, and you reinvent anyway.
principles.quote: For 33 years, Nvidia had reinvented itself over and over again, each time asking, "How hard can it be?" And each time learning, "It's harder than we thought."

principles.text: AI amplifies human capability; the risk is being outpaced by people who use AI better.
principles.quote: AI is not likely to replace you. But someone using AI better than you might.

sources.title: Jensen Huang on AI factories: the five-layer cake and why AI elevates jobs
sources.originalTitle: NVIDIA's Jensen Huang on Building the Dynamo of the Intelligence Age
sources.summary: Jensen explains AI from first principles: computing shifted from retrieval to real-time generation, so the world needs vast AI factories producing tokens, like the dynamo and the internet before. He gives a five-layer model for investing and argues task versus purpose shows AI elevates jobs.

principles.text: Go back to first principles: computing shifted from retrieving pre-recorded files to generating intelligence in real time.
principles.quote: Went from a computer industry that was largely based on retrieval for 60 years, and all of a sudden, one day, it's completely generated in real time. We call it intelligence.

principles.text: Reason upstream (industrially) about a new capability, not only about downstream industries, to position in large markets.
principles.quote: But you should go upstream, meaning industrially, what does that mean? And so, the first thing you realize is this. Go back to first principles.

principles.text: Think of AI as a five-layer cake (energy, chips, infrastructure, models, applications) to decide where to invest.
principles.quote: And so, this five-layer cake is the industrial version. And I think that's a good way to think about where to invest.

principles.text: AI can learn anything with predictable structure, so the opportunity reaches far beyond language models into the physical world.
principles.quote: we hear we talk about all the language, but don't forget we learn any you can learn anything with structure.

principles.text: Separate task from purpose: automating tasks doesn't remove the job, it elevates it.
principles.quote: Typing is not the job of a software engineer. Coding is not their job. Solving problems is their job.

principles.text: Don't fear AI, engage it. You lose out to people who use AI, not to AI itself.
principles.quote: You may or may not lose a job to an AI. But you will absolutely lose a job to someone who uses AI.

sources.title: Jensen Huang at Startup School: how a wrong bet, textbooks and "how hard can it be?" built NVIDIA
sources.originalTitle: Jensen Huang: The Mindset That Built NVIDIA
sources.summary: Jensen tells how NVIDIA's founding technology was wrong, how a Sega contract and three textbooks saved it, and why accelerating algorithm domains beat building chips. He covers first-principles curiosity, fitting the company to the founder, systems thinking, agents, physical AI, and resilience: get through today.

principles.text: Confront reality and learn: technology changes, so willingness to learn matters more than your starting technology.
principles.quote: technology is changing all the time and so long as you're able to confront the reality so long as you are able to learn the technology itself actually doesn't matter.

principles.text: Great companies come from a unique, deeply held perspective on the future, not just the chip or the market.
principles.quote: what makes great companies is a unique perspective about the world that you deeply believe in. It's not so much the technology, it's not so much uh the market even

principles.text: Accelerate an algorithm domain, not just build a chip.
principles.quote: it's not about building a great chip, it's about accelerating an algorithm domain.

principles.text: Fit the company to the founder, like an F1 car built so you can drive it; keep tweaking it.
principles.quote: You're going to build an F1 racer, but you're going to build it in a way that you can drive. You should adapt the car to you.

principles.text: Reason from first principles about what you observe: if this, then what? Live 5 to 10 years in the future.
principles.quote: asking questions, reasoning about things to first principles, asking you know questions like if this then what?

principles.text: Resilience: take on the problem with 'how hard can it be?' and just get through today.
principles.quote: You don't have to overcome life in one day you just have to overcome that morning

sources.title: Jensen Huang on AI capex: first-principles demand, safety as engineering, and why fungibility beats specialization
sources.originalTitle: Jensen Huang | Does AI Revenue Justify Capex, '27 AI Bottlenecks, Singularity, Open vs Closed & more
sources.summary: Jensen breaks the AI capex question down from first principles, showing buildout doesn't hinge on two labs. He argues safety must accelerate with capability, and that Nvidia's moat grows through fungible, durable full-stack infrastructure. He also describes new software-licensing and revenue-share growth vectors.

principles.text: Safety and security are part of the technology. Accelerate capability, safety and security together as one package.
principles.quote: You can't separate capability, functionality from safety and security. They go us one.

principles.text: Alignment is a forever problem, so build safety by engineering: zero-trust containment plus out-of-band monitoring you can escalate or shut down.
principles.quote: You start out with zero trust. When you hire somebody, you start out with zero trust.

principles.text: Take action quickly on what is first rather than arguing about what is perfect.
principles.quote: The best way to get to the future is uh uh uh take action quickly.

principles.text: Break big questions down to first principles. Don't extrapolate two labs into trillions when the buildout has many demand legs.
principles.quote: Break it down back down to first principles

principles.text: Specialization is the enemy of fungibility and durability. General-purpose compute lowers risk, which drives rentability, financeability and lowest TCO.
principles.quote: So specialization is the enemy of fungibility. Specialization is the enemy of durability.

principles.text: Intelligence demand is insatiable. Falling costs open more doors and more ambition, so consumption more than makes up for it.
principles.quote: Every time you learn, it opens a new door. And every time you open a new door, you see more opportunity.

sources.title: Jensen Huang at HKUST: AI factories, leading 60 reports with transparency, and life's work
sources.originalTitle: Fireside Chat with Jensen Huang and Harry Shum on Technology, Leadership, and Entrepreneurship
sources.summary: Jensen frames AI as a reinvention of the computing stack and a new industry that turns energy into digital intelligence. He shares leadership lessons: confidence without certainty, strength with vulnerability, reasoning in public, and serving others' success. He also covers robotics and universities.

principles.text: Treat your work as your life's work, not a job, and keep reinventing yourself by learning daily.
principles.quote: the way of thinking about about whatever you do as your life's work rather than your job I think it it it is a a very big difference in your mind

principles.text: Confidence and certainty differ: be confident in direction, leave room for uncertainty so you keep learning.
principles.quote: confidence and certainty are not the same idea it is possible for you to be completely confident in pursuing a direction and not and allow room for uncertainty

principles.text: Strong leaders can be vulnerable and ask for help; this lets the whole team do the same.
principles.quote: vulnerability uh doesn't is not the absence of strength uncertainty is not the absence of confidence

principles.text: Leaders earn trust when every decision serves the mission and other people's success, not themselves.
principles.quote: leaders leaders are are fundamentally trusted when every single decision that is made is in the interest of the mission it's an interest of others

principles.text: Run a flat org by reasoning in front of everyone so the team reaches strategy together and hears the same thing.
principles.quote: I reason in front of everybody uh what we need to do uh we work together to come up with a strategy whatever strategy it is everybody hears at the same time

principles.text: Nvidia's biggest contribution was cutting the marginal cost of computing a million times, which changes behavior.
principles.quote: we've taken the marginal cost of computing MH and we reduced a buy a million times

sources.title: Jensen Huang on character, resilience and first principles: building NVIDIA through the AI phase shift
sources.originalTitle: Jensen Huang - CEO of NVIDIA | Podcast | In Good Company | Norges Bank Investment Management
sources.summary: Jensen explains why NVIDIA reinvented the whole computer stack for deep learning, why AI is an iPhone moment and a new industrial revolution of producing intelligence, and how company character, forged by 15 years of adversity, drives lasting success. He closes with advice to think from first principles.

principles.text: When a new computing model appears, rethink the whole stack from chips to applications instead of patching the old one.
principles.quote: what is the implications to um everything about computer science from chips to systems to operating systems to Data Centers to networking to the algorithms all the way to applications

principles.text: Platform shifts arrive slowly, then abruptly like a phase change, and each one makes computers easier to program.
principles.quote: at first slowly and all of a sudden abruptly just like the just like water turning to ice or water turning to Vapor

principles.text: Innovation is about timing: the technology brews for years, and innovators realize the time is now and industrialize it.
principles.quote: the innovators are the ones that realize the timing is now and to jump on it and um industrialized it and turned it into a really great product

principles.text: Approach hard new things with 'how hard can it be?' and learn the missing skills; reason from first principles.
principles.quote: we started with the attitude how hard can it be and and so if it's a solvable problem how hard can it be and we reasoned about everything from first principles

principles.text: A company's character, meaning resilience, agility and willingness to suffer, is what makes it succeed in the long run.
principles.quote: the character of a company um is what makes it ultimately successful and you know how resilient is it um how does it deal with adversity

principles.text: Think for yourself from first principles; you can learn to love what you do rather than hunting for something to love.
principles.quote: think for yourself think from first principles

sources.title: Jensen Huang on Nvidia's 33 years: first principles, empty chairs, character forged by suffering
sources.originalTitle: Jensen Huang: Founder and CEO of NVIDIA
sources.outlet: A Bit Personal with Jodi Shelton
sources.summary: Jensen explains how he reasons from first principles, runs about 60 direct reports, refuses to fill a chair with the wrong person, and builds corporate character through shared pain. He also covers ignorance as a superpower, CEO vulnerability, and why AI makes problems look smaller and people busier.

principles.text: Build belief on first principles, then keep re-checking that the foundation is still sound; if it changes, re-evaluate and move on.
principles.quote: You have to reason through for what reason do you believe this and break down um your reasoning into into sound first principles and and then you have to you have to check it on a regular basis

principles.text: Inventing technology is not enough; you must also invent products, strategies, and the market itself.
principles.quote: You have to shape the market to receive your products that you invented and the strategies that you developed

principles.text: Never fill a chair with the wrong person; the company keeps moving, so wait for the right one.
principles.quote: an empty empty chair is better than a chair filled with the wrong person and so I'm never in a hurry.

principles.text: Great companies are defined by corporate character, forged by enduring pain together, not by intelligence or hard work alone.
principles.quote: it's just corporate character and that character comes from somewhere. That's what defines great companies.

principles.text: Make speed so large that a phase change happens: when computing gets vastly faster, hard problems look small.
principles.quote: when the tool when the instrument when the tool is way way faster then the problem looks way smaller

principles.text: Ignorance and optimism are superpowers for founders; approach hard things with 'how hard can it be?'
principles.quote: I approached everything with this attitude how hard can it be?

sources.title: How Jensen Huang runs NVIDIA: flat, first-principles, no one-on-ones, continuous planning
sources.originalTitle: Leading the teams behind the world’s fastest AI | Jensen Huang | Strange Loop
sources.summary: Jensen explains designing NVIDIA from first principles: attract great people with barely-possible problems, stay small and flat, skip one-on-ones and status reports, plan continuously, and empower people by avoiding commodity work and sharing information openly.

principles.text: Start company design from first principles: define the machine, its inputs, outputs and industry conditions.
principles.quote: you start from first principles. What is this machine that we're trying to create? What is this output? What is this input?

principles.text: Pick barely-possible problems; they attract amazing people.
principles.quote: Our company's mission is to solve computing problems that are barely possible. And if a problem could be solved by normal computers, we don't do it.

principles.text: Keep the company as small and flat as possible so information travels fast and people are empowered.
principles.quote: You want a company that's as small as possible, not as large as possible. It needs to be as large as necessary to do the job well, but to be as small as possible.

principles.text: Strategy is action: sample raw 'top five things' emails instead of status reports to check actions match strategy.
principles.quote: strategy is action. And so if the company has a set of strategies, but the people's actions, their top five things are not that, then they're obviously not executing the strategy.

principles.text: Plan continuously, not in five-year plans, and admit when you're wrong.
principles.quote: there's no five year plan, there's no one year plan, there's no plan. There's just what we're doing.

principles.text: Empower people by avoiding commodity work and walking away from commoditized businesses.
principles.quote: The most important way of realizing that mission is to not cause people to have to do commodity work.

sources.title: Jensen Huang's NTU Commencement: failure, humility, and strategic retreat at NVIDIA
sources.originalTitle: Jensen Huang NVidia CEO NTU Commencement Speech
sources.summary: Jensen tells three NVIDIA stories: admitting the Sega console architecture was wrong and asking for help, persevering through years of CUDA losses to create accelerated computing, and abandoning the phone market to create robotics. He frames AI as a rebirth of computing and urges graduates to run after their ideas.

principles.text: Confront your mistakes with humility and ask for help; it can save the company.
principles.quote: confronting our mistake and with humility asking for help save Nvidia these traits are the hardest for the brightest and most successful like yourself

principles.text: Creating a new computing model is hard; solve the chicken-and-egg problem by building an installed base with an existing product.
principles.quote: so to solve the chicken or the egg problem we used G-Force our gaming GPU which already had a large Market of gamers to build the installed base

principles.text: Persevere through years of skepticism and poor results when you believe the time will come.
principles.quote: we persevered we believe the time for Accelerated Computing would come

principles.text: Realizing a vision requires enduring pain and suffering, which forges corporate character.
principles.quote: a journey forged our corporate character to endure the pain and suffering that is always needed to realize a vision

principles.text: Strategic retreat is core to success: decide what to give up so you can create a new market.
principles.quote: strategic retreat sacrifice deciding what to give up is at the core the very core of success

principles.text: Run after your ideas urgently, either for food or from being food.
principles.quote: run after it like we did one don't walk remember either you're running for food or you are running from being food

sources.title: Jensen Huang on flat management, living in peril, and keeping humans in the loop (HBR)
sources.originalTitle: Jensen Huang on Leading Nvidia, Developing a Flat Management Style, and Keeping Humans in the Loop
sources.summary: Jensen explains why Nvidia keeps a flat structure so information moves at the speed of accelerated computing, why healthy paranoia beats assured survival, and how he reasons from first principles on weak signals. He also covers diversity, redundancy and human oversight in AI safety.

principles.text: Design the org architecture around the work: flatten so information reaches the top fast and avoids layers of hierarchy.
principles.quote: the last thing you want is for it to be information to to pass along hierarchically.

principles.text: Remove management layers by keeping the top as flat as possible.
principles.quote: the best way to do that uh is to put the most at the highest level to be as flat as possible up there. And so we probably reduced, you know, three three or four layers of management

principles.text: Let information flow freely, not trapped in silos, so the company stays alert to weak signals from adjacent fields.
principles.quote: the ability for information to be moving freely in your organization um without being trapped in silos is is something that's really important as the company gets larger and larger

principles.text: Distill observations from adjacent fields back to first principles, then extrapolate to useful applications elsewhere.
principles.quote: be able to somehow distill it back down to first principles and then extrapolate to to useful applications in in other domains.

principles.text: Don't manufacture paranoia. A company is always in peril, and staying between aspiration and desperation beats pure optimism or pessimism.
principles.quote: If you if you don't think you're in peril, it's probably because you have your head in the sand. There are no no companies that are that are assured survival.

principles.text: Build resilience through diversity and redundancy, in machines and in companies, with humans in the loop above them.
principles.quote: Diversity and redundancy is is an important part of intelligence, autonomous intelligence in a lot of ways.

sources.title: Why Jensen Huang wouldn't build Nvidia again: pain, CUDA, and forgetting yesterday
sources.originalTitle: Jensen Huang: The Man Behind NVIDIA (April 2026)
sources.outlet: How I Built This and Guy Raz
sources.summary: Jensen explains why he would not start Nvidia again knowing the pain, then walks through NV1's failure, the Sega deal, the emulator bet, and carrying CUDA on GeForce for years. He also covers first-principles reasoning, leadership by values, and why AI fear harms young people.

principles.text: Greatness requires pain and suffering; if you knew the full cost up front you would not start, so ignorance is a feature.
principles.quote: the pain and suffering necessary, the endurance necessary to do something great

principles.text: Learn from setbacks, codify the lesson, then let the past go and look forward with belief.
principles.quote: somehow learn from it codify that learning make sure it goes into every fiber in your body but leave it behind just let it go.

principles.text: A CEO's first job is keeping the company alive; when funds run short, be honest with partners and make bold calm bets.
principles.quote: my first job as a CEO is to make sure we don't go out of business.

principles.text: Solve the architecture chicken-and-egg problem by building an installed base: ship CUDA on GeForce everywhere, accept margin pain, and evangelize.
principles.quote: let's have GeForce carry on its back CUDA to every single computer in the world.

principles.text: Break new developments down to first principles and bring the organisation along before announcing direction.
principles.quote: I break things down to first principles and and and you ask yourself, uh, what did I learn? Why is it why is it impactful?

principles.text: Leadership style matters less than consistent values: be tough on the same things, then let it go, and make clear you are on their side.
principles.quote: I don't think people care about style. I think people care about your values and what you care about

sources.title: Jensen Huang in Kazakhstan: Ambition, sovereign AI and programming AI
sources.originalTitle: NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang: What Quality Will Help You Succeed in the Age of AI?
sources.summary: At a fireside chat in Kazakhstan, Jensen argues that ambition is the one quality that decides whether AI lifts you. He makes the case for sovereign AI built from national data, for physical AI as the next wave, and for investing in people. His advice to an 18-year-old: become the world's best programmer of AI.

principles.text: Ambition is the only thing that matters; AI and robotics amplify whoever has it.
principles.quote: The only thing that matters is do you have ambition? If you have ambition, then AI and robotics will lift you. It will empower you to do more.

principles.text: Leaders and parents must instill ambition in people, families, companies and nations.
principles.quote: the most important thing we need to do as country leaders like yourself, as CEOs like myself and my friends, as parents, is to instill upon our people, our families, our companies, our nation, instill upon them ambition.

principles.text: When investing, back people over companies and pick the best people.
principles.quote: you invest in people, not companies.

principles.text: A nation's data is its natural resource; it should build its own intelligence rather than import it.
principles.quote: You cannot export something as fundamental as your people's culture and values and export that to import the intelligence from someone else. It makes no sense.

principles.text: Adapting open technology is far easier than inventing it, so build on open source for your own language and culture.
principles.quote: the invention of the technology is difficult. But the application, the adaptation of the technology is not so difficult.

principles.text: To get the most from AI, learn how it works; the best user understands the machine.
principles.quote: The best user of a machine is someone who understands how the machine works. The best driver of a race car is someone who understands how the car works.

sources.title: Jensen Huang at Davos 2026: AI as a platform shift and a five-layer cake
sources.originalTitle: Conversation with Jensen Huang, President and CEO of NVIDIA | WEF Annual Meeting 2026
sources.summary: Jensen explains AI from first principles as a platform shift that reinvents the computing stack. He describes it as a five-layer industrial cake and the largest infrastructure buildout in history. He argues AI creates jobs when you separate a job's purpose from its tasks, and urges every country to build its own AI.

principles.text: Reason back to first principles: AI is a platform shift that reinvents the computing stack, and new applications get built on top.
principles.quote: it's helpful to reason back to the first principles of of fundamentally what is happening to the computing stack this is a platform shift a platform is something where applications are built on top of

principles.text: AI is a five-layer cake: energy, chips, cloud, models, applications. Economic benefit lands at the top layer.
principles.quote: industrially AI is actually essentially a five layer cake. At the bottom is energy.

principles.text: To judge AI's impact on a job, separate the job's purpose from its tasks. Automating tasks can amplify the purpose.
principles.quote: the easiest way to think about whether what is the impact of AI on a particular job is to understand whether the job what is the purpose of the job and what is the task of the job.

principles.text: Every country should treat AI as infrastructure and build its own AI from its language and culture.
principles.quote: AI is infrastructure and there's not one country in the world I can't imagine that you need to have AI as part of your infrastructure

principles.text: Learning to direct, manage and evaluate AI is a core skill, much like managing people.
principles.quote: it is essential to learn how to use AI how to direct an AI how to prompt an AI how to manage an AI how to guard rail the AI evaluate the AI. These skills are no different than leading people

principles.text: You don't write AI, you teach it. Fuse industrial capability with AI to enter physical AI and robotics.
principles.quote: AI is software that doesn't need to write software. You don't write AI, you teach AI.

sources.title: Jensen Huang on OpenAI, extreme co-design and why accelerated computing wins (BG2, 2025)
sources.originalTitle: NVIDIA: OpenAI, Future of Compute, and the American Dream | BG2 w/ Bill Gurley and Brad Gerstner
sources.summary: Jensen explains the OpenAI partnership, the three scaling laws, and why general-purpose computing is giving way to accelerated computing and AI. He covers extreme co-design as Nvidia's moat, how to build a market as a startup, sovereign AI, China, immigration, and why AI augments jobs.

principles.text: Optimize model, algorithm, system and chip together. When the chip stops getting faster, innovate outside the box.
principles.quote: Extreme code design means that you have to optimize the model, algorithm, system, and chip at the same time.

principles.text: Create a startup before the market grows. Take 100% of a tiny market, and hope it gets big.
principles.quote: You're supposed to take 100% of a tiny company, a tiny industry, which is what Nvidia did did, right?

principles.text: The 'take a few percent of a huge market' idea is a fallacy.
principles.quote: You're not supposed to come up as a startup when the market's a trillion dollars large.

principles.text: Nvidia sees itself as an AI infrastructure company, not a chip company. It sells in whatever way customers prefer to buy.
principles.quote: NVIDIA is really an AI infrastructure company. You know, we are your AI infrastructure partner

principles.text: When Moore's law stalls, the cost of tokens only falls if performance rises every year. That is why Nvidia moved to an annual cadence.
principles.quote: we have to increase our per performance annually at a pace that keeps up with that exponential.

principles.text: Facing a fast exponential, get on early and figure out the rest on the way. Don't try to predict where it will be.
principles.quote: If you have a train that's about to get faster and faster and go exponential, the only thing that you really need to do is get on it.

sources.title: Jensen Huang on reinventing computing, being a market maker, and first-principles reasoning (BG2)
sources.originalTitle: Ep17. Welcome Jensen Huang | BG2 w/ Bill Gurley & Brad Gerstner
sources.summary: Jensen explains why Nvidia's moat is a full-stack, flywheel-wide system rather than a chip, why it makes markets instead of taking share, and how he reasons about AI demand from first principles. He also covers AI-augmented flat organisations, safety, and staying relevant by learning.

principles.text: Optimise the whole flywheel, not one step; Amdahl's law means speeding up one part barely helps the whole cycle.
principles.quote: you really want to create a system that accelerates every single step of that because only in doing the whole thing can you really materially improve that cycle time

principles.text: Be a market maker, not a share taker; share takers are capped by the existing pond.
principles.quote: Nvidia is a market maker not share taker if you look at our company slides we don't we don't show not one day does this company talk about market share

principles.text: Reason about the future from first principles: establish ground truths, then ask what follows.
principles.quote: the best way to to think about the future is reason reason about it from first principles correct okay so so the the question is what are the first principles of what we're doing

principles.text: A singular, meaningful mission lets you be transparent with partners, even ones building competing products.
principles.quote: if you have a sole purpose and your purpose is Meaningful and your mission is is is dear to you and is dear to to everybody else then you could be transparent

principles.text: Productivity gains from AI lead to growth and more hiring, because there are more ideas than people to explore them.
principles.quote: we have more ideas than we can explore and we need people to help us think through it before we automate

principles.text: Leading is not always fun; take the work seriously, not yourself.
principles.quote: I don't take myself too seriously I take the work very seriously I take our responsibility very seriously

sources.title: How Nvidia built a deliberate full stack: Jensen Huang on shaders, CUDA and manufacturing intelligence
sources.originalTitle: An Interview with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang about Manufacturing Intelligence
sources.summary: Jensen Huang explains how Nvidia deliberately moved from fixed-function graphics chips to programmable shaders, CUDA and a full integrated stack. He covers the pain of building for a future market, the ARM bid, his upbringing, and why every company will produce intelligence.

principles.text: Reinvent yourself before commoditization forces you to; fixed-function efficiency eventually becomes a dead end.
principles.quote: if we don’t reinvent computer graphics, if we don’t reinvent ourselves, and we don’t open the canvas for the things that we can do on this processor, we will be commoditized out of existence

principles.text: Building for the future market has a cost: you pay overhead before new applications exist to justify it.
principles.quote: you created something for the future, which means that the current applications don’t benefit. Until you have new applications, your chip is just too expensive and the market is competitive.

principles.text: Creating a new computing platform means building the whole ecosystem yourself: compilers, SDKs, libraries, developer outreach, even marketing.
principles.quote: we had to create a compiler team, we have to think about SDKs, we have to think about libraries, we had to reach out to developers and evangelize our architecture

principles.text: Stay backwards compatible so the install base attracts developers, and developers make the platform valuable.
principles.quote: If you want developers, they’re going to want install base, and if you want install base, they have to be compatible with each other.

principles.text: Build one thing, generalize it, then build the next thing from it; that's how the company grew.
principles.quote: You build one thing and you generalize it and you realize it could be used for other things, and then you build that thing derived from the first thing and then you generalize it

principles.text: Don't squander scarce resources on what already exists; partner or reuse, and only do what others won't.
principles.quote: One of the rules of our company is to not squander the resources of our company to do something that already exists.

sources.title: Jensen Huang on ChatGPT as AI's iPhone moment, full-stack computing and doing what only Nvidia can
sources.originalTitle: An Interview with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang About AI's iPhone Moment
sources.summary: Huang explains why ChatGPT created a new computing platform, how Nvidia responded with inference products and DGX Cloud, and why it builds full stack but goes to market disaggregated. He also covers resilience through redundancy, not competing where everyone can, and why full-stack beats a slowing Moore's Law.

principles.text: A new computing platform is defined by how you program it, what apps it enables, and who can use it.
principles.quote: These three properties that I just described characterize computing platforms.

principles.text: Build a great company by doing what others can't, not by fighting over what everyone can do.
principles.quote: You build a great company by doing things that other people can’t do. You don’t build a great company by fighting other people, a whole bunch of other people, to do things that everybody can do.

principles.text: Build full stack and vertically integrated, then disaggregate at go-to-market to fit the world's ecosystem.
principles.quote: we built it in a full system, vertically integrated, but when we go to market, we disaggregate everything and we integrate it into the world’s computing fabric.

principles.text: Communicate your direction transparently so partners can prepare and you can prepare for them.
principles.quote: that’s only possible if I communicate to the ecosystem at all times what I intend to build so that they could be prepared for us on the one hand, we could be prepared for them on the other.

principles.text: Resilience comes from diversity and redundancy, and it is a cost worth paying.
principles.quote: Ultimately every company needs to have diversity and resilience, that resilience comes from diversity and redundancy

principles.text: With Moore's Law slowing, big gains require redesigning every layer of the stack.
principles.quote: Every single layer from the chip to the system to the interconnect to the algorithms, all completely redesigned and so this way of doing full-stack computing

sources.title: Jensen Huang on AI factories, platform flywheels and why blocking China backfires (2025)
sources.originalTitle: An Interview with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang About Chip Controls, AI Factories, and Enterprise Pragmatism
sources.summary: In a Computex 2025 interview, Huang explains why AI is a full-stack platform whose install base and developer flywheel decide who leads. He frames AI as a new industry built on factories, argues for competing everywhere, and shows how Nvidia is integrated yet disaggregated to serve customers however they buy.

principles.text: Reinvent the company constantly to stay ahead of where the industry is going and take on hard problems.
principles.quote: we’re trying to reinvent Nvidia so that we could be ahead of the puck so that we could be where the industry will go and we want to solve problems that are hard and contribute to the industry.

principles.text: AI is a new industry, not just IT: it augments labor and runs on factories.
principles.quote: for the very first time that we’re building computers, not just for the technology industry, we’re building computers for a new industry called AI.

principles.text: A computing platform wins through a self-reinforcing loop of install base and developers.
principles.quote: The larger, the more capable your platform, the larger the install base, more developers run and develop on it. When more developers develop on it, it makes the results, the applications, that run on your computing platform better.

principles.text: Winning means running faster, not holding rivals back; aspiring to be great deserves respect.
principles.quote: When some company aspires to be great, I don’t begrudge them. It causes us to all rise above and do even better than we could, and so I love watching people who aspire to be great.

principles.text: Build fully integrated, but with enough discipline to disaggregate, so customers can buy any part.
principles.quote: we’ve always built things in a fully integrated way because software needs to be integrated with hardware somehow, but we do it with enough discipline that we can then disaggregate the software from the hardware

principles.text: In an AI factory, power is fixed, so throughput per watt decides economics; a weak architecture is costly even if free.
principles.quote: in the world of AI factories, the math would suggest that if an architecture is not as good, sometimes depending on how poor it is, even free is not cheap enough.

sources.title: Nvidia's unifying theory: full-stack accelerated computing, AI factories, Groq and open horizontals
sources.originalTitle: An Interview with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang About Accelerated Computing
sources.summary: Post-GTC 2026 interview with Ben Thompson. Huang explains why Nvidia is an accelerated computing company, not a chip or GPU company. He covers building vertically then opening horizontally, the Groq deal, CPUs for agents, and why he opposes doomerism and bundling the AI stack.

principles.text: Start from what you need to become, not what you are not; hard problems need full-stack solutions.
principles.quote: my mind doesn’t start with, “What I’m not”, it starts with, “What do we need to be?”.

principles.text: Accelerate the application, not the chip. Nvidia is an accelerated computing company, not a GPU company.
principles.quote: We’re not obsessed about where computing is done, we just want to accelerate the application. Remember, Nvidia is an accelerated computing company, not a GPU company.

principles.text: A company moves fast when the CEO supplies a unifying theory and builds an organism that delivers it.
principles.quote: The reason why Nvidia can move so fast is because we always have a unifying theory for the company, and that’s my job

principles.text: Build vertically, integrate and optimize, then open it horizontally so others can use any piece.
principles.quote: We create a thing vertically and then we open it horizontally and so everybody could use whatever piece they would like.

principles.text: Great products come from feeling the pain point yourself and knowing where the market will go.
principles.quote: I think most great products are kind of because you see a pain point and you feel the pain point and you know that that’s where the market’s going to go.

principles.text: Teams that don't talk over-design their parts; working as one team pushes the limits.

sources.originalTitle: NVIDIA's Jensen Huang on Securing American Leadership on AI (CSIS fireside, Rev transcript)
sources.summary: Jensen explains NVIDIA as a platform company and frames AI as a five-layer stack from energy to applications. He argues that whoever diffuses technology first builds sticky ecosystems, and that AI changes tasks, not necessarily jobs. He closes on optimism and his immigrant story.

principles.text: A platform is something other people build upon; NVIDIA's business model is purely technology, so it works with every company in the stack.
principles.quote: A platform is something that you build other things upon.

principles.text: Think of AI as a five-layer cake: energy, chips, infrastructure, models, applications. Judge competitiveness layer by layer, not as one race.
principles.quote: Let's simplify AI into a five layer cake. Energy, chips, infrastructure, models, and applications.

principles.text: Whoever applies a technology first and most wins the industrial revolution; diffusion matters as much as invention.
principles.quote: in the end, whoever applies the technology first and most wins that industrial revolution.

principles.text: Getting there first lets you build ecosystem and become sticky, an essential and dependent part of it. Early patience paid off for NVIDIA.
principles.quote: the sooner you get there, the sooner you build the ecosystem on top, the sooner you become a sticky.

principles.text: Don't be complacent even when several generations ahead; compounding growth closes gaps fast.
principles.quote: We're several generations ahead, but don't be complacent.

principles.text: Separate the task from the job. AI automates tasks, but the purpose of the job remains, so people get busier, not obsolete.
principles.quote: what is the task versus what is the job?

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jensen explains how Nvidia went from a parallel-plus-sequential computing insight, through gaming, CUDA and AlexNet, to reinventing the computing stack. He covers staying committed for a decade on core beliefs, physical AI, energy efficiency, and advice to students to use AI.

chunks.heading: Why Nvidia started with parallel computing and video games
chunks.text:
- Early 1990s observation: in a software program, roughly 10% of the code does 99% of the processing, and that 99% can run in parallel. The other 90% of the code must run sequentially.
- Jensen concluded the "perfect computer" does both sequential and parallel processing, not one or the other. Nvidia was founded to solve problems normal computers can't.
- Why games first:
  - 3D graphics needs parallel processing.
  - He loved the application, a simulation of virtual worlds.
  - He judged games could become the largest entertainment market ever, and that proved true.
- A large market funds a large R&D budget. That budget creates new technology, which grows the market. He calls this technology-and-market flywheel what made Nvidia one of the most important technology companies.
- He calls a GPU a "time machine" because it lets you see the future sooner. A quantum chemistry scientist told him: "Jensen because of Nvidia's work I can do my life's work in my lifetime." Weather prediction and simulating self-driving cars in virtual cities are the same kind of time travel.

chunks.heading: How CUDA came about and why he bet the company on it
chunks.text:
- CUDA came from a mix of sources, which he describes as "some of it is aspiration and inspiration, some of it is just desperation":
  - Researchers at Mass General were using Nvidia graphics chips for CT reconstruction.
  - Other researchers were "horsing around" using GPUs for general-purpose acceleration.
  - Nvidia's own games needed fluid dynamics and particle physics, which a graphics-only pipeline handles poorly.
- Before CUDA, researchers had to trick GPUs into treating their problem as a graphics problem. CUDA let programmers use languages they already knew, such as C.
- Why he was certain, and put the whole company behind it: the video game market was so large that the GPU would be the highest-volume parallel processor in the world, so the architecture had a good chance of reaching many people.
- His framing of the risk: the cynic says "if you build it they might not come." The optimist says "if you don't build it they can't come." Nvidia's approach was "a strategy based on Hope," but "reasoned hope."

chunks.heading: AlexNet in 2012 and reinventing the computing stack
chunks.text:
- In 2012, Ilya Sutskever, Alex Krizhevsky and Geoff Hinton at the University of Toronto got a GeForce GTX 580 because they had learned of CUDA, and used it to train AlexNet.
- Nvidia was already struggling to get CUDA to work well for computer vision internally. AlexNet's giant leap on computer vision therefore got its attention.
- He asked: "if it can do this with computer vision how far can it go?" His reasoning:
  - If deep learning scales, most machine learning problems can be represented with deep neural networks.
  - That has the potential to reshape the entire computer industry and its architecture.
- This led Nvidia to re-engineer the entire computing stack "layer by layer by layer", which is where DGX came from. He frames it as reinventing computing 65 years after IBM System 360 introduced modern general-purpose computing.
- Result he points to: computer vision, speech recognition and language understanding were each solved in turn.

chunks.heading: Core beliefs, first principles and staying committed for a decade
chunks.text:
- Why it took about 10 years: he says the middle of the decade "probably felt like today." There is always some problem, some reason to be impatient, and some reason to be happy and carry on.
- His method:
  - Have core beliefs and reason from first principles (physics, deep understanding of the industry or the science).
  - "At some point you have to believe something."
  - If the principles and assumptions don't change, there's no reason to change the beliefs.
  - Evidence of success arrives along the way. Sometimes you go a long time without it and may need to course correct a little.
- He says staying committed was not hard to explain: "there was no reason to not be committed because we believed it."
- Costs of conviction: nobody else believed in it, it cost a lot of money, and investors might prefer you keep the profit or lift the share price. His answer: "you have to believe in your future, you have to invest in yourself." Nvidia invested tens of billions of dollars before it really happened.
- His three core beliefs:
  1. Accelerated (parallel) computing, adding accelerators to general-purpose processors.
  2. Deep neural networks learn patterns and relationships from many types of data. They scale: bigger models and more data learn more nuanced features, empirically true, and no physical, architectural or mathematical limit has been found.
  3. Data is "digital versions of human experience", and AI can learn almost any modality and translate between modalities.
- Examples of modality translation: text to text (summarise, translate), text to image, image to text (captioning), amino acid sequence to protein structure, words to video, and words to action tokens for a robot. "From the computer's perspective how is it any different."
- He says the last 10 years were the science of AI and the next 10 will be the application science of AI: digital biology, climate, agriculture, fishery, robotics, transportation, logistics, teaching and more.

chunks.heading: Betting on general-purpose architecture instead of burning in Transformers
chunks.text:
- The question: build chips tuned to one AI architecture (Transformers) or stay general. He says it comes down to core belief: is the Transformer the last AI architecture ever discovered, or a stepping stone to evolutions "barely recognizable as a Transformer"? Nvidia believes the latter.
- His reasoning: no idea in software, engineering or algorithms has stayed on top that long. A computer's beauty is that it can do something today that no one imagined 10 years ago. If you "turned that computer 10 years ago into a microwave" the applications would stop coming.
- Example: the attention mechanism compares every word with every other word, which becomes impossible at million-token context windows. This led to many variants since, such as Flash Attention and hierarchical attention.
- Strategy: build an architecture that lets inventors, programmers and AI researchers "swim in the soup" and come up with new ideas. Flexibility for research and innovation is "fundamentally the most important thing."

chunks.heading: Working with partners and pushing physical limits
chunks.text:
- Nvidia has its chips made by TSMC but still assumes it needs deep expertise of its own:
  - It employs people very good at semiconductor physics, to have an intuition for the limits of what current semiconductor physics can do.
  - It then works closely with TSMC to discover those limits together.
- The same applies to systems: it has plumbing expertise for liquid cooling and aerodynamics engineers designing fans to move the most air with the least noise. Nvidia doesn't make these parts but designs them, and needs deep knowledge of how to have them made.
- Limit he names: "everything in the end is about how much work you can get done within the limitations of the energy that you have." Energy efficiency is Nvidia's number one priority.
- Data point: the first DGX (DGX-1) was delivered to OpenAI in 2016 at $250,000. The new mini version uses 10,000 times less power than the 2016 one, according to him, and has six times more performance.
