He frames this as 10,000 times better energy efficiency in eight years, and compares it to a 100-watt light bulb producing the same light on 10,000 times less power.
- He plans $3,000 mini AI supercomputers so students and schools can own one, since AI has gone from researchers to every engineer and student.

chunks.heading: Physical AI: Omniverse plus Cosmos, and AI safety
chunks.text:
- His analogy from language models:
  - ChatGPT's first stage was generative AI that could hallucinate.
  - The next stage grounded it with context (an uploaded PDF, search), which becomes the ground truth.
- The physical-world equivalent:
  - Cosmos is a world foundation model that encodes physical common sense: gravity, friction, inertia, geometric and spatial awareness, object permanence, cause and effect.
  - Omniverse is a physics simulator built on principled solvers (Newtonian physics) that grounds Cosmos.
  - Together they can generate effectively unlimited physically plausible futures for robots to train on, in different lighting, times of day and conditions, instead of costly and slow real-world training.
- Prediction: "everything that moves will be robotic someday and it will be soon." Pushing a lawn mower will be "kind of silly", every car will be robotic, and humanoid robots are "just around the corner." He expects a personal R2-D2-like companion that lives across glasses, phone, PC, car and home.
- AI safety concerns he lists: bias, toxicity, hallucination, fake information, impersonation, and AI that tries to do right but performs wrong (for example a failed sensor in a self-driving car).
- His engineering answer is redundancy and community architecture. Like aviation (triple-redundant flight computers, two pilots, air traffic control, other pilots watching), AI safety systems must be built so that failures don't put people in harm's way. Break the problem into parts and "build them as engineers."
- Other bets he names: digital biology (a digital twin of the human body), and climate science with high-resolution regional weather prediction.

chunks.heading: Advice for individuals: AI makes people superhuman
chunks.text:
- Mental exercise: suppose the effort of drudgery in your work goes toward zero. He compares this to the interstate highway system, which created suburbs, gas stations, fast food and motels. Ask what new capabilities and economies appear.
- He is already surrounded by thousands of people better than him at what they do, and says it never made him feel unnecessary: it "empowers me and gives me the confidence to go tackle more and more ambitious things." He expects the same from AI: "we're going to become super humans because we have super AIs."
- Concrete advice:
  - Get an AI tutor right away to teach, program, write, analyze and reason with you.
  - Learn to prompt well. It resembles being good at asking questions and takes some artistry.
  - A student should keep asking "how can I use AI to do my job better?" (lawyer, doctor, chemist, biologist, in any field). His generation was first to ask this about computers (he entered the industry in 1984); the next generation must ask it about AI.
  - If you don't know how to use ChatGPT, just ask it to teach you.
- Example of AI freeing attention: the GeForce RTX 50 Series computes about 500,000 pixels of an ~8 million pixel 4K frame (ray traced) and AI predicts the rest. Humans, like the card, should spend scarce attention on the few things that matter most and let AI fill in the rest.

chunks.heading: What he wants Nvidia remembered for
chunks.text:
- In his words: "they made an extraordinary impact."
- He credits core beliefs held a long time ago and stuck with. He says Nvidia takes the responsibility seriously because of its consequential work.
- He wants the capability available as pervasively as possible: to large companies and individual researchers across every field, "no matter profitable or not, big or small, famous or otherwise."
- His hoped-for legacy: digital biology and life sciences transformed, materials science revolutionized, robots handling dangerous and mundane work, and people learning that the company at the epicenter is "the company that you grew up playing games with."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jensen tells his immigrant path and Nvidia's founding thesis: general-purpose CPUs can't be the only computing platform, so he solved the chicken-and-egg adoption problem via 3D gaming. He also covers suffering for belief, returning to first principles, and advice to young people.

chunks.heading: Founding Nvidia: two ideas and the chicken-and-egg problem
chunks.text:
- Jensen and co-founder Chris Malachowsky (the transcript renders the name inconsistently, so it is not named here) started Nvidia at the beginning of the PC and CPU era, when "everything was about general purpose computing" and Moore's law.
- **Idea one:** a CPU cannot be the right format for every interesting problem, such as real-time computer graphics (one of the hardest problems in computer science at the time) or simulation. They imagined a second tool that would offload work unsuited to general-purpose computing and turn the computer into a supercomputer. His analogy: there is a right tool for the right job, and a house, garage or company with only one tool is badly equipped.
- **Idea two:** how to get the company started at all. General-purpose computing is about 64 years old, and a positive cycle of install base, sales and applications reinforces it. Getting developers to consider a new architecture is a chicken-or-egg problem that "has never been solved" apart from Nvidia.
- His answer was to find a first application that needed the new architecture and also had enough volume to spread it. Computer graphics was a tiny market at the time (essentially Silicon Graphics), so they chose 3D graphics for video games.
- He calls the business plan "impossible to fund", with multiple chicken-and-egg problems. Sequoia Capital and Sutter Hill still invested, and the company attracted top computer scientists.
- Conviction rested on first principles: "the general-purpose computer cannot possibly be the only computing platform."

chunks.heading: Finding new markets for accelerated computing, from graphics to deep learning
chunks.text:
- Jensen frames computer graphics as a simulation of the world, and AI as a simulation of the mind. Simulation happens concurrently and in parallel, so it suits a different architecture from step-by-step "recipe" execution.
- The first application was computer graphics. The second was seismic processing, or inverse physics, along with CT reconstruction and ultrasound. The third was molecular dynamics (Newtonian physics). "We just kept finding one problem after another."
- The GeForce 3 had a 57 million transistor GPU, and Jensen says it was the first time the graphics processor was as programmable as the CPU, with an instruction set game programmers could target.
- Deep learning arrived when researchers including Andrew Ng (Stanford), Geoff Hinton (Toronto) and Yann LeCun (NYU) reached out to Nvidia. Jensen says he was alert enough to see a problem Nvidia could contribute to.
- The resulting computer vision capability was something "no one had ever imagined". It prompted questions about why it worked, what else it could do, how far it could go and what it meant for computer science and the industry.
- His method: "step by step by step, we broke everything down to its first principles", then rebuilt where Nvidia should be in that world.
- Nvidia built for about a decade before anyone paid attention.

chunks.heading: Conviction, grit and keeping a team motivated without feedback
chunks.text:
- Jensen says Nvidia "suffered our way here" because nobody believed in it. He describes the work as endeavoring something with "no positive feedback, no external motivation."
- His traits for it: reasoning, vision, strategy, discipline, patience and belief, "at the core of grit."
- Leadership recipe for keeping people going:
  1. Go back to core values and core beliefs, and ask why you believe the future will happen.
  2. Show you are determined to pursue it.
  3. See the future in your mind's eye, even though nobody else can.
  4. Tell the story so everyone else can see it too.
  5. Believe it yourself.
- He applies the same logic to America, Stanford and Nvidia: each has core foundations that explain its purpose.
- He says an entrepreneur must be "desperate to succeed": "If you don't work hard every single day, you will perish." He compares this to his immigrant parents, who had "nothing to fall back to", and says his constant desperation to do better at Nvidia is the same feeling.

chunks.heading: First principles as the response to uncertainty
chunks.text:
- When he is uncertain about the future or things are moving too fast, "you always go back to first principles."
- The questions he asks: What are my core values? What makes me great today? What do I aspire to?
- He says it is possible to feel three things at once: grateful for what you have, unsatisfied with where things are, and aspiring to greatness.
- He argues that "during technology change, during world change is the only opportunity for greatness. Status quo, it's really hard to make a difference."
- The same first-principles approach was behind Nvidia's founding thesis that general-purpose computing could not be the only platform.

chunks.heading: Advice to students worried about AI and jobs
chunks.text:
- Dive deeply into AI and use it in every possible way. The goal is mastery of using AI in your own field, not only mastery of the science.
- Separate the tasks of a job from its purpose. Examples:
  - A doctor's purpose is to care for people, which is different from reading a radiology scan.
  - An engineer's purpose is to solve a known problem, or discover problems that have never been solved and are worth solving.
- His rule: "every job's purpose consists of tasks but not defined by the tasks."
- He tells young people that AI is a moment of opportunity rather than a reason for fear.

chunks.heading: Cautious optimism and the five-layer AI cake
chunks.text:
- Jensen calls himself a "cautious optimist". Intelligence is the foundational ingredient of almost everything in society and industry.
- "Cautious" means advancing the technology quickly so that it works as promised, is functional, and doesn't produce something that sounds intelligent but is flawed. His point: "Functional things are safer", and AI needs to function as promised like a car does.
- He defines AI as a five-layer cake, and says the US has to win every layer:
  1. Energy
  2. Chips (his layer)
  3. Infrastructure (cloud services)
  4. Models (where "everybody talks", but not the only layer)
  5. Applications: healthcare, military and defense, cybersecurity, transportation, manufacturing
- The application layer matters most to the nation, and whoever advances it most will exploit the industrial revolution the most.
- Leadership can change during a technology inflection, even for a leader. Policy should not hinder the application layer.

chunks.heading: Why America enabled Nvidia
chunks.text:
- Jensen calls his path "a chain of extremely low probability events" and says America "provides tailwind, not headwind."
- What entrepreneurs rely on:
  - Understandable, dependable laws and rules.
  - A business environment where everyone plays by the rules, so you can find underserved market segments.
  - Confidence that a market you serve "won't be foreclosed on you randomly, arbitrarily, unknowingly, unpredictably."
  - Risk-taking and a willingness to fail, with the chance of a second chance.
- Immigrants arrive by choice with little expectation and great hopes, and appreciate everything. He says the immigrant and entrepreneurial spirits are "rather similar".
- He calls Nvidia "genuinely an only in America story", achieved in one generation, and says he is "the embodiment of the American dream."

chunks.heading: Designing with simulation, and the Nvidia campus as an example
chunks.text:
- The new Nvidia building was fully designed in simulation first, using a supercomputer.
- They simulated the building for every hour of the day across an entire year and kept adjusting until it was "perfect."
- Design choices from the simulation:
  - Light wells in the roof let in sunlight only where needed, since extra sunlight means extra heat to remove.
  - An undulating roof tracks the sun.
  - Sloped walls (the "baseball cap") move offices further back from the low afternoon sun.
- The goal was maximum use of California sunlight with high energy efficiency.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jensen tells Nvidia's origin story: an impossible 1993 mission, three wrong technology bets, Sega's $5M lifeline, and an untested chip tape-out. He explains leading through vulnerability, first-principles reassessment and fear of failure, and why AI, energy and jobs will change gradually.

chunks.heading: How Nvidia nearly died in 1995 and what Jensen learned
chunks.text:
- Nvidia started in 1993 with a mission "that has no chance of success": build a new kind of computer for problems normal computers can't solve. The catch is that apps for such a computer don't exist, so the company had to create the problem as well as the chip.
- With no customers, the three founders spent afternoons in arcades studying Sega's 3D games (Virtua Fighter, Daytona). Jensen went to Japan and pitched Sega: port your games to the PC, and Nvidia builds a chip for your game console.
- About two years in, the first architecture proved wrong. It used forward texture mapping instead of inverse, curved surfaces instead of triangles, and no Z-buffer. Meanwhile Silicon Valley was full of 3D graphics startups (3dfx, Rendition, Silicon Graphics, Intel), which Jensen put at eventually about 100.
- His call on strategy: "we don't know what the right strategy is, but we know what the wrong technology is." So stop doing it the wrong way and give the company a chance to work out the strategy.
- He told Sega's CEO Shoichiro Irimajiri (his own account of the pitch):
  - The technology doesn't work.
  - He should be let out of the contract and Sega should find another partner.
  - Nvidia still needed the last $5 million, as an investment instead of a payment.
- Irimajiri said yes after a couple of days. Jensen says the odds of getting that money back looked like 0%, and he would not have invested himself. Sega sold the stake at the IPO, at a valuation of about $300 million.
- He laid off most of the company. He bought three Silicon Graphics 3D-graphics textbooks with the $200 in his pocket ($60 each) and gave one to each architect: "Read that and let's go save the company."

chunks.heading: Narrow focus and platform strategy: how Nvidia beat about 30 competitors
chunks.text:
- The team learned the best-known art from Silicon Graphics, then reimplemented it from first principles.
- Silicon Graphics ran its geometry engine as general-purpose software on processors. Nvidia stripped out the generality and hardcoded only what video games needed into the chip.
- The result was one chip producing images about as fast as a $1 million image generator. That was the RIVA 128, which Jensen says saved the company.
- The strategic choices were:
  - Build a 3D chip for one application, video games, not CAD or flight simulators. Jensen "bet the farm" on it. Narrowing the problem let him reject all other complexity.
  - Build an ecosystem with game developers, porting and adapting their games to Nvidia silicon. That turned a technology business into a platform business.
  - GeForce was, at heart, a game console inside the PC.
- Nvidia was the first technology company to serve one audience, gamers, and the gaming industry itself didn't exist in 1993. Doom and Quake later made it take off.

chunks.heading: Surviving on fumes: the emulator and the unproven chip
chunks.text:
- With $5 million draining monthly, a normal cycle of tape-out, silicon back, test, bug, tape-out again was unaffordable.
- The workaround was an emulator, a machine that pretends to be your chip so software can be tested before the fab. Jensen spent about half of the roughly $1 million left in the bank on one. The maker (he names it as IOS) was already out of business, and he bought the unit from inventory.
- He then asked TSMC to go straight to production with no first-silicon test. They told him nobody had ever taped out a working chip first time. Morris Chang backed him anyway. Jensen says the company had a strong purchase order from a customer (Diamond Multimedia) but not all the money, so the risk was real.
- The chip was a hit, and Nvidia became the fastest-growing technology company in history to go from zero to $1 billion, by his account. He says the emulator-first methodology is now used across the chip industry.
- What he says the crisis taught:
  - How to develop winning strategies and how to create a market (3D gaming then, AI later: "exactly the same blueprint").
  - How to stay calm and think systematically in a crisis.
  - How to cut all waste and work from first principles, doing only what is essential, "living on fumes at all times."

chunks.heading: Fear, vulnerability and daily operating habits
chunks.text:
- Jensen still feels "30 days from going out of business" every morning. He has used the phrase for 33 years. He says "I have a greater drive from not wanting to fail than the drive of wanting to succeed."
- On vulnerability as a leader:
  - The company doesn't need him to be a genius who was right all along.
  - The more vulnerable a leader is, the more people will tell him "that's not exactly right" or bring information he hasn't considered.
  - "If you're always right, how can you possibly pivot? Because pivoting requires you to be wrong."
- His method is to reason from first principles all the time and reassess continuously. He admits the constant reassessing is partly what causes continuous anxiety.
- His image for the job is surfing: you can't predict the waves, you deal with the ones you have, and skill matters.
- He calls himself the longest-running tech CEO in the world. His two goals: don't get fired, don't get bored. What keeps him going is not always enthusiasm. Sometimes it is fear or frustration, "whatever keeps you moving."
- Habits: up at 4am reading emails, which he says run to several thousand a day. He sleeps six to seven hours. He works every day, including Thanksgiving and Christmas, even on vacation. Both of his kids work at Nvidia.
- He pushes back on the idea that success is all joy. Much of it is "long periods of suffering and loneliness and uncertainty and fear and embarrassment and humiliation." People often disbelieve you when you invent something new. He thinks it's healthy to say this openly, and says the suffering makes the good outcomes far more deeply appreciated.

chunks.heading: Seeing the future: how Nvidia spotted deep learning and bet on it
chunks.text:
- In 2012, Alex Krizhevsky and Ilya Sutskever, in Geoffrey Hinton's Toronto lab, built AlexNet. It beat 30 years of hand-built computer-vision algorithms, and they trained it on two Nvidia GTX 580 cards in SLI. Jensen calls that "the big bang of modern AI."
- Nvidia was already working on computer vision, and he noticed deep learning cropping up at many universities. He reasoned that a deep neural network is a "universal function approximator": give it inputs and outputs and it learns the function in between, for almost any problem.
- Two things had to be true. It had to scale, and it had to learn without human-labelled data. Unsupervised learning (for example, predicting masked words in text) arrived a few years later.
- His point is that a flash like that is brief, and the company succeeded because it paid attention to it.
- In 2016 he built the DGX-1, eight chips linked with NVLink. It cost "a few billion dollars" to develop and sold for $300,000. At launch the audience was silent and there were no purchase orders. Elon Musk was the first taker, for a nonprofit AI lab (OpenAI). Jensen drove one to San Francisco and delivered it himself.
- The DGX Spark he gave Musk in 2025 delivers the same 1 petaflop at about $4,000 and the size of a small book.
- His radar for what comes next:
  - Surround yourself with the best computer scientists. He says Nvidia's culture draws people who want to serve the technology itself, not an advertising or social business.
  - Run one of the largest industrial research labs and partner with universities and outside researchers.
  - Use customers across every industry as signals, which he calls the broadest radar of any company.
  - Stay alert by paying attention: "I haven't found a single way of being able to stay alert without paying attention."

chunks.heading: Betting on conviction: CUDA
chunks.text:
- Around 2005-2006, Nvidia added CUDA to its chips. Nobody paid for it, but costs about doubled. Nvidia's valuation fell from about $12 billion to roughly $2-3 billion, by his recollection.
- At CUDA's launch the audience was silent, no customer wanted it and nobody understood it.
- His rule for the team: ask "do we believe this or not?" If the belief is grounded in first principles and not hearsay, the thing is really hard, and Nvidia is the right company to do it, "we owe it to ourselves to go pursue it." Not acting on a belief you hold means a lifetime of regret.
- He notes that every Nvidia invention (GPUs, programmable shaders, real-time ray tracing, CUDA) was undervalued by the market at first while costs rose.
- CUDA is what enabled AI on Nvidia hardware.

chunks.heading: AI, jobs and safety: how Jensen frames them
chunks.text:
- **Purpose versus task:** He argues a job's purpose is not its tasks. AI now sweeps radiology, and Hinton predicted radiologists would disappear, yet their numbers have grown. Their purpose is diagnosing disease, not studying images. Faster, cheaper image analysis means more scans and patients, better hospital economics and more hiring. "If your job is the task," AI replaces you. If your job has a purpose beyond the task, it changes but survives.
- **New industries:** He expects robots to create maintenance, manufacturing and even apparel jobs, as cars created mechanics.
- **Technology divide:** He hopes AI narrows the divide, because anyone can use it in their own language. He expects yesterday's AI to be excellent and to run on phones. Only frontier AI needs vast energy.
- **Energy:** Moore's law cut the cost and energy of computing about 10x every five years. He says accelerated computing improved performance about 100,000x in the last 10 years. He expects AI's energy needs for most people to become "minuscule", and expects small nuclear reactors of hundreds of megawatts to power AI factories within six or seven years.
- **Safety:** He says most added AI capability goes toward safety and accuracy, such as step-by-step reasoning, research before answering, reflection and tool use, which cut hallucination. He compares it to car horsepower going into handling, ABS and traction control.
- **Cybersecurity as the model:** Defenders share breaches and patches across companies. He expects AI defence to work like this, with millions of AI agents defending against attackers. He also expects postquantum encryption to be developed.
- **Consciousness:** He rejects the idea that today's AI is conscious. It has knowledge and intelligence, not experience, and its blackmail-style outputs are pattern generation. He is wary of doomsday scenarios and says there will likely be gradual progress, not one AI that arrives with no one else's matching it.
- **Synthetic knowledge:** He predicts that within a couple of years about 90% of the world's knowledge will likely be AI-generated, which he is fine with as long as it is fact-checked against first principles.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jensen recounts founding NVIDIA, the OpenGL pivot that saved it, and creating markets alongside technology. He explains first-principles thinking, early indicators of future success, his flat organization with about 50 direct reports, and how he steadied the company through an 80% stock drop.

chunks.heading: Founding NVIDIA: the mission and the first killer app
chunks.text:
- Jensen left LSI Logic in 1992-93 because Chris and Curtis (then at Sun) wanted to start a company and insisted he work out with them how to build it. They met at Denny's.
- The mission was to build computers that solve problems normal, general-purpose computers can't. Jensen says that is still the focus.
- The founding bet was accelerated computing, with 3D graphics as the technology and video games as the application. At the time 3D graphics meant million-dollar image generators from Silicon Graphics, and the video game market was "$0 billion".
- Don Valentine of Sequoia warned that "startups don't invest in startups". NVIDIA needed another startup, Electronic Arts, to succeed too.
- Jensen skipped writing a business plan (Gordon Bell's book was about 450 pages, and he and Lori had about six months of money in the bank). Wilf Corrigan of LSI Logic phoned Valentine on his behalf.
- His lesson: "you can't run away from your past, and so have a good past." He says he was Denny's best dishwasher and busboy: organized, "mise en place", never left the station empty-handed.

chunks.heading: Create the technology and the market together
chunks.text:
- NVIDIA had to invent a new way of doing computer graphics that took a $1 million system down to a $300-$500 card that fits in a PC. It also had to create the market that would buy it.
- Jensen says this defines NVIDIA: "we create technology, we create markets." People call it a stack or an ecosystem.
- This is why NVIDIA was early in autonomous driving, deep learning and computational drug design.
- For roughly a decade (10-15 years), the markets that fuel NVIDIA today did not exist. Graphics was the only market.
- The hard part was bringing management, engineers, shareholders, the board and partners along with no evidence of a market.
- Technology that solves interesting problems is not enough. The question is whether those problems can also be interesting markets, because otherwise the company is not sustainable.

chunks.heading: Surviving the Direct3D reset: "how hard can it be?"
chunks.text:
- Microsoft introduced Direct3D, which spawned hundreds of companies. NVIDIA found itself with 89 competitors, and its own architecture turned out to be incompatible with Direct3D.
- The company had to reset or go out of business, and nobody knew how to build it the Microsoft way.
- Jensen bought three copies of the OpenGL manual at Fry's Electronics for about $68 each. He handed them to the founding team, and they implemented the OpenGL pipeline "like nobody had ever implemented" it.
- The lesson was that you can succeed at inventing a future even when you start uninformed. His reflex on anything new is "how hard can it be?" He thinks it is probably "a textbook away" or "one archive paper away".
- Learning how something is done is not the same as copying it. He then returns to first principles and asks how he would reinvent it today, given current tools and conditions.

chunks.heading: First principles, core beliefs and early indicators of future success
chunks.text:
- Jensen says to go back to first principles constantly, for software, computers and company structure. Software used to be monolithic and built for supercomputers, and is now disaggregated.
- NVIDIA's moves rest on core beliefs: CPUs and general-purpose computing have limits, and there are important problems a different computer can solve. Unless something changes his mind, he keeps believing and looks for evidence.
- He rejects KPIs like gross margin as results, not signals. NVIDIA instead uses "early indicators of future success" (EIOFS), which are the earliest signs of being on the right road. He used them to give the company hope while the markets did not exist.
- Examples of early indicators:
  - Programmable shaders, then Cg (about 2003, roughly three years before CUDA), written up with textbooks by Mark Kilgard.
  - Doctors at Mass General using Cg for CT reconstruction, and a computational quantum chemist using it for his algorithms.
  - Deep learning researchers needing a domain-specific language, which became cuDNN, "the SQL" of neural network computing.
  - Andrew Ng's cat detection and AlexNet, from which NVIDIA reasoned that deep learning "could change everything".
- Project selection: NVIDIA is inspired "not from the size of a market, but from the importance of the work", and the importance of the work is the early indicator of a future market. Nobody needs a business case or a P&L.
- The test is whether the work is important and whether it would happen without NVIDIA. If someone else will do it, he is happy to let them ("ultimate laziness"). NVIDIA picks things that would not happen without it, because that gives a sense of purpose.

chunks.heading: Staying steady through crisis
chunks.text:
- When the share price dropped 80%, he says his pulse was the same as any other week. It was embarrassing, and he admits not wanting to get out of bed.
- His routine is to wake up at the same time, prioritize the day the same way, and "gut-check back to the core": what do I believe, and did anything actually change?
- The stock price changed, but physics and gravity did not. If the assumptions behind a decision haven't changed, "you change nothing, keep on going." If they have, you change everything.
- Leaders must be seen. Jensen says he is shy and dislikes public speaking, but he had to face employees at a company meeting after the drop, explain it without knowing how long or how bad it would be, and know some were thinking "we're doomed" or "you're an idiot".
- He credits NVIDIA's leadership team for staying, and calls it the deepest technology management team the world has seen.

chunks.heading: Flat organizations and management
chunks.text:
- Jensen has about 50 direct reports. He argues a CEO should have the most direct reports, because people at that level need the least management.
- He rejects the idea that a CEO's information is so valuable it can be shared with only two or three people. He doesn't believe in a culture where information is the source of power.
- Management exists in service of everyone else. His stated job: "to create the conditions by which you could do your life's work".
- Empowerment requires context, so he keeps as few layers of "information mutilation" as possible. He reasons out loud in front of people: the facts, the data, the assumptions, the knowns and unknowns. NVIDIA has 30,000 people, which he calls "the smallest large company in the world".
- No task is beneath him (he was a dishwasher and cleaned toilets). When people send him something for review, he shows how he reasons through ambiguity, forecasting and breaking down problems. It costs him emotional and intellectual energy to get into their headspace, but he learns from it.
- He is transparent and trusts people with hard information: "you're adults here, you can handle this."
- Design the organization from first principles, not from other companies' org charts:
  - Old hierarchies existed to keep soldiers short on information. He wants employees to "question everything".
  - Organizational machinery should fit what the company builds, so computers and health care services shouldn't be organized identically.
  - Ask what the inputs and outputs are, and whether the environment is stable or constantly attacked.
  - The CEO's job is to architect the company. Culture is the operating system, set by which behavior you encourage and which you discourage. He did this reset at age 29.

chunks.heading: Generative AI, working backwards, and advice
chunks.text:
- Jensen's reasoning on generative AI: everything was digitized (words, sound, images, video, genes, amino acids), and models now learn what the data means. Because they learn modalities in the same context, they can translate between them (text to image, video to text, text to text), and translation is generation of information.
- He then asks what this means for every layer of computing. Computing will shift from retrieval of pre-recorded information to generation from a seed prompt. This changes chips, systems, software and applications. He tells entrepreneurs to ask which industries get disrupted, for example networking and storage.
- Next markets he is excited about:
  - Computer-aided drug design, as EDA was for chips. He says we are close to representing and understanding what a cell means, like a paragraph.
  - Humanoid robotics, by tokenizing manipulation the way speech is tokenized.
- On regulation: he says we need technology for guardrails, fine-tuning, alignment, safety and cybersecurity to advance much faster, and he gives the aviation example of diversity and redundancy. He favors existing product and service regulators (FAA, FDA, NHTSA) adapting to AI rather than a single "super regulation", and says he has no great answer for the social implications.
- How he thinks about the future: he goes forward in time and looks backwards, working back from the end result. He wants NVIDIA remembered for one insanely hard thing it is great at and loves: advancing computing, which he calls "the single most important instrument of all humanity". He says the company is 31 years in and "still just beginning".
- Advice: "Have a core belief, gut-check it every day. Pursue it with all your might, pursue it for a very long time. Surround yourself with people you love, and take them on that ride."
- On purpose: make a unique contribution, so that people say the world was better because you were here.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jensen explains why Nvidia moved from chips to rack and AI-factory scale design, and how he builds a company around the output. He covers betting CUDA on GeForce, pre-shaping belief before big announcements, first-principles "speed of light" thinking, and handling suffering by decomposing problems. He also gives career advice on AI and jobs.

chunks.heading: Extreme co-design: why the company is organised like the system it builds
chunks.text:
- Jensen says extreme co-design is necessary because the problem no longer fits in one computer or on one GPU. Adding 10,000 computers should make things a million times faster, so you must shard the pipeline, the data and the model.
- Amdahl's law bites: if computation is 50% of the problem and you speed it up a million times, the total workload only speeds up about 2x. CPU, GPU, networking, switching and workload distribution all become problems at once.
- Moore's law has largely slowed, so he says every technology has to be brought to bear. Over the last 10 years Moore's law would have given about 100x; Nvidia scaled computing about a million times.
- He treats co-design as three questions: what it is (optimising across architectures, chips, systems, system software, algorithms and applications, plus power and cooling), why it is needed, and how to do it.
- On the "how": he says org charts at hamburger, software and car companies all look the same, and that makes no sense to him. "The architecture of the company should reflect the environment by which it exists." The company is the machinery that produces the product.
- His direct staff is about 60 people. He does no one-on-ones: "no conversation is ever one person." A problem is presented and everyone attacks it, and people tune in or out as relevant. He calls out anyone who could have contributed and didn't.
- Most of the staff have a foot in engineering: memory, CPUs, optics, GPUs, architecture, algorithms.
- He says the Vera Rubin pod has 7 chip types, 5 rack types and 40 racks, and Nvidia builds about 200 pods a week. An NVL72 rack has about 1.3 million components, and about 200 suppliers contribute to the Vera Rubin rack.
- His complexity rule: "as complex as necessary but as simple as possible." Test and challenge every bit of complexity, and treat the rest as gratuitous.

chunks.heading: Speed of light thinking and rejecting continuous improvement
chunks.text:
- About 30 years ago Jensen started a method he calls "the speed of light". It means comparing everything against the limit of what physics allows: memory speed, math speed, power, cost, time, effort, headcount and manufacturing cycle time.
- Test each constraint separately against its limit. For example, find the speed of light for a high-throughput system and for a low-latency system, which are architected fundamentally differently. Then make trade-offs across the whole system.
- He doesn't love continuous improvement. Engineer from first principles first, and improve afterwards.
- Example: if someone says a task takes 74 days today and can be done in 72, he would rather strip it back to zero. Ask why it's 74, then ask how long it would take built from scratch. It might be 6 days. The gap between 74 and 6 can then be discussed as explicit compromises, which he says is much more effective.
- He admires Elon Musk's approach to the Memphis Colossus build for the same reasons. Elon questions whether each thing is necessary, whether it has to be done this way and whether it has to take this long. He strips things to the minimum, is present at the point of action, and his personal urgency makes suppliers treat his project as top priority.

chunks.heading: Becoming a computing company: CUDA on GeForce and installed base
chunks.text:
- Nvidia started as a narrow accelerator company. Narrow specialisation limits market size, and market size sets R&D capacity and ultimate influence. Becoming a computing company meant walking a narrow path that expanded the aperture without losing specialisation.
- The steps he lists: the programmable pixel shader, then IEEE-compatible FP32 in shaders, then C on top (Cg), then CUDA.
- Putting CUDA on GeForce was the strategic decision closest to an existential threat. It raised the GPU's cost by about 50% when Nvidia was a 35% gross-margin company, and it consumed all the gross profit dollars. He says market cap fell from roughly $6-8 billion to about $1.5 billion, and recovery took about a decade.
- His reasoning: "install base defines an architecture." Developers go where the install base is large. x86 won despite criticism, while elegant RISC architectures largely failed.
- The plan was to put CUDA in every PC whether customers used it or not, then attract developers by going to universities, writing books and teaching classes. Researchers and gamers discovered CUDA on GeForce. He calls Nvidia "the house that GeForce built." GeForce is still his number one marketing strategy because people learn the brand as teenagers.
- He sold the board on the idea that workstations and supercomputers could later capture more margin.
- His moat answer: the CUDA install base, amplified by yearly execution on very complex systems. Developers know it will be 10x better in about 6 months and will be maintained indefinitely. It took 43,000 people and millions of developers, not three people, to make CUDA succeed.
- The second advantage is the ecosystem: vertically designed, but horizontally integrated into every cloud, OEM, supercomputer, car, robot and satellite. Nvidia doesn't sell a finished product; it is a platform company.

chunks.heading: Shaping belief before announcing a bet
chunks.text:
- Jensen's method for big bets: reason to a conclusion, then spend months or years shaping the belief system of the board, management, employees, partners and customers. He avoids annual manifestos, big layoffs and reorganisations.
- He uses each new piece of external information, discovery or milestone to move people step by step. He says he's "laying down the bricks" so that the day he announces a move (buying Mellanox, going all in on deep learning), everyone's reaction is "what took you so long?" Leading this way can look like leading from behind.
- GTC keynotes do the same for partners and industry. He says he talked about the Groq stepping stones for two and a half years, and showed agentic systems resembling OpenClaw two years ago at GTC.
- Reasoning in the open: he explains his steps in meetings so people can disagree with a reasoning step rather than the conclusion, and pull him in other directions. He describes this as a "collective patriarchal method" and ties it to staying humble and open-minded.
- Specification as leadership: he describes strategy specifically enough to be actionable but under-specifies on purpose so 43,000 people can make it better than he imagined.
- No succession planning in the usual sense: instead, pass on knowledge continuously. Nothing he learns sits on his desk for more than a fraction of a second. Every meeting is a reasoning meeting.

chunks.heading: Anticipating architectures and aligning the supply chain
chunks.text:
- AI model architectures change about every six months, while system and hardware architectures change about every three years, so he has to anticipate what will matter 2-3 years out.
- His three tools:
  - basic and applied research, including building Nvidia's own models (such as Nemotron, a transformer-plus-SSM hybrid)
  - working with essentially every AI company in the world
  - keeping CUDA flexible enough to adapt (the interview mentions CUDA 13.2)
- Example: mixture of experts led to NVLink 72 instead of NVLink 8, so a 4-10 trillion parameter model runs in one computing domain. The Vera Rubin rack adds storage accelerators, the Vera CPU and Groq racks because agents "bang on tools", not just run LLMs.
- He says he reasons about the future through thought experiments. A digital worker needs ground truth (files), research and tools. A humanoid robot would use your microwave and read its manual rather than turn its hand into a microwave.
- Supply chain: he tells upstream and downstream CEOs the business conditions and growth drivers, and flies out to explain, draw pictures and reason from first principles. About three years ago he convinced several DRAM CEOs to invest in HBM and in low-power LPDDR memory for data centres. Several hundred CEOs attended his GTC keynote.
- He moved supercomputer integration from the data centre into the supply chain with NVLink 72, shipping racks of 2-3 tons, which required partners to make capital investments of several billion dollars each.
- Why he doesn't lose sleep over bottlenecks: he told partners what he needs, they told him what they'd do, and he believes them. He says he sleeps because he has listed everything that could harm people and told someone who can act on it.
- Power: push tokens per second per watt up by orders of magnitude yearly, so token cost falls about an order of magnitude a year even as computer prices rise. He also wants to use the idle capacity of the grid, which he says runs at about 60% of peak most of the time. His proposals are:
  - make customer CEOs aware of the uptime guarantees in their contracts
  - build data centres that degrade gracefully
  - have utilities sell lower-guarantee power sooner

chunks.heading: Resilience, suffering and a first-principles mindset
chunks.text:
- He attributes success partly to a child-like "how hard can it be?" mindset. If you simulated all the setbacks in advance you wouldn't start, so go in fresh and expect it to be great. Then bring endurance and grit, because the setbacks, embarrassments and humiliations will still surprise you.
- His method for pressure and anxiety:
  - decompose the problem into parts
  - separate what you can act on from what you can't
  - either do it or get someone else to do it
  - tell the person who can fix it, so the burden is shared
  - after that, "stop crying about it" and go to sleep
- Forget setbacks quickly, like an athlete worrying about the next point, and let the next opportunity pull you forward.
- He keeps reassessing: if the assumptions behind his picture of the future haven't materially changed, the expected outcome hasn't either.
- Humility: because he works publicly, he's often visibly wrong, and he says that keeps him humble. He emulates and learns from everyone he watches.
- He says he has hit psychological low points "all the time."

chunks.heading: Strategy, new markets and AI's economics
chunks.text:
- Four scaling laws: pre-training, post-training, test-time and agentic. He argues synthetic data means training becomes limited by compute, not data. Inference is thinking, which is harder than reading, so it won't commoditise into tiny chips.
- Agentic scaling means spawning sub-agents, which he compares to hiring more employees being easier than scaling himself.
- Why he sees Nvidia's growth as inevitable: computing shifted from retrieving pre-written files to generating contextual tokens in real time, which needs far more computation. And the computer has changed from a warehouse into a factory that generates revenue.
- He says tokens are segmenting like iPhones into free, premium and high-end tiers, and that $1,000 per million tokens is "just around the corner." He calls OpenClaw "the iPhone of tokens."
- He says Nvidia is not in the market-share business because the markets he's addressing mostly don't exist yet. He recalls being told a fabless semiconductor company couldn't exceed $1 billion, and later that Nvidia would never top $25 billion, and calls such claims not first-principles thinking. He says $3 trillion in revenue is not limited by any physical limit he can see.
- His mental unit of what he builds has grown from the chip to the computer, the cluster and the gigawatt AI factory, and he hopes to think at planetary scale next.
- Open source: Nvidia builds open models (it open-sources weights, data and method for Nemotron 3) to learn how models evolve, to let every industry and country join AI, and to push non-language AI (biology, weather, physical AI). "We don't build cars, but we want to make sure every car company has access to great models."
- On TSMC, he says the biggest misunderstanding is that its technology is all it has. He credits its orchestration of customer demand, its balance of technology and customer service, and its trust. Nvidia has done business with it for three decades without a contract. In 2013 he declined Morris Chang's offer to run TSMC.

chunks.heading: Jobs, intelligence and advice to students
chunks.text:
- Purpose versus tasks: "the purpose of your job and the tasks and the tools that you use to do your job are related, not the same." If your job is a task, you are highly exposed. If your job's purpose includes tasks, learn to use AI to automate them.
- Radiology example: computer vision became superhuman around 2019-2020, yet the number of radiologists grew and there is now a shortage. The purpose is diagnosing disease, and faster scan reading means more patients seen and more radiologists needed.
- Nvidia's software engineer headcount will grow, not shrink. He wants engineers to solve problems, not write lines of code. He says coding is becoming specification, so the pool of people who can code goes from about 30 million to potentially 1 billion.
- Advice: every student should graduate expert in AI, and every worker, from carpenter to pharmacist, should use it. Given two graduates, one AI-expert and one not, he'd hire the expert.
- He argues intelligence is becoming a commodity. He's surrounded by 60 people who are superhuman in their areas, yet he orchestrates them. What matters more is character, compassion, generosity, tolerance for pain and determination.
- He says he has been CEO for 34 years and that his tools have changed continuously while the purpose of his job hasn't.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jensen tells the Caltech class of 2024 how NVIDIA bet on deep learning from first principles, and how repeated setbacks pushed it into robotics. He argues that resilience, tolerance for suffering, a chosen craft and strict prioritisation matter more than raw intelligence.

chunks.heading: Why accelerated computing became necessary
chunks.text:
- Jensen traces modern computing to the IBM System 360, which he learned from. He says its architecture and strategy still govern the industry.
- In the 1980s he was in the first generation of VLSI engineers, trained on Mead and Conway's textbook from Carver Mead's work at Caltech.
- CPUs and Moore's Law drove the mass production of software, which became a "$3 trillion industry". When he was a student, "the concept that you could make money selling software was a fantasy."
- Transistor scaling and instruction-level parallelism have slowed CPU gains while demand keeps growing exponentially. He says the widening gap, left unaddressed, means computing energy use and cost inflation "would eventually stifle every industry."
- After two decades of CUDA, accelerated computing is the path forward. Offloading time-consuming algorithms to a GPU built for parallel processing routinely gives 10x, 100x, sometimes 1,000x speedups, saving money, cost and energy.
- Domains accelerated include:
  - ray tracing and computer graphics
  - gene sequencing
  - scientific computing and astronomy
  - quantum circuit simulation
  - SQL data processing and pandas
- He calls it NVIDIA's "first great contribution" to the industry and to society. Costs can keep falling while computing requirements grow.
- His reasoning: a 100-fold saving in time, cost or energy will trigger a new development somewhere else. The industry did not know what until deep learning arrived.

chunks.heading: Betting on deep learning after AlexNet
chunks.text:
- In 2012, Hinton, Krizhevsky and Sutskever trained AlexNet on NVIDIA CUDA GPUs and won the ImageNet Challenge. Jensen calls it the "big bang of deep learning."
- His point is that NVIDIA's decisions after AlexNet transformed the company. They were based on principled thinking and the company's own analysis of how deep learning scales.
- The belief: deep learning might be a "universal function learner" for problems that are hard or impossible to express from first principles. Its limits might be set only by model and data scale.
- The dilemma:
  - NVIDIA was small then, and massive GPU clusters could cost hundreds of millions of dollars.
  - There was no assurance scaling would work, and no one knew how far it could go.
  - His logic: "if we don't build it, they can't come."
- His rule: "when the company believes something, we should go act on it."
- Over the next decade NVIDIA reinvented every computing layer: the modern GPU, interconnects, systems, networking and software.
- It invested billions "into the unknown," with thousands of engineers working for a decade without knowing how far the technology would go.
- In 2016 NVIDIA announced DGX-1, its first AI supercomputer. Jensen delivered the first one to OpenAI, then a startup nobody knew.
- In 2022, 10 years after AlexNet and about a million-fold more computing later, OpenAI launched ChatGPT.

chunks.heading: The new computing model and AI factories
chunks.text:
- NVIDIA went from a graphics company building GPUs to an AI company building data-center-scale supercomputers.
- The stack changed: GPUs process large language models trained on supercomputers, instead of CPUs executing instructions written by programmers.
- Computers are now "intention-driven rather than instruction-driven": tell a computer what you want and it figures out how.
- Future AI applications will understand the mission, reason, plan and orchestrate teams of large language models. They will assemble teams of experts and use tools, much as people do.
- AI's inputs and outputs are tokens, floating-point numbers that embed intelligence.
- Companies are building a new kind of data center that produces tokens: "AI factories." He compares AI token generators to Tesla's AC generators as the factories of a new industrial revolution.
- He says this model and industry emerged because "we reasoned from first principles, formed our belief about the future, and we acted on them."
- On AI's pace: it is the only technology he knows that is advancing on multiple exponentials at once. He told students to "run, don't walk" to engage with it.

chunks.heading: Setbacks that led to robotics
chunks.text:
Jensen contrasts the AI factory strategy, which came from reasoning and deliberate action, with robotics, which came from a series of setbacks.

- NVIDIA invented the GPU and programmable shading in 2000, and wanted GPUs in every computer.
- A sequence of markets was built, then lost:
  1. **Chipsets for AMD CPUs:** went from zero to about a billion dollars almost overnight. AMD bought ATI and no longer needed NVIDIA.
  2. **Intel connection license:** led to work with Apple on what became the first MacBook Air. Intel then terminated the agreement.
  3. **Mobile SoC built on an ARM license:** the world's first SoC that was a full computer. It excited Google and led to work on Android devices. Qualcomm then refused modem connections. There were no other LTE modem companies, so NVIDIA had to exit mobile.
- This repeated roughly yearly: build something successful, then be pushed out a year later.
- With no markets left, he chose one with no customers, reasoning that "where there are no customers, there are also no competitors, and nobody cares about you." That was a "$0 billion market": robotics.
- NVIDIA built the world's first robotics computer, running deep learning, over 10 years ago. Today's robotics computer does not even need graphics.
- The next wave of AI is robotics, where AI has a physical world model as well as a language model. NVIDIA works with hundreds of companies on robots, robotic vehicles, pick-and-place arms, humanoids and robotic warehouses.
- The lasting gain was agility and a culture of resilience: "Our company is really hard to distract and really hard to discourage, and no setback that comes our way doesn't look like an opportunity these days."
- His advice: "Swiftly, shake it off." There is another opportunity out there, "or create one."

chunks.heading: Resilience as a superpower
chunks.text:
- Of his abilities, he says intelligence is not top of the list. What he values most:
  - enduring pain and suffering
  - working on something for a very long time
  - handling setbacks and seeing the opportunity around the corner
- He calls these his "superpowers" and says pain and suffering strengthen character, resilience and agility.
- Setbacks strengthen a company's character as well as a person's: "Each time, we gained skills and strengthened our character."
- He says sacrifice, enduring pain and suffering are qualities graduates will need.
- He also cites a strategic retreat as one of NVIDIA's best strategies. He credits intellectual honesty and humility with saving the company during the canceled Sega game console project.
- He says his own longevity comes from not going out of business, not getting bored and not getting fired. He has run NVIDIA for 31 years and is the longest-running tech CEO.

chunks.heading: Craft, priorities and having time
chunks.text:
- At the Silver Temple in Kyoto, he met a gardener picking dead moss with a bamboo tweezer in a garden about the size of a courtyard. The gardener said, "I have cared for my garden for 25 years. I have plenty of time."
- Jensen's lesson: when you dedicate yourself to a craft and your life's work, you have plenty of time.
- His morning routine, identical every day:
  - He keeps a clear priority list and does the highest-priority work first.
  - Before he gets to work, his day is already a success, and he can spend the rest of it helping others.
  - When people apologize for interrupting, he says "I have plenty of time", and he means it.
- He hopes graduates find a craft to spend a lifetime perfecting. It need not be decided on day one or soon.
- He says to prioritize your life and you will have time for the important things.

chunks.heading: Advice to graduates
chunks.text:
- Believe in something unconventional or unexplored, but let it be "informed" and "reasoned." Then dedicate yourself to making it happen.
- You may find "your GPU, your CUDA, your generative AI, your NVIDIA."
- See setbacks as new opportunities.
- Engage with AI now: use it, play with it and enjoy it, because it is changing so quickly.
- Understand that computing is being rebuilt "from studs on up," because computers are "the single most important instrument of knowledge" and will transform every industry.
- Jensen says he does not love giving advice, especially to other people's children, so he frames it as stories from his own experience.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jensen rebuts AI doom predictions by pointing to failed forecasts, argues regulation should solve real problems via engineering root-cause, and explains why Nvidia runs every model and builds only what customers need. He also covers open models, supply chain foresight, and long-horizon thinking.

chunks.heading: Judging AI doom predictions: track the record and demand root-cause engineering
chunks.text:
- Jensen calls the quantified extinction predictions "made up". He says they come from researchers, are not grounded in science, and are "irresponsible" to publish.
- He argues the track record of such predictions is poor, and people should be held to it:
  - Radiology would be fully taken over by AI with no radiologists left. The opposite happened: AI automated scan reading, and the world needs more radiologists than ever.
  - Within 6 to 12 months, 90% of code would be AI-generated. He says this proved wrong.
  - Within 6 to 9 months, 50% of entry-level jobs would be wiped out. He says this proved wrong.
- His line: "We have to take accountability for all of the stupid predictions that were made."
- He says safety and leadership are "false choices". America can innovate, execute fast, lead and be safe at once.
- On whistleblowers, he says they must be taken seriously, and he credits the one in question with courage. He separates that from the scientific forecasting, which he says is not grounded in science.

chunks.heading: Regulation should solve actual problems, and safety is an engineering discipline
chunks.text:
- His rule: "regulation should solve actual problems." So the first question is which actual problems have occurred.
- He notes the real incidents so far came from the frontier labs, because they have the most compute and work on the hardest problems. A high school student or a startup lacks the compute to cause a frontier-scale incident.
- He describes the labs as moving from research to engineering while building the company, culture, technology and products at once, so he understands it is "a little bit hair on fire".
- His prescription after any incident:
  - Root-cause it from an engineering perspective.
  - Ask what could have been done differently.
  - Implement and institutionalise the fix in technology, methods and processes.
- He bets the labs now have sandboxes, runtimes and continuous monitors. If a lab truly had no control, other companies should send engineers in, but he doubts that is the case.
- He supports third-party evaluators, comparing them to financial auditors:
  - They need not be as expert as the company, only ask the right questions.
  - He agrees there should be several, so one cannot be captured or influenced.
- On recursive self-improvement (RSI), he calls it a combination of sensible ideas: in-context learning, skills, reflection, reinforcement learning, synthetic data, and LoRA-style weight improvements, with the base model retrained later on that experience.
- He says RSI will not spiral out of control, because a product must still be evaluated and regression-tested before release. Better control comes from methods, tools, verification and evals.

chunks.heading: Open and closed models: use both, and win by exploiting the technology
chunks.text:
- He says the world needs both. He uses as many closed frontier models as he can, and used four the weekend before.
- His analogy: closed models are like bottled water. Water is free, and "you use the right water in the right places". It is the same as electricity and other commodities.
- Reasons open models are needed: sovereignty, privacy and proprietary technology.
- He cites that $400 billion of venture funding went into AI-native companies in the last 6 months, and 80% of them use open models. Without open models, they could not build their dream.
- He argues winning the AI race is not about a few tech companies. It is about every company, industry, researcher, teacher, student and startup.
- On Chinese open models, he says much of the world's open-source contribution now comes from China, which has far more engineers. But once you download a model, "it's yours": you fork it, improve it and make it your own, as with Linux and Kubernetes.
- His view of the race: it is about who exploits the technology best. The last industrial revolution's inventors (Maxwell, Volta, Ampère) were not American, yet America took social advantage of it better than anyone.
- He says China's narrative is pragmatic, an economic and social advance, with no groups saying it will end civilisation.
- He advises engineers that coding is "just typing". His favourite key is backspace, because "the best software is the smallest software". He expects engineering to continue and grow after typing.

chunks.heading: Nvidia's strategy: go as high as needed and as low as possible
chunks.text:
- His strategy: "go up as far as we need to and as low as possible", then "let a thousand flowers bloom".
- He would rather help everybody succeed than take a slice. That is why Nvidia runs every model: a year and a half earlier it ran essentially only OpenAI, and now it runs Gemini, Grok, Meta's models and others, with Anthropic scaling up on its platform.
- Examples of building the layer others need:
  - Without cuDNN, the frameworks would not exist.
  - Without Megatron-Core, large-scale training would not have happened.
- He builds frontier models in five domains, out of need rather than to disrupt anyone:
  - Alpamayo, the first "thinking" self-driving model. It reasons about novel situations, so it needs less road data. Many car, ag-tech and truck makers cannot build the whole stack, so Nvidia builds it and they adapt the last mile.
  - Biology models: ESM2 protein language model, ESMFold, OpenFold, cuEquivariance, and Proteina-Complexa for synthesising next-generation proteins. He says Lilly and Merck need these and cannot build them yet.
- His test: build it because Nvidia has the skills and customers need it.

chunks.heading: Capital allocation: find ecosystem bottlenecks and fund them early
chunks.text:
- He calls AI a new industrial revolution that needs manufacturing: intelligence is produced, so infrastructure must be built.
- He says the industry is mostly about applications and the infrastructure layers (data centres, construction, electricity, power generation), not just models and chips.
- His method: look across the whole ecosystem for bottlenecks and constraints, and back extraordinary companies being built where supply must scale, such as land, power and shell.
- He thinks about the long-term supply chain more than most, because Nvidia's scale means many companies must support it (Corning, Lumentum, TSMC, memory makers). He started working with them long before the growth arrived so the growth could happen.
- He is "surprisingly uncompetitive" in the sense of not wanting to own every layer. He would be happy with five hyperscalers.
- Why he backs regional clouds (NCPs):
  - Their early customers were the hyperscalers, which plan once a year while the market is so volatile that they are almost always wrong.
  - Regional clouds are agile and know their state or country, so they can secure land, power and shell better than someone in Seattle or Palo Alto.
  - Countries now see compute as strategic, with some reserving power for domestic companies. Nvidia helps neoclouds there grow, for example in Australia and Southeast Asia, bringing on gigawatts.

chunks.heading: Company culture: quiet, apolitical and consistent
chunks.text:
- He says companies like these "ought to be built the way we used to build companies, which is in silence".
- No one speaks for the whole organisation. He says employees accepted this when they joined, and told them how people behave in the company.
- Nvidia is apolitical and bipartisan. It wants America to succeed and will help whatever government is in place.
- No political discourse inside the company. He tells staff to "take it home", and the same goes for race and religion.
- Core values he says attract people: taking care of families, creating conditions for people to do their life's work, meaningful work done quietly, and contributing to everyone else's success.
- He values consistency and stability, and says employees are very happy.

chunks.heading: Long-term thinking and the pace of the frontier
chunks.text:
- He thinks in decades: "I've got to think about what happens next decade and decade after that", so two or three years "is just a click".
- On China's lithography, he expects it to get there by 2030. He says China is very good at high-volume production, so it is a matter of time.
- On Elon Musk's Terafab, he says "if anybody could do it, he can". He notes Nvidia knows process technology and memory well. He says Musk's superpower is that once he decides to do something, it is hard to stop him.
- He says slowing down is "definitely the wrong strategy".
- He says AGI is already here. Superintelligence is here in narrow domains, such as self-driving (he cites one-tenth the accident rate of humans) and protein synthesis and virtual screening.
- He is having fun on the frontier and wants "all of America to come with us". He asks for less drama and says the future is "too good not to be" part of.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jensen explains Nvidia's moat as ecosystem, install base and programmable co-design, not scarce supply. He covers shaping the supply chain by educating CEOs, refusing to pick winners or auction GPUs, owning misses like Anthropic, and defending selling to China.

chunks.heading: "As much as needed, as little as possible": Nvidia's operating philosophy
chunks.text:
- Jensen's mental model of Nvidia: the input is electrons, the output is tokens, and Nvidia sits in the middle. Its job is to "do as much as necessary as little as possible" to enable that transformation.
- Anything he does not need to do himself, he partners on and makes part of the ecosystem. Nvidia has ecosystems across all five layers of the "AI cake" (energy, chips, infrastructure, models, applications), upstream and downstream.
- What Nvidia does do is "insanely hard", and he believes it would not get done otherwise. His examples:
  - 20 years of CUDA, "losing money most of that time".
  - Building NVLink and the whole stack.
  - Creating domain-specific CUDA-X libraries (ray tracing, data processing, cuLitho for computational lithography) about 15 years ago.
- Applied to clouds: Nvidia backs neoclouds such as CoreWeave, Nscale and Nebius so they exist, but does not become a cloud or a financier. "There are people in the financing business and we'd rather work with all of them." He keeps the business model "as simple as possible".
- He thinks the transformation from electrons to tokens will not be commoditized. Making one token more valuable than another takes "artistry, engineering, science, invention", and the journey is "far from over".

chunks.heading: Supply chain: informing partners, prefetching bottlenecks, no contracts
chunks.text:
- Upstream partners invest for Nvidia because Jensen explains how big the industry will be and why, and because Nvidia's downstream demand is large enough to buy what they build.
- He spends much of his time educating the supply chain, directly or indirectly. Keynotes include a deliberately "torturous" educational part so that suppliers and the ecosystem can reason about the opportunity "just like I reason about it". GTC brings upstream and downstream into one place so each can see the other.
- Bottlenecks get swarmed. CoWoS got "double, double, double" for two years and people no longer talk about it. CoWoS and HBM went from specialty to mainstream.
- Nvidia now prefetches bottlenecks years ahead. For silicon photonics it:
  - partnered with TSMC on COUPE;
  - invented new technology and new test equipment (e.g. double-sided probing);
  - licensed the patents to the supply chain;
  - invested in companies such as Lumentum and Coherent to scale capacity.
- His view is that no bottleneck lasts longer than 2-3 years: "once you can build one you can build 10." The slow constraints are downstream of Nvidia, such as energy. Plumbers and electricians can also limit data center builds.
- He wants a market where instantaneous demand exceeds total supply.
- Nvidia and TSMC have had no legal contract in nearly 30 years, only "rough justice". He says he can "completely trust them".
- He recalls the Micron team doubling down early after a meeting where he laid out the predictions.

chunks.heading: Pricing and allocation: be dependable, don't auction
chunks.text:
- Nvidia sets a price and sticks to it. It does not sell to the highest bidder or raise prices when demand spikes. "That's a bad business practice."
- Allocation is forecasting first, then purchase orders, then mostly first in, first out. If a customer's data center isn't ready, Nvidia may serve another customer first to keep its factory throughput up.
- He denies that Larry Ellison and Elon Musk "begged" for GPUs at a dinner. They just had to place an order.
- He wants Nvidia to be "the foundation of the industry": a public annual roadmap (Vera Rubin, Rubin Ultra, Feynman, then a name not yet announced) and a "no second-guessing" price.
- Customers can buy at any scale: one graphics card, one rack, $10M, $100M, $1B, or a $100B AI factory.
- He also says every year Nvidia delivers a big leap, and customers can count on token cost falling by an order of magnitude.

chunks.heading: Why CUDA and the architecture moat persist
chunks.text:
- Moore's law gives about 25% a year. 10x-100x leaps need algorithm and architecture change every year, which needs a programmable, extreme codesign company.
- Hopper to Blackwell: transistors improved about 75% over 3 years, yet Blackwell delivers about 50x Hopper's energy efficiency. Jensen originally claimed 35x and says Dylan Patel found it was actually 50x. It came from new models, parallelism, disaggregation and offloading compute into NVLink and Spectrum-X, changed across processors, system, fabric, libraries and algorithms at once.
- Why developers pick CUDA first:
  1. Ecosystem richness. It supports every framework (Triton, vLLM, SGLang, RL frameworks such as Verl and NeMo RL). If something breaks, it is more likely in your code than in the stack below.
  2. Install base. Developers want their software to run on as many machines as possible, and Nvidia has several hundred million GPUs, from robots to every cloud.
  3. Presence in every cloud and on-prem, so AI companies do not have to choose a CSP.
- Nvidia engineers work with AI labs to tune their stacks. He says they often get 2x, and sometimes 50% to 3x, out of a kernel or stack. For a lab with a large fleet, a 2x speedup directly doubles revenue. He uses the analogy that a CPU is a Cadillac and an accelerator is an F1 car.
- He claims the best performance per TCO and per watt, pointing to InferenceMAX and MLPerf and inviting TPU and Trainium to show their cost advantage.
- On ASIC margins: he argues that an ASIC vendor's margin is also high (about 65% vs his 70%), so "what are you really saving?"
- On TPUs and Anthropic: Anthropic is "a unique instance, not a trend". Without Anthropic there would be no TPU or Trainium growth. Nvidia is not offended by others trying alternatives.
- His own admitted miss: he did not realize Anthropic and OpenAI needed supplier investments of $5-10B, which VCs would not provide, and Nvidia could not have afforded it then. He says he will not make that mistake again and now invests in OpenAI and Anthropic.
- Without AI, Nvidia would still be very large because general-purpose computing has run its course and accelerated computing serves molecular dynamics, seismic processing, data processing, graphics and more.

chunks.heading: Don't pick winners
chunks.text:
- Nvidia invests in all the foundation labs: "when I invest in one of them, I invest in all of them." It isn't Nvidia's job to pick winners.
- His reasoning is humility from Nvidia's own history. There were about 60 3D graphics companies at the start, and Nvidia was the only survivor.
- He says Nvidia would have been at the top of the list of companies not to make it. Its first graphics architecture was "precisely wrong", reasoned from good first principles but landing on the wrong solution.
- Investments in neoclouds and labs happen because they ask, have a plan and passion, and the world needs them. He does not want to be in the financing business.

chunks.heading: Software companies, agents and tools
chunks.text:
- He argues the opposite of the "AI commoditizes software" view. Most software companies make tools (Excel, PowerPoint, Cadence, Synopsys), and agents are tool users.
- He expects agents to grow exponentially, so instances of tools like Synopsys Design Compiler, floor planners and design-rule checkers will "skyrocket". Today usage is limited by the number of engineers.
- It hasn't happened yet because agents aren't good enough at using the tools. He expects it to come from software companies building agents, agents improving, or both.
- He expects engineers to be supported by agents exploring the design space far more widely.

chunks.heading: Product segmentation: Groq and premium tokens
chunks.text:
- Nvidia added Groq and is folding it into the CUDA ecosystem, because token value has risen enough to support different price points by response time.
- Jensen says he would pay for faster, more responsive tokens for Nvidia's own software engineers.
- Nvidia chose to expand the Pareto frontier and add a faster, lower-throughput inference segment, expecting high-ASP tokens to make up for lower factory throughput.
- He decided against running parallel exotic chip projects (wafer-scale, a Dojo-style big package, one without CUDA) because Nvidia simulates them and finds them "provably worse". He would put extra money behind the existing architecture.

chunks.heading: China, export controls and American tech stack leadership
chunks.text:
- He says Nvidia wants the US to be ahead, and notes the US has about 100 times more compute than anywhere else, with the newest Nvidia hardware available in abundance there.
- His arguments against export controls:
  - China already has plenty of compute. Huawei just had its largest year. China has abundant energy ("ghost data centers"), makes about 60% of mainstream chips and has about 50% of the world's AI researchers.
  - Abundant energy can substitute for chip efficiency, and AI is a parallel computing problem, so 7nm chips can be ganged together. He says Mythos was trained on fairly mundane capacity.
  - The key lever is computer science. Most AI advances came from algorithms, so researchers with less compute build smarter algorithms.
- His strategic fear is that China is the largest contributor to open models, and if models like DeepSeek run best on Huawei first, that is "a horrible outcome". He does not want two ecosystems, open source on a Chinese stack and closed on an American stack.
- He argues that 50% of AI developers are in China. Conceding the market (about 40% of the technology industry, the second largest market) hurts American leadership, as telecoms did. Ecosystems like x86 and ARM are sticky, and "computing is not like a car".
- He says export controls accelerated China's chip industry and forced its AI ecosystem onto internal architectures, and that Nvidia's China share has fallen rather than grown.
- He wants US dialogue with Chinese researchers on what not to use AI for, and says AI cyber defense needs an open ecosystem with thousands of safety agents watching each powerful agent.
- He rejects the enriched-uranium analogy and calls "extremes" and "absolutes" childish. He calls for "nuance" and "maturity".
- He says the US should win at all five layers, including chips, and most of all at the application layer.

chunks.heading: Warning against doomer narratives on jobs
chunks.text:
- He worries that telling people not to become software engineers will leave a shortage of them. He compares it to predictions 10 years ago that radiologists would disappear, when there is now a shortage.
- His distinction: a radiologist's job is patient care, while reading a scan is just one task.
- He says scaring people about AI hurts the US, since the layer that diffuses AI into society benefits most from this industrial revolution.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jensen argues AI is a revolution best understood as software and engineering, not myth. He separates a job's purpose from its tasks, says safety is part of accelerating AI, and backs open models and diffusion across every industry. He also rejects doomer narratives as harmful.

chunks.heading: The five-layer cake model of AI
chunks.text:
- Jensen frames AI as a new industrial revolution with five layers: energy, chips (the AI factory hardware), infrastructure/cloud, models, and applications.
- Models are not just language models. He lists chemistry, biology, physics, robotics, navigation and self-driving models.
- The application layer is the one he cares about most: legal, health, manufacturing, every industry. "Every single industry has to benefit": Walmart, Safeway, FedEx, banks, healthcare, drug discovery, construction, power generation.
- His mental model of the industry is this cake, and Nvidia invests across all of it.
- Framing: electricity let us power anything, the internet let us find anything, AI lets us "know everything and do anything". You give it a question and get an answer, give it a project and get a solution.
- He calls the technology engineering: "It's software." Agents are algorithms optimizing an objective, and words like spawn, kill and fork are decades-old operating system terms.
- His definition of intelligence from computer science: perception, reasoning (decomposing a scenario into elemental parts), and planning toward an objective.

chunks.heading: Jobs: purpose versus task, and ambition
chunks.text:
- Every job has a purpose and a set of tasks. AI automates tasks, not purpose.
- Radiology example: reading scans was automated, but the purpose (diagnose disease, help patients) stayed. Radiologists handle more cases, hospitals earn more, and they need more radiologists.
- Software engineering: he calls the prediction that 90% of code written by agents means no engineers "completely false". The purpose of an engineer is to invent, discover and solve problems. There was engineering before software and will be after.
- Jobs where task and purpose are the same, like phone customer service, can be automated away.
- He says AI "will change every job" but he rejects "destroy jobs". He expects net job creation and new industries, as luxury and wellness industries appeared in his lifetime.
- His missing ingredient in the job-loss math is human ambition: "the power of ambition is the greatest force."
- Evidence he cites: in the last six months AI became useful after 15 years of effort, and $500 billion of venture capital went into AI natives.
