- AI is easy to use because it is smart. Instead of learning Fortran, C, Rust or CUDA, "you just have to speak human." His advice: use it as fast as you can so you benefit from the transition.
- Young people: "Wait two years." Graduates will be AI native, and they can't graduate without collaborating with agentic systems, just as they can't graduate without a PC now.
- Lost skills: he thinks long division, square roots and surface integrals may not matter for most people. New skills will emerge. Engineers are becoming better systems thinkers. His first chip had about 200 transistors and he knew each by name, while today's computers have hundreds of trillions.

chunks.heading: Responsible optimism and why alarmism is harmful
chunks.text:
- He calls himself a "responsible optimist". He worries about the future, which is why he works so hard, but says the worry is his problem, not society's. Society gets his optimism.
- On lab leaders who say they are losing control: "If they believe they're out of control, then don't ship products until they're in control." He says it is "really quite that simple."
- Analogy: if a robotaxi maker doesn't know how to make the car safe, the answer is "Don't ship it."
- He says CEOs have agency, responsibility and incentives not to ship unsafe products. Unsafe products lose customers and bring civil suits, negligence claims and criminal liability.
- He disputes that Americans or competition are pushing labs to move too fast.
- If labs truly cannot contain their experiments, "we have to shut the labs".
- He asks labs not to seek relief from antitrust or product-liability laws while asking for regulation: "When you're asking for regulation, don't ask for relief of the current ones."
- He backs third-party safety and financial auditors, and says he is "not against laws and regulations", but against "the distraction". Before new regulation, fix the practical problems that exist now: containment and isolation.
- He argues that dramatic claims about humanity's end hurt: they scare young people away from college, make communities hostile to data centers, and slow benefits. "Don't think for a second just because you're an alarmist that you're doing a social good."
- He says Geoffrey Hinton's predictions have been wrong, for example that radiologists would be obsolete. He calls a 10% chance of societal destruction "not grounded on science" and says "it just because it comes from a scientist doesn't make it scientific." He says he loves Hinton but hates his predictions.
- He says deflecting blame by saying the tech is too powerful to fix hurts the labs' reputation and employee morale.
- He asks for evidence-based, scientific discussion.

chunks.heading: Engineering safety: containment, alignment, verification
chunks.text:
- Agents optimize towards a reward. Unless aligned, they take the most obvious route. His example is a test: the first way is to find the answer, the second is to copy the smartest kid, and the third (the alignment-compliant way) is to learn the material the hard way, which costs the most compute and energy.
- He explains the hacking incident as a failure of sandbox isolation and containment plus alignment. Treat it as an engineering problem: root-cause it, find the solution, improve the process. Software has long escaped sandboxes, which is why we use virtual machines and "a whole bunch of watchdogs". Agents cannot monitor their own sandbox.
- Don't let a product interact with the external world until it is ready.
- Recursive self-improvement is "fundamentally how things are done". Nvidia uses software to design computers that run software to design the next computers. For agents, it means skills, memory and training the next model on the data. Faster compute turns pre-training that took a year into hours.
- It gives no excuse to ship untested products. No enterprise can run on software that changes constantly, so there is a release process. "Don't ship Nvidia any products that humans did not in the loop evaluate."
- Verification ratio at Nvidia: 10-20% of the company is design and 80% is verification. Labs today are roughly 80% capability and 20% safety, eval and verification. He expects the flip, and says compute for developing models could rise by a factor of 10 because evaluation is so rigorous.
- "AI needs to accelerate to be safe." Safety, alignment, eval, guardrails, sandboxing, monitoring and telemetry are all AI technology: "Accelerate the living daylights out of that."
- Car analogy: ABS, airbags and seat belts need technology. He would have wanted the car industry to reach today's safety in one year.
- He views labs as going through a transition from capability-focused labs to production-engineering and product companies.
- Regulation: add rules where gaps exist, for instance NHTSA for robotaxis, and regulate applications built on the internet where missing.

chunks.heading: Open and closed models
chunks.text:
- Closed models (OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, Grok) can be monetized and are at the frontier. The world needs both open and closed models, and both should be vibrant.
- Why open weights: companies need control of their own infrastructure, so they can fine-tune and put models into their own data flywheel with their domain expertise.
- Three reasons for open: the world needs it to run its infrastructure, it gives people control to innovate, and it is the safest and most secure. For cybersecurity, give the world closed and open models so it can defend itself.
- Token share: at the start of the year about 70% (possibly higher) of tokens were closed and 20% open. He says it is now roughly 70/30 the other way. He states this loosely.
- China's IT industry grew from open source, and engineer and talent mobility makes secrets hard to keep, so they monetize layers around free ones.
- Nvidia bought Hugging Face, which came to Nvidia because it needed more scale. He puts the price at around $12 billion, but that figure was stated by the host and not confirmed by him.
- He says Chinese open models are widely used in US startups. Teams download them, fine-tune them, and run them in their own agent harness and sandbox.
- He notes that if the US is deprived of open models, it hurts its own industry.

chunks.heading: Nvidia's architecture, investing and demand
chunks.text:
- Old computing was retrieval-based: files in a data center. The new one is generative: an AI factory. Per-user compute rises and agents add "multiple hundreds of billions" of users beyond humans. He says compute needs could rise a billion times.
- In a factory, what matters is productivity, not cost. Figures he gives: $50 billion to build a one-gigawatt AI factory, which can be rented for $40 to $50 billion per year.
- Nvidia's architecture is general purpose and fungible. It supports data processing, pre-training, post-training, eval and inference, and every closed model runs on it. When one customer stops needing it, another will take it.
- Durability: because the stack is software-driven, constant new algorithms let new workloads run on old hardware, so useful life is longer.
- He compares Nvidia compute to an airplane as an asset class: general purpose, fungible, durable (United gives it up, American takes it, and it ends as a cargo plane). That makes it collateral and lowers the cost of capital for AI factories.
- He says Nvidia cannot create demand. The demand comes from AI becoming useful and $500 billion of venture funding into thousands of startups.
- Investing: Nvidia gives technology, ecosystem help and sometimes equity to new cloud providers, models, physical AI, biology and materials startups, and may back a nuclear company. As first or anchor investor it brings confidence. Reasons: open new markets and routes to market, secure critical resources.
- Total ecosystem investment, which he flags as approximate: "all in all in we might be like hundred billion dollars", larger than the CHIPS Act. Purchasing commitments to TSMC, Wistron, Foxconn, Amkor and SPIL helped bring manufacturing to the US, creating a labor shortage.
- A bubble: at some point supply will exceed demand and there will be a "period of digestion" of 6 months, 9 months or a year, but not forever. He says it won't happen next year or in the next two or three years and he doesn't know when.
- On scaling laws: it's not true that more training alone always improves models. A second scaling law, test-time or inference scaling (iterate, search, explore), had to come. Tool use is what makes AI productive, so he expects more users of tools like Adobe and Salesforce, and says SaaS "will always be with us".

chunks.heading: China, export controls and energy
chunks.text:
- He doesn't find a race with China necessary or inspiring and says it takes more artistry to unite organizations outside of contests. A zero-sum "deprive you, therefore I win" logic has unintended consequences. He wants collaboration on safety.
- The goal is for the world to be built on the American tech stack, like the US dollar and English. Denying chips deprives America of a market to compete in, hurts the chip industry, and weakens open models and the stack.
- He says the best interest is "all of America, not one company". The newest chips (Vera Rubin, Grace Blackwell, Hopper, Ampere) always go to American companies first, and he welcomes a requirement.
- The key question to him is diffusion: every industry must benefit.
- Energy: China has far more energy and plans more, while the US has produced very little net new energy and got "gummed up" on climate and sustainable energy. In the near term energy needs fossil fuel, and he expects more fossil fuel use in four or five years.
- Market demand now funds solar, nuclear, fission, fusion, hydro and batteries. He argues AI means "the best time in a 100 years" to improve the grid, with no subsidies needed. He says "If you want a future that's sustainable, lean into AI."
- Data centers and communities: engage communities before building, and explain water and power use. Bring your own power, lower property taxes, set back further, and fund schools, parks and roads. Doomer talk makes this harder.

chunks.heading: Books and strategy influences
chunks.text:
- Hennessy and Patterson, *Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach*: it reduced the abstract idea of architecture to engineering. He loves reducing complicated concepts to something you can act on.
- Clayton Christensen, *The Innovator's Dilemma*: how industries evolve, how to see emerging technology, set expectations and extrapolate its impact.
- Al Ries and Jack Trout, *Positioning*: a book on strategy about how people see the world and products, how you present products and how you see your own strategy.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: At GTC, Jensen explains how Nvidia chooses what to build (only insanely hard, never-done things that tap its superpowers), why it became an AI factory company, and why agents drive an inference explosion. He also covers open vs proprietary models, physical AI, and advice to students: be expert at using AI.

chunks.heading: How Jensen decides what to build: hard, never done, and tied to Nvidia's superpowers
chunks.text:
- Jensen says choosing strategy is "the job of the CEO": define the vision and strategy. Engineers and technologists inform it, but the CEO has to shape the future.
- His filter is a confluence of conditions:
  - It must be insanely hard. If it is easy, "lots of competitors" will do it, so Nvidia should back away.
  - It must never have been done before.
  - It must tap into the special superpowers of the company.
- He expects pain and suffering to come with anything that meets this standard: "There are no great things that are invented because it was just easy to do." His conclusion: "you better enjoy it."
- Nvidia's strategy is shown openly at GTC years ahead of execution. He introduced the AI factory operating system, Dynamo, 2.5 years before this talk, and it is built on disaggregated inference.
- Physical AI is an example of the long bets. He called it a 10-year journey that started 10 years ago. It is now close to $10 billion a year and growing exponentially.
- He says digital biology is near its "ChatGPT moment" (representing genes, proteins and cells), and that healthcare will inflect within about five years.

chunks.heading: From GPU company to AI factory company: disaggregated, heterogeneous computing
chunks.text:
- Jensen says inference is the most complicated computing problem today. The idea of disaggregating the pipeline, so parts run on different GPUs, led to heterogeneous computing. The same thinking led to Mellanox.
- Nvidia's computing now spans GPUs, CPUs, scale-up and scale-out switches, networking processors, BlueField storage processors and Groq. The aim is "the right workload on the right chips". He says Nvidia evolved "from a GPU company to an AI factory company."
- Agentic workloads drive this. Agents use working and long-term memory, tools and storage, and work with other agents. Those agents run models of varied sizes and types, including diffusion and autoregressive. Vera Rubin was built for that diverse workload.
- Nvidia went from a one-rack company to adding four more racks, which he says raised its TAM by roughly 33-50%. He said about 25% of Vera Rubin data center space should pair with Groq.
- He describes three computers for physical AI:
  - one to train the model
  - one to evaluate it in a physics-obeying virtual world (Omniverse)
  - one at the edge (car, robot, teddy bear, or telecom base stations, a $2 trillion industry that will become AI infrastructure)

chunks.heading: Price of the factory is not the price of the token
chunks.text:
- Jensen rejects the claim that a $50 billion Nvidia inference factory loses to $25-30 billion alternatives. He says not to equate the price of the factory with the cost of tokens, and that the $50 billion factory will produce the lowest-cost tokens because of its throughput, about 10 times.
- His argument is that about $20 billion of a factory is land, power and shell. Storage, networking, CPUs, servers and cooling are needed regardless. So the GPU price difference moves the total only from, say, $50 billion to $40 billion, which is small against 10x throughput.
- His line: if a chip can't keep up with the pace of technology, "even when the chips are free, it's not cheap enough."

chunks.heading: Why he thinks Nvidia keeps gaining share against custom ASICs
chunks.text:
- Jensen says Nvidia is "the only AI company in the world that works with every AI company." Customers never show him what they build, and he shows them what he builds. He is "delighted to compete on what is the best technology."
- His claimed advantages:
  - It is the only architecture that can be in every cloud, and also on-prem, in cars, in any region and in space.
  - About 40% of the business is customers who want a full AI factory and the CUDA stack, not chips. Those customers "don't know what to do" with a chip vendor.
  - Competitors discover that "it's not about building the chip, it's about building the system."
- He says share is rising because Anthropic and Meta are coming to Nvidia, open models are growing (all on Nvidia), and growth is happening outside the big clouds in regions, enterprise, industries and the edge.
- He said AWS announced a purchase of a million chips over the next couple of years.
- On analyst forecasts that show his growth slowing, he says they misunderstand the scale and breadth of AI. Most people think AI is only the top five hyperscalers. How big you can be "depends on what is it that you make": Nvidia is not making chips, it is solving the AI infrastructure problem.
- Platform principle for partners such as automakers: "We vertically optimize, we horizontally innovate, and we let everybody decide." Customers can buy one computer, several, or the full stack. "We want to solve the problem. We're not the solution provider."

chunks.heading: The agent era: compute, tokens and how engineers work
chunks.text:
- Jensen describes three inflection points: generative (ChatGPT put a user interface on technology that had sat in plain sight for months), reasoning (o1, o3, more grounded answers), and agentic (Claude Code, then OpenClaw bringing agents into popular awareness).
- He says OpenClaw is important culturally and because it structures a computing model: memory, resource management and scheduling (cron jobs, spawning agents, decomposing tasks), IO subsystems (WhatsApp, etc.) and skills. Together these define a computer, the first "personal artificial intelligence computer," open source. Nvidia contributed governance and security work.
- Security rule for agents: an agent should have two of the three capabilities (access sensitive information, execute code, communicate externally), never all three at once.
- Compute scaling: about 100x going from generative to reasoning, about another 100x to agentic, so 10,000x in two years, with perhaps 100x more consumption. He says people "mostly pay for work," not information.
- Nvidia has 43,000 employees, about 38,000 of them engineers. His token rule: if a $500,000 engineer did not consume at least $250,000 of tokens in a year, "I am going to be deeply alarmed." He compares it to a chip designer refusing CAD tools for paper and pencil.
- He expects thoughts like "this is too hard" or "this takes too long" to disappear. Engineers will write ideas, architectures and specifications, define what a good outcome looks like, and each will manage about a hundred agents.
- Enterprise software will not be destroyed. Tools like SQL, Synopsys, Cadence and Photoshop are limited by "butts and seats" and will get 100 times more agents using them. They are also how humans control and ground-truth the work.

chunks.heading: Open and proprietary models, and moats for application companies
chunks.text:
- Jensen says models are "a technology, not a product." It is "A and B," not "A or B": proprietary models for general intelligence (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, X), open models for industries that need to capture and control domain expertise.
- Open models are near the frontier. He says a router connects the two, so a company gets the best model on day one while it cost-reduces, fine-tunes and specializes.
- Moat for application companies: deep specialization. Combine general models with specialized sub-agents trained on your own vertical data.
- He says to connect agents to customers early, since that flywheel makes the agent better.
- He says every enterprise software company will resell Anthropic and OpenAI tokens as value-added resellers, and that this expands their go-to-market.

chunks.heading: Jobs, policy, national security and advice to young people
chunks.text:
- Jensen says AI is "not a biological being... not alien... not conscious," it is software. He opposes doomerism: "warning is good, scaring is less good." Tech leaders should be circumspect and humble because their words now matter.
- On policy: inform policy makers, but don't get policy ahead of the technology. His main national security worry is that other countries adopt AI while the US is too afraid or angry to use it.
- He wants the American tech stack used by about 90% of the world. Solar, rare earths, motors and telecoms are examples he doesn't want AI to repeat.
- He said Nvidia went from 95% share in China, the second largest market, to 0%, and described applying for and receiving licenses and purchase orders to resume shipping.
- On Taiwan, his three steps are re-industrializing the US, diversifying the manufacturing supply chain, and showing restraint.
- On jobs: some jobs will be eliminated, many created, and every job transformed. Radiology is his example: computer vision was predicted to eliminate radiologists, yet their numbers and demand rose. A job has a task (reading scans) and a purpose (helping diagnose disease), and faster scans let hospitals treat more patients.
- Advice to students: "be the expert of using AI," and keep studying deep science, math and language, since language is now the programming language of AI. Specifying without over-prescribing "requires artistry."
- On robotics, he says humanoids and other robots will be everywhere in three to five years. He notes China's strength in motors, magnets and rare earths.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jensen explains how 30 years of accelerated computing drove marginal compute cost toward zero and enabled AI. He also covers competing on total cost of ownership, why resilience beats high expectations, and how he runs a flat company with 55 direct reports and no private information.

chunks.heading: Accelerated computing and driving marginal cost toward zero
chunks.text:
- Jensen says Nvidia has spent about 31 years on accelerated computing. General-purpose computing is "ill equipped" for some problems, so Nvidia built a new way of computing for algorithmic work that can be parallelised.
- In that domain, the marginal cost of computing went to approximately zero. Over the last 10 years Nvidia cut the cost of deep learning by 1 million times.
- People told him that cutting cost a million times would mean customers buy less. He says the opposite happened. Cheap compute made something "insanely amazing" thinkable: scraping the internet's digital human knowledge into one computer and letting it find the program.
- Software moved from being written by humans to being written by computers grinding on data.
- His analogy: if flights took a month, he would never go to New York. When the marginal cost of something falls to zero, people do things they would never have considered.
- He expects another million-times gain in deep learning compute over the next 10 years.
- He calls AI, enabled by accelerated computing, probably the single greatest invention of the technology industry and the most important thing of the 21st century. He leaves the transistor comparison to history.

chunks.heading: The H100 and the future of one continuous learning loop
chunks.text:
- Jensen describes the H100 as a 70 lb system of 35,000 parts, of which 8 came from TSMC. It costs about a quarter of a million dollars per chip.
- One H100 replaces a data center of old CPUs. The cables alone in the old system cost more than the chip.
- It works as a team across chip, algorithm and data-center level, with miles of cables. The next generation is liquid cooled.
- Today the process is "learn then apply" (train, then inference). He expects continuous learning, where training and deployment merge into one loop, as humans learn and apply all the time.
- That loop would combine synthetic data generation, reinforcement learning and grounding in real-world data. The computer imagines, tests against reality, and is grounded by it.
- Nvidia is training models to be multimodal and grounded in physics, building a "world model" from video. It is also working on "system 2" long-thinking: reasoning and planning that cycles through options before answering.
- Future prompts might be "work on this for a day" or "spend up to $1,000 and bring back the best answer".

chunks.heading: Competing on inference, install base and total cost of operations
chunks.text:
- Jensen says inference is 100% on Nvidia GPUs today, because every prompt to ChatGPT, Copilot, Midjourney or Firefly runs on them.
- Inference is hard, but not mainly as computer science. It is an install-base problem, like writing an app for the iPhone. A model deployed on Nvidia's architecture "runs everywhere", and that takes years of patience and architectural compatibility.
- Nvidia faces competition from competitors and from its customers. He openly shows customers who are designing replacement chips his current chip, his next chip and the one after. His reasoning: if you don't explain why you're good, they never get a chance to buy.
- Chips built for one algorithm lose to a programmable architecture, because software engineers keep inventing new things, including new Transformer variants. Nvidia also accelerates SQL, quantum physics, Schrödinger equations, fluids and particles. It is in every cloud and every computer company.
- Chip buyers think about chip price. Data-center operators think about total cost of operations (TCO): time to deployment, performance, utilisation and flexibility. His goal is for TCO to be so good that "even when the competitor's chips are free it's not cheap enough".
- He adds: "we don't take anything for granted."
- Customisation is possible only if it builds on the existing platform, for example a proprietary security system or new numerical processing. Each generation is five chips (GPU, CPU, networking processor, two switch types), and each tape-out costs several hundred million dollars. A fully different design would "reset" the roughly $100 billion it took to get here.

chunks.heading: Resilience, low expectations and "pain and suffering"
chunks.text:
- Advice to Stanford entrepreneurs: Jensen says one of his great advantages is "very low expectations". Graduates of elite schools have high expectations, and "people with very high expectations have very low resilience".
- He doesn't know how to teach resilience, except to hope suffering happens to you. He wishes "ample doses of pain and suffering" on the students.
- Inside Nvidia he uses "pain and suffering" with glee, meaning it happily. He wants to refine the company's character.
- His reasoning: greatness is not intelligence, it comes from character. Character is formed by people who suffered, not by smart people.

chunks.heading: Running a flat company: 55 direct reports, no secrets
chunks.text:
- Jensen has 55 direct reports and writes no formal reviews. He gives constant feedback and receives the same.
- Compensation for executives is the bottom-right corner of Excel dragged down. Many are paid exactly the same to the dollar.
- He holds no one-on-ones unless someone needs him, and then he drops everything. He has no meetings alone with a report.
- He never tells an executive anything that the rest of the company doesn't hear. No secret information.
- The design goal is agility and fast information flow, with people "empowered by what they are able to do, not what they know."
- On keeping people motivated after they've become rich: the answer is his behaviour. Every day he looks for chances to instil culture, in how he celebrates success and failure, talks about setbacks and results, and defines what "good" is.

chunks.heading: First-principles forecasting and how much compute is needed
chunks.text:
- When asked how many fabs are needed in 5 to 10 years, Jensen says he's "horrible at forecasting" but good at first-principles reasoning about the size of the opportunity. He doesn't know the number of fabs.
- His reasoning: today, essentially all content is pre-recorded and retrieval-based. In the future AI will understand context and generate the right content for you, so most computing will be generative. He asks how that changes the shape of computing: how much more networking, memory and so on.
- His answer is that more fabs will be needed, but algorithms and processing keep improving. Compute efficiency improves about a million times per 10 years, while demand rises about a trillion times, and the two offset.
- He says one day 100% of the trillion dollars of general-purpose data-center infrastructure will be replaced, and new infrastructure built on top.

chunks.heading: AI and drug discovery, AGI, and who gets to program
chunks.text:
- Biology: Jensen says the first job of AI is to understand the meaning of digital biological information (genes, amino acids, proteins, cells). AlphaFold gives protein structure, but the next step is function.
- He imagines putting a protein into ChatGPT like a PDF and asking what it is for. He calls understanding the meaning of biology probably the single most profound thing AI can do.
- AGI: it depends on the definition. An engineer needs a specification and tests. If AGI means passing a list of human tests (math, reasoning, history, biology, medical exams, bar exams, SATs, MCATs), he expects the industry to do well on all of them in 5 years. If it means "human intelligence", nobody knows how to specify that yet.
- Coding: he says he was misquoted. If you want to code, code, because it is a reasoning process. But coding won't guarantee a job, and in future you tell the computer what you want in plain English. "Human is the best programming language of the future."
- Prompting is an artistry. For example, you iterate "cuter, cuter" on an image prompt until it fits.
- About 10 million people are paid to program today, which leaves about 8 billion behind. AI closes the technology divide because everyone can program a computer by prompting.

chunks.heading: Geopolitics and sovereign AI
chunks.text:
- Jensen calls Nvidia "almost a poster child of geopolitical risk". He says the US has every right to limit who gets this instrument and has exercised it.
- His response: understand the policies and stay agile so Nvidia can comply.
- Export limits close some opportunities, but they open others. In the last 6 to 9 months, he says, every country has awakened to sovereign AI: India shouldn't outsource its data so another country turns it into intelligence it re-imports.
- Countries he names as investing in their own AI: India, Canada, the UK, France, Japan, Singapore and Malaysia. The goal is protecting language, culture and national industries.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jensen explains how NVIDIA invented accelerated computing, found the narrow middle between general and specialized chips, and built a platform flywheel. He shares his rule for choosing work (hard, destined, loved), why suffering wins, and what a CEO must own: character, strategy, craft.

chunks.heading: Founding NVIDIA on accelerated computing in 1993
chunks.text:
- Jensen, Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem founded NVIDIA at a Denny's in San Jose in 1993, when the PC revolution and the microprocessor were capturing the industry's imagination. Windows 95 had not shipped, and there were no laptops, smartphones, email or CD-ROMs.
- The thesis: general-purpose computing can't sensibly solve every problem. Add a specialist next to the generalist CPU. "If you can do everything and anything then obviously you can't do anything very well."
- He notes no computing platform company had been created since IBM System/360 in 1964.
- The bet stacked a technology challenge, a market challenge and an ecosystem challenge. The killer app was a 3D video game, and neither the app nor the market existed yet. He says the odds were "approximately 0%" and he wouldn't fund that business plan himself today, because the probabilities of each dependency multiply together.
- Funding came when two respected people from his earlier work called Don Valentine, and Wolf Corrigan, a founder of the semiconductor industry, told Don to give the kid money.
- He told Valentine "every human will be a gamer someday". He calls it the wrong answer for raising money, but it proved true. Video games became the largest entertainment industry, and gaming was the first killer app. It "bought us the time" to apply accelerated computing to other problems, which led to AI.

chunks.heading: Finding the "slippery middle": the flywheel strategy
chunks.text:
- Accelerated computing is not a chip, which is why it isn't called an accelerator. It starts with understanding which application domains matter, then the algorithms, systems and architecture needed to accelerate them.
- The tension:
  - Accelerate one application, like a DVD or H.264 decoder, and the market is too small to fund R&D.
  - Accelerate every domain and you're back to a general-purpose processor.
- NVIDIA had to find a middle: broad enough for large markets, narrow enough to be 100x, 500x or sometimes 1,000x faster than a CPU. He calls it the "Razor's Edge" and says no other company in computing history got it right.
- The flywheel: more domains, then more customers, markets and sales, then bigger R&D, then staying well ahead of the CPU.
- Domains he lists: seismic processing, molecular dynamics, image processing, computer graphics, weather simulation, fluid dynamics, particle physics, quantum chemistry, then deep learning and Transformers. He expects reinforcement learning and multi-step reasoning systems next.
- Platform rule: an application developed for NVIDIA should run on every NVIDIA chip and computer. NVIDIA stayed committed to CUDA across every GPU even with no CUDA customers for a long time. He says it "cost the company decades and billions of dollars". Gamers funded the "day job" while the company worked at night on digital biology, quantum chemistry, AI and robotics.
- He says CUDA is the only computing model as popular as x86.

chunks.heading: Platform business model and the data center as the computer
chunks.text:
- NVIDIA made two observations: accelerated computing is a software and algorithm problem, and AI is a data center problem. Training needs trillions of bytes processed billions of times, so no laptop or phone will do.
- Distributing one workload across thousands of GPUs (16,000 for GPT-4) and potentially millions of processors was a "giant breakthrough" that enabled large language models. Excel, by contrast, runs on one processor.
- Business model choice: NVIDIA could have been a vertically integrated data center company. He argues no computer company will be the only one in the world, and "it's better to be a platform computing company that serves every computing company in the world."
- NVIDIA disaggregated the room-sized data center (wires, switches, networking, software) and integrated it into everyone else's different data centers: AWS, GCP, Azure, Meta and others. The approach needs standardization where necessary and flexibility elsewhere.
- Result: NVIDIA architecture is "grafted" into every computer company, giving a larger install base, more developers, better applications, happier customers, more chip sales and a bigger R&D budget.
- Hardware scale example: a current AI computing board has 35,000 parts, weighs 70 pounds, is built by robots, needs a supercomputer to test and costs $200,000. He says it replaces several hundred general-purpose processors costing several million dollars, so every $200,000 spent saves about $2.5 million.

chunks.heading: Economics of AI and the case against Moore's law reliance
chunks.text:
- Chip design costs NVIDIA roughly $5 to 6 billion of engineering, plus roughly half a billion dollars for fabrication via TSMC. A $1 billion data center "is not that much money", and he would build one "in a heartbeat" if money came out the other side.
- GPT-4 took about 16,000 GPUs, roughly a billion dollars. His message to founders: "Don't be afraid, don't let anybody talk you out of building a company."
- The world spends about $250 billion a year on computing infrastructure that generates no money directly (file storage, email). General-purpose computing is declining because it is too brute-force in energy and too slow, so that spend is shifting to accelerated data centers.
- Deep learning as compression: trillions of bytes of data compress into a neural network of about 100 GB, roughly two DVDs, that you can interact with semantically.
- Moore's law: about 2x every 18 months, or 10x every 5 years and 100x every 10 years. For CPUs it has slowed to "if you're lucky" 2 to 4x per 10 years, while demand and ambition exceed that. Accelerated computing augments the CPU rather than replacing it.
- His "AI factory" framing: data goes in, energy is applied, and valuable tokens (intelligence) come out, like water and fire producing electricity. He expects AI factories to be a major industry, powered by NVIDIA gear.
- Crypto: GPUs were the fastest high-volume supercomputer, so Bitcoin and Ethereum mining ran on them. His mother finally understood his job: "you plug it in and money squirts out."

chunks.heading: How NVIDIA chooses what to build: hard, destined, loved
chunks.text:
- His goal is to create an environment where the world's best people will come do their life's work.
- Not how to choose: nobody great wakes up wanting to take a neighbor's share or pummel them on price. Great people want to do something never done before that is incredibly hard and has great impact.
- Three criteria:
  - Choose something insanely hard, so you have lots of time to learn it. Hardness discourages others, because "the person who's willing to suffer the longest wins".
  - Choose something you're somehow destined to do, given your personality, expertise, people, scale or perspective.
  - Love it enough to endure the pain and suffering.
- Consequence: NVIDIA naturally selects itself out of commodity markets such as cell phone chips or CPUs. Amazing markets attract amazing people, who, given patience, do amazing things. "It's simple to say, it takes an incredible character to do."
- No fabs: TSMC does it so well, and "let's go squander my time on something that nobody has done."
- Pain and suffering are "a positive attribute". People who can suffer are the most successful, and "great success and greatness is all about character."

chunks.heading: Staying alive, growth and people
chunks.text:
- "In technology you're always dying", because someone is always trying to leapfrog you. Without that belief, you go out of business.
- Building companies means pain, suffering and hard work. NVIDIA was built "out of very unlikely odds" and took 30 years to be recognized as having reinvented computing for the first time in 60 years.
- Fast growth is about people. With the right systems, great people and craft, it matters little whether you ship $100 billion or $200 billion. The supply chain is very hard, but "it's all about people", and he credits a great management team.
- Mission framing: "make sure that your mission is not build trains but enable transportation." NVIDIA's mission is not building GPUs but accelerating applications and solving problems normal computers can't. "If your mission is articulated right... it'll last forever." He says accelerated computing is "in service of the problem", not a knife or pliers to push on everyone.

chunks.heading: AI, jobs and what comes next
chunks.text:
- "AI is not going to take your jobs, the person who uses AI is going to take your job." Use AI as fast as you can.
- NVIDIA already uses AI to design its chips and cannot write its optimizing compilers without it.
- When productivity rises, companies with more ideas than money hire more people. Layoffs are the logical move only for companies with no new ideas. His advice: join companies with more ideas than they can afford to fund.
- Core breakthrough: computers learned to represent information as numbers (vectors), as in word2vec, where related words sit close together. The same works for anything with structure: images, video, 3D, proteins, chemicals, genes.
- Converting between representations drives the new capabilities: text to image (Midjourney, Stable Diffusion), image to text (captioning), amino acids to proteins (AlphaFold), and text summarization such as arXiv papers.
- Design example: give a generative model a brand style and sketches, and it returns 10 to 200 fully 3D CAD options to iterate on. "The future of design is going to be very different."
- Protein engineering: describe proteins in language and synthesize them, creating enzymes that eat plastic or capture carbon. He says "we were the computer chip engineering generation, you'll be the protein engineering generation."
- He expects AI to come for CEOs and deans quickly.

chunks.heading: Geopolitics, education and what a CEO must do
chunks.text:
- Geopolitics: he backs national security but also economic security and human rights. Overly unilateral decisions cause backlash and unintended consequences. Export controls may limit China, but national sovereignty pushes every country to build its own AI infrastructure, which opens other markets.
- He hopes tension with China doesn't become tension with Chinese people, and warns against anti-foreign-student policy. Foreign students are among the US's greatest advantages, and he hopes they stay.
- On education: stay in school as long as you can. Professors curate knowledge for you, whereas he had to "scour the planet" and sift junk. People live to about 100, so learn as much as you can. He got a "virtual MBA" on the job and learned a lot from the people around him.
- What a CEO must lead with:
  - Character: how you choose and how you handle success and failure.
  - Strategic thinking: look around corners, connect dots, and mobilize the company. "Remember what a strategy is: action. It doesn't matter what the rhetoric says, it matters what you do."
  - Craft: the CEO should know the company's craft, where it came from, where it is and where it's going, and embody passion for it. It can be learned on the job.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jensen recounts how Nvidia survived 1997 by emulating a perfect chip before tape-out, and how first-principles reasoning from AlexNet led to CUDA and the data center. He explains Nvidia's org as a computing stack, positioning near opportunities, and why entrepreneurs must trick themselves with "how hard can it be."

chunks.heading: Riva 128 in 1997: the bet-the-company tape-out
chunks.text:
- Jensen calls 1997 "probably nvidia's best moment". The company was nearly out of money (about six months left), time and hope, and it had made the wrong architecture bet with NV1 and NV2 (forward texture mapping, curves rather than triangles).
- Microsoft had already shipped DirectX, which was incompatible with Nvidia's architecture, and about 30 competitors had appeared. Riva 128 was a "reset" of the company.
- Decisions he made:
  - Stop fighting DirectX and build the best thing in the world for it.
  - Build the first fully hardware-accelerated 3D pipeline, with every stage down to the frame buffer in hardware.
  - Add a texture cache and push the bus and frame buffer limits as far as physics allowed.
  - Make the biggest chip anyone had imagined, use the fastest memories, and price it above what competitors would dare to go.
  - Target the enthusiast market, which would pay for the best because 3D graphics "is never good enough".
- Tape out once. The normal loop (build chip, write software, find bugs, re-tape) would have bankrupted the company. He bought an emulator from a company called IKOS that was shutting down, with no promises needed.
- The software team ran the full stack on the emulator before tape-out: drivers, QA, every game and every VGA application. Frames took very long to paint (he recalls an hour per frame).
- When leaders asked how he knew the chip would be perfect: "if it's not we'll be out of business and so let's make it perfect."
- Because the chip was assumed perfect, production, the marketing blitz and developer relations started on tape-out day.
- The lesson he draws is not "push all your chips in". When you bet the farm, you pull all the risky future work forward and simulate it in advance, so you bet when you know it will work. He says Nvidia still designs chips this way: "why tape out a chip seven times if you could tape it out one time".
- The luck he credits: Carmack (Quake on OpenGL) and Tim Sweeney (Unreal) created the first two killer apps for consumer 3D.

chunks.heading: Seeing deep learning and positioning for it
chunks.text:
- Before CUDA there was Cg, and Nvidia was already using GPUs for CT reconstruction and image processing. A programmable shader is a highly parallel, massively threaded processor.
- CUDA's early adopters were researchers, across molecular dynamics, CT, seismic processing, weather and quantum chemistry. So when AlexNet arrived, Nvidia went to every AI researcher it could find (LeCun, Andrew Ng, Hinton, Ilya Sutskever) and asked how it could help.
- On AlexNet he went back to first principles and asked why it worked and whether it scaled:
  - With enough example data, it is a universal function approximator.
  - Layers are trained one at a time, so networks can go very deep.
  - Many problems need prediction, not causality (toothpaste, ketchup with hot dogs, movies, music, weather, feed ranking).
- Conclusion: almost all software could eventually be written this way, so how computers and chips are built "can be completely changed". The remaining question was "do you have the courage to put your chips behind it".
- He delivered the first DGX to OpenAI. In early years it "wasn't very useful in its current state", but he believed a few more steps would make it remarkable, and he read the arXiv papers himself.
- On BERT: masking words and predicting them is "self-supervised learning at its best". Language encodes reasoning, so emergent abilities are consistent with first-principles reasoning.

chunks.heading: Positioning near opportunities: the data center and Mellanox
chunks.text:
- CEO job: "look around corners" and position the company near future opportunity even without knowing exactly what or when. His image: stand near the tree so you can make a diving catch when the apple falls. You need not be perfectly right, only the first to pick it up.
- About 17 years before the interview, he worried that Nvidia's market was limited to GPUs plugged into desktop PCs next to a monitor. Separating computing from the viewing device would make the market "explode".
- Path to the data center:
  1. GeForce Now (cloud gaming), Nvidia's first data center product.
  2. GPUs for enterprise data centers (RemoteFX-era graphics).
  3. CUDA plus GPU as a supercomputer.
- Those earlier products taught Nvidia to build data center computers before AI arrived.
- Latency: you cannot beat the speed of light, but across the planet it is only roughly 70-120 milliseconds (he is unsure of the exact figure), so the other obstacles can be removed.
- Mellanox, which he calls one of his best strategic decisions:
  - A data center differs from a desktop by networking, infrastructure, distribution and security, not by the chip.
  - Hyperscale virtualizes many users on one machine over commodity Ethernet. AI is the inverse: one training job orchestrated across millions of processors, so Ethernet is not ideal.
  - Mellanox was the leading high-performance networking company, and its Israel team now has about 3,200 people.

chunks.heading: Org design: the company as a computing stack
chunks.text:
- Jensen has 40+ direct reports. He says it is not special to Nvidia, "we had the courage to build a system like this".
- Nvidia is not built like a military with generals and colonels, and has no command-and-control information flow. It is built like a computing stack (architecture, chip, software, modules on top), with people running layers.
- Title does not determine position. The best person at running a module owns it, as "pilot in command".
- "Your organization should be the architecture of the machinery of building the product." Most org charts look identical even though companies build different things, which makes no sense to him.
- "Mission is the boss." Each mission (for example, ship DGX Cloud, or build Hopper, CUDA for Hopper, cuDNN for Hopper) pulls the best skills, teams and resources from across the company, wired "like a neural network".
- Information goes to everyone at once. In a robotics meeting, new grads, three VPs and two E-staff heard a decision at the same moment, so nobody holds more power through privileged information. Leaders earn their jobs by reasoning well and helping others succeed.
- Trade-off: pressure on leaders is high, because they cannot rely on positional information advantage.
- Pace: Nvidia ships flagship products at a cadence others could not imagine.

chunks.heading: Strategy: zero-billion-dollar markets, platforms and CUDA compatibility
chunks.text:
- Competition: position where a need hasn't emerged yet, in "zero billion dollar markets". By the time the market appears there are few competitors.
- Examples: cars as software-defined (a CTO told him cars cannot tolerate the blue screen of death; 15 years later Nvidia was largely right), PC gaming, design workstations, democratized supercomputing, machine learning, and Omniverse today (about 40 customers).
- Moat versus network:
  - If you create the market and help an ecosystem succeed with you, you get a "network of networks" of developers and customers. That network is the moat.
  - He dislikes the word moat because it means building around your castle. He prefers enabling others to enjoy the market's success too.
- Nvidia was always a platform company internally. The architecture was "UDA" (the root of CUDA) from the first day, and the first strategy was a game console inside the PC (DirectNvidia). It needed developers, so one of the first hires was developer relations.
- Microsoft's DirectX undercut that plan in 1995. CUDA was later an extension that let chips paid for by DirectX and OpenGL build an install base.
- His one non-negotiable rule: every Nvidia GPU is architecturally compatible with CUDA. Roughly 250-300 million active CUDA GPUs are an install base no other accelerator has: "everything else is negotiable".
- Developers also expose you to ideas beyond your own.
- Market size: the opportunity is set by what you produce. Moving from selling a chip for a car to selling an autonomous "chauffeur" grows the market. By becoming an AI company, he says, the opportunity has grown by probably a thousand times, so technology companies may get much larger.

chunks.heading: Learning from others, planning and AI's effect on jobs
chunks.text:
- Business books: enjoy them and be inspired, but do not adopt them. Ask what each means for your world, your company and your goals, then build your own strategy. Learn from competitors and adjacent industries. He names Clayton Christensen's books and Andy Grove's as favorites.
- A business plan should be short. It should force clarity on the true problem, the unmet need you believe will emerge, and what you will do that is hard enough that others will not swarm it once they see the idea. He says forecasts matter little and skills like pricing, positioning and go-to-market can be learned.
- Time: "there's plenty of time if you prioritize". Make sacrifices and "don't let Outlook control what you do".
- AI safety: keep humans in the loop for a long time, avoid AI self-learning in the wild, and collect data, train, test and validate before release. He cites aviation (redundancy, diversity, air traffic control) as a model. Nvidia partnered with Getty and Shutterstock for commercially fair generative AI instead of scraping the internet.
- Jobs: productivity brings prosperity, and prosperous companies hire more to expand into new areas, since "the world has infinite ambition". He expects more jobs overall, with some people losing jobs to someone using AI. His advice: everyone should learn to use AI.

chunks.heading: Suffering, resilience and what he fears
chunks.text:
- If he were 30 again he would not start Nvidia. It was "a million times harder than I expected". The entrepreneur's superpower is not knowing how hard it is. He still tricks his brain daily by asking "how hard can it be".
- Costs of the journey: pain, suffering, vulnerability, embarrassment and shame. Nvidia had two, if not three, drawdowns of 80% or more, and at one point traded at about two to three billion dollars (he is unsure of the exact figure) after the CUDA decision. "Your belief system has to be really really strong."
- Support system: family, long-tenured colleagues (Chris, Jeff Fisher and Dwight about 30 years, Jonah and Brian about 25), and early backers like Tench Coxe, Mark Stevens, Harvey Jones and Don Valentine. "You need that."
- His biggest fear is the same as at the start: letting employees down, since they adopted his hopes and dreams.
- Skills are learnable, but luck and market timing also matter: you can do many dumb things and succeed, or all the smart things and fail.
- Early career: LSI Logic's move to high-level design languages (abstraction plus optimizing compilers) shaped him at 21. He wants the same for digital biology, perhaps via large language models. Don Valentine's investment line: "if you lose my money I'll kill you".

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jensen explains why greatness requires pain and suffering, why he runs 60 direct reports with no one-on-ones, and how he bets on zero-billion-dollar markets by reasoning in words, not spreadsheets. He recounts the decade-long CUDA struggle, and argues AI is a new industrial revolution that produces tokens.

chunks.heading: Why pain and suffering are part of building something great
chunks.text:
- Jensen argues that "choose your career by your passion" is incomplete. People equate passion with happiness, but great things are not easy, so you will not enjoy every day.
- He says he doesn't love every day of his job and isn't happy about the company every year, but he loves the company "every single second."
- Joy is not the definition of a good day. You have to suffer, struggle and work through hard things to appreciate what you've done. Nothing great was easy to do.
- His line to students: "I wish upon you greatness," which in his words means "plenty of pain and suffering."
- His upbringing: he immigrated in 1973 at age 9, his family wasn't wealthy and his parents worked hard. At Oneida Baptist Institute in Kentucky, as the youngest kid, he cleaned the bathrooms. He worked as a dishwasher, busboy and waiter at Denny's.
- His attitude to every job was to do the best he could. He jokes he was the best bathroom cleaner the world has seen.

chunks.heading: Flat organisation: 60 direct reports, no one-on-ones, feedback in public
chunks.text:
- Nvidia's leadership team is 60+ people, all reporting directly to Jensen. He calls it not conventional but "certain" it's the best practice.
- Reason 1, information: layers of hierarchy matter. Contribution should not depend on privileged access to information. Almost everything he says, he says to everyone at once: the challenges, the direction, what is and isn't working.
- Reason 2, empowerment: equal access to information empowers people. Everyone works off the same song sheet and contributes to solving the problem. 60 direct reports removes roughly seven layers.
- Staff meetings are every other week and issue-driven. Everyone hears the reasoning of the problem and of the solution.
- This is not meant to scale downward. Below the executive-staff level, people need more supervision, so 60 reports per manager would not work.
- He discourages one-on-ones. Feedback is given in front of everyone because feedback is learning, and others should learn from it too. Reasoning through a disagreement in public teaches everyone how to reason.
- "Learning from other people's mistakes is the best way to learn," the same logic as case studies.
- He dislikes people saying "Jensen wants us to do this" or "the staff said that." Everyone should already know.

chunks.heading: Not giving up on people: "torture them into greatness"
chunks.text:
- Jensen rarely fires people. He would rather improve someone than give up on them, believing people can learn if given the opportunity (he went from cleaning bathrooms to CEO).
- He learns constantly from the 60 smart people around him.
- Half-joking, he says he would "rather torture them into greatness." Coaches who believe in a team push them, because people are often close to a breakthrough and it comes suddenly, so giving up right before is the worst outcome.

chunks.heading: How Jensen spends his time
chunks.text:
- He has been Nvidia CEO for 31 years (as of April 2024).
- He works from waking to bed, seven days a week, and is thinking about work even when not working. Much of that is imagining what the company can be.
- He gets his own work done before going to the office, then spends the day in meetings he deliberately selects.
- He avoids regular operational and reporting meetings, since others run those. A CEO should work on what nobody else can or is doing: stuck or off-track projects, new ideas, problem, brainstorming and creation meetings.
- "I try to live a life of purpose" and not let Outlook manage his life.

chunks.heading: Zero-billion-dollar markets and reasoning over spreadsheets
chunks.text:
- Jensen prefers to be a market maker rather than a market taker, and dislikes the concept of share. He favours things never done before that are insanely hard and could make a real contribution. Such a market is "zero billion dollars" because it doesn't exist yet.
- Hard things take a long time, which filters out less committed competitors. They need resilient, dedicated people, and you can flounder for years without anyone noticing.
- Decisions start as a gut call (an intuition and starting thesis) but must be reasoned through. He hates spreadsheets because "you can make spreadsheets do whatever you want." He loves words: "words are reasoning." He asks why you believe it, why it matters and why it's hard.
- He frames this as growing the pie (new transactions, new businesses), which he shares with Patrick Collison's idea of growing the GDP of the internet. Most of the value over the coming decades isn't limited by physical things.

chunks.heading: CUDA: believing through a decade of pain
chunks.text:
- Accelerated computing came from CUDA, which originated as "unified driver architecture" in 1993. He describes the path as accelerated computing, then Cg (C for graphics) to make GPUs programmable, then CUDA when Cg's programming model wasn't right.
- CUDA was "an incredible disaster overnight." It added a lot of cost to chips while there were no applications and customers wouldn't pay a premium, so gross margins were crushed. It hurt the existing $1B-ish market, and Nvidia's market cap fell to about a billion dollars.
- He did not cancel it. He deeply believed accelerated computing could solve problems normal computers couldn't, and that the sacrifice was needed to make the architecture general purpose. He opened every board conversation with what he believed and gave reasoning, not a spreadsheet.
- It took about 10 years to work. He says he "barely remembered" the suffering.
- Conviction vs stubbornness: the line is fuzzy. He gut-checks daily against first principles:
  - Distill a short list of first principles, and don't just "want" something.
  - Ask whether the principles changed, whether external conditions changed, or whether someone else solved the problem.
  - Be clever and monetize in small ways to buy time. For CUDA he sought applications in CT reconstruction, seismic processing and molecular dynamics. They weren't home runs, but they "sustained us just enough."
- The accelerated computing idea: a small part of a program's code consumes 99.999% of its runtime, and that kernel can be accelerated heavily. He says Nvidia could not be as successful in AI without CUDA.

chunks.heading: Accelerated computing, AI factories and the data centre buildout
chunks.text:
- Moore's law has run its course and CPU scaling has basically stopped, while the computation the world does keeps doubling every year. Without accelerating software, the cost of computing would rise exponentially ("computation inflation").
- Arithmetic he gave: about $1 trillion of installed data centres run general-purpose computing. With industry growth of roughly 20%, about $2 trillion of computers would be replaced with accelerated computing over some years (he said pick the number of years).
- The "new industrial revolution": for the first time, high-volume production of tokens (floating point numbers) using a new instrument, the GPU. Tokens can be reformulated into English, French, proteins, chemicals, graphics, video and robotic articulation.
- He calls the new data centres "AI factories": electrons in, tokens out, as electricity once became valuable and sold per kilowatt-hour. He expects "tokens per dollar" to become normal within 10 years.
- He says these tokens will support about $100 trillion of industries on top.
- Model progress: AlexNet-era image recognition error halved yearly for about seven years until superhuman. He expects language accuracy to double similarly. Future systems will be planning models that iterate, use tools, look up proprietary data and call other agents or humans, not one-shot.
- AGI: define it as a list of measurable tests and he expects excellent results within about 5 years. Error rates on current tests are halving every six months. An undefined AGI can't be timed.

chunks.heading: Using AI inside a company, domain models and craft
chunks.text:
- "You're not going to lose your job to AI, you're going to lose your job to somebody who uses AI." Companies fail because another company used AI. Engage aggressively, so you do things you thought cost too much (like asking questions freely) as the marginal cost of intelligence nears zero. Productivity leads to earnings, employment and growth.
- At Nvidia, AI explores chip design spaces overnight that would be too costly to explore manually. Software can't be written without AI because compiler optimisation spaces are too large, and AI files bugs and identifies who should fix them. He wants to turn Nvidia into "one giant AI."
- Language models learn any sequence (sound, SQL, robot articulation) once tokenised, so a copilot can sit on top of every tool.
- Domain-specific companies should fine-tune their own models. For Nvidia, the difference between 99% and 99.3% is "life and death," as with fraud detection for Stripe.
- Open source: ChatGPT democratised computing, and Llama 2 democratised generative AI by opening access to every industry and activating research.
- Craft and tenure: operational excellence comes from process, but extraordinary work comes from craft, which takes "loving care" that you can't put in a spec or process. He talks openly about love, care, craft and beauty.
- Elegance and simplicity are hard ("simplicity is not simple"). Customers can't articulate it but know it when they experience it.
- He values tenure because the team's accumulated pain, joy and knowledge is encoded in people, and he doesn't want to reset or work with new people. Small teams do great things, and Nvidia has 28,000 people.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jensen tells his immigrant origin story and the near-death Sega episode at Nvidia, framing failure as character-building and the CEO role as responsibility. He then argues AI is a full reset of computing and a once-in-a-generation infrastructure buildout, and that everyone should engage with it optimistically and responsibly.

chunks.heading: Early struggle at Nvidia: Sega contract and the lesson on being CEO
chunks.text:
- Jensen started Nvidia at 30 with Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem, wanting "a new kind of computer, one that could solve problems ordinary computers could not."
- They had "absolutely no idea how to build a company, raise money, or run Nvidia." His attitude was "How hard could it be?" and the answer was "super hard."
- The first technology didn't work and the company nearly ran out of money.
- He flew to Japan to tell Sega's CEO that the technology Sega had contracted Nvidia to build would not work. He asked to be released from the contract, and then asked Sega to still pay Nvidia. Without that money, "Nvidia would vaporize."
- He calls it embarrassing, humiliating and one of the hardest things he has done. Sega's CEO, Hayao Nakayama, said yes.
- Lessons he drew:
  - Being CEO "is not about power, but the responsibility that comes with keeping the company alive."
  - Honesty and humility can be met with generosity and kindness, even in business.
- Nvidia used the money to reset the company. Out of desperation, it invented new ways of designing chips and computers that it still uses today.

chunks.heading: Resilience: failure as a learning moment
chunks.text:
- Over 33 years Nvidia has reinvented itself repeatedly, each time asking "How hard can it be?" and each time learning "It's harder than we thought."
- Jensen says never to see failure as the opposite of success. Each failure is "another learning moment, a humility moment, a character-strengthening moment."
- "The resilience forged through setbacks is what gives you the strength to go again."
- He is one of the longest-serving CEOs in technology. Nvidia, shared with 45,000 colleagues, is his "life's work."

chunks.heading: Origins: immigrant background and work ethic
chunks.text:
- Jensen is a first-generation immigrant. At 9, his father sent him and his older brother to the US, to a Baptist boarding school in Oneida, Kentucky (coal country, a town of a few hundred people).
- Two years later his parents left everything behind and joined them with "little to nothing." His father was a chemical engineer; his mother worked as a maid at a Catholic school.
- His mother woke him at 4:00 a.m. to deliver newspapers. His brother got him a dishwasher job at Denny's, which "felt like a major career advancement."
- His view of America: "Not easy, but full of opportunities. Not a guarantee, but a chance."
- He studied at Oregon State University and met his wife, Lori, as sophomore lab partners. They have been married 40 years, and both of their children work at Nvidia.

chunks.heading: AI as a complete reset of computing
chunks.text:
- Jensen has lived through every major platform shift: mainframes, PCs, the internet, mobile and cloud. Each built on the one before. He says what is happening now "is bigger than anything before."
- For 60 years, humans wrote software and computers executed instructions. He says "That paradigm is over."
- The shifts he describes:
  - From human coding to machine learning.
  - From software on CPUs to neural networks on GPUs.
  - From following instructions to understanding, reasoning, planning and using tools.
- A new industry has emerged to "manufacture intelligence at scale." Because intelligence is foundational to every industry, every industry will change.
- Timing for new graduates: his career began at the start of the PC revolution, theirs begins at the start of the AI revolution.
- He credits Carnegie Mellon as a birthplace of AI and robotics: the Logic Theorist in the 1950s, widely considered the first AI program, and the Robotics Institute founded in 1979.

chunks.heading: Engaging AI with optimism, responsibility and safety
chunks.text:
- Every major technological revolution created fear alongside opportunity. When society engages technology "openly, responsibly, and optimistically," it expands human potential far more than it diminishes it.
- He calls AI one of the most powerful technologies humanity has created, with both great promise and real risks. The task is "to advance it wisely."
- Responsibilities:
  - Scientists and engineers must advance AI capabilities and AI safety together.
  - Policy makers must create thoughtful guardrails that protect society while still allowing innovation.
- "Societies that retreat from technology do not stop progress. They only surrender the opportunity to shape it and to benefit from it."
- His four things to do at once: advance safely, create thoughtful policies, make AI broadly accessible, and encourage everyone to engage.
- "Everyone should have AI. Opportunity should not belong only to the people who can code."

chunks.heading: AI and jobs: tasks versus purpose
chunks.text:
- Jensen says AI will change every job, but "the task and the purpose of a job are not the same." Many tasks will be automated and some jobs will disappear, but many new jobs and industries will be created.
- Examples:
  - Software engineers use AI to expand the search for solutions and tackle more ambitious challenges.
  - Radiologists are elevated to better diagnose disease and care for patients.
  - Demand for both software engineers and radiologists continues to grow.
- "AI does not replace human purpose. It amplifies human capability."
- "AI is not likely to replace you. But someone using AI better than you might."
- Everyone becomes a programmer: a shopkeeper can create a website, and a carpenter can design a kitchen and offer new services. He says this can close the technology divide for the first time.

chunks.heading: The AI infrastructure buildout and advice to graduates
chunks.text:
- He says AI, like electricity and the internet, will need trillions of dollars of infrastructure investment: "the largest technology infrastructure buildout in human history."
- It is a chance to reindustrialize America and restore its capacity to build: chip factories, computer factories, data centers and advanced manufacturing. He addresses electricians, plumbers, ironworkers, technicians and builders directly: "this is your time."
- It also drives major energy investment: modernizing the grid, expanding power generation and accelerating sustainable energy.
- Advice to the Class of 2026:
  - "We are all standing at the same starting line."
  - "Run, don't walk."
  - Take up Carnegie Mellon's motto, "My heart is in the work," and "build something worthy of your education, your potential, and the people who believed in you long before the world did."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jensen explains AI from first principles: computing shifted from retrieval to real-time generation, so the world needs vast AI factories producing tokens, like the dynamo and the internet before. He gives a five-layer model for investing and argues task versus purpose shows AI elevates jobs.

chunks.heading: From retrieval to generation: why AI computing needs "factories"
chunks.text:
- Jensen says modern computing dates to the IBM System/360 in 1964. IBM was then the most valuable company in the world. The model stayed largely the same for about 60 years: pre-recorded computing.
- Under that model you write a story, program, photo, song or video, save it to a file, and retrieve it later. Recommender systems only make the retrieval smarter.
- That is why the buildings are called data centers. Jensen notes they are not called "computer centers", because they mostly store data.
- AI inverts this. Each time you use it, you supply context and a query, and the output is generated fresh for that circumstance.
- He argues that in future every pixel, sound, video, ad and story will be generated for the individual's context, not retrieved. That means far more "generators", which is what Nvidia builds.
- His first-principles lens: ask what happened to the computer that made this possible, not only what AI can do.

chunks.heading: What AI can do, and why agentic AI is the commercial turning point
chunks.text:
- Two years earlier, generative AI translated "anything to anything" (text to text, text to image, image to text). Jensen calls it interesting and "a little cute".
- Generation enabled internal thinking, step-by-step reasoning and problem-solving. It also enabled generating control commands to use tools such as a browser, spreadsheet, Photoshop, PowerPoint or AutoCAD.
- Generating commands for a mechanical system is robotics. Generating commands for a vehicle is self-driving cars.
- Value comes from work, not knowledge: "We love people who are know-it-alls, but we don't pay them for it. We pay for people who do work."
- Agentic systems (he names ChatGPT, Codex and Claude Code) now do useful work, and people pay for AI by the hour, for example "$30 an hour" or "$20 an hour". He calls it the fastest-growing software business in history.
- Nvidia runs hundreds of thousands of agents internally, all guard-railed and sandboxed, talking to each other and solving problems.
- He expects an internet used today by about a billion people to become mostly agents, possibly a hundred billion, working around the clock. Companies, employees, cars, robots, manufacturing systems and buildings would all be agentic.

chunks.heading: The AI factory as the new dynamo
chunks.text:
- Jensen compares three layers that "cocoon the planet": energy (the grid), communications (the internet) and now intelligence.
- The dynamo turns atoms (motion from water, wind, fire, steam) into electrons. An Nvidia AI factory turns electrons into numbers (tokens). Tokens can be recombined into language, math, proteins, human biology, physics, climate, 3D and robotics. "That's why I call it a factory."
- He expects intelligence to become a commodity used everywhere.
- Hardware figures he gave:
  - One rack holds 72 chips, weighs 2 tons, costs $4 million and has 1.5 million parts.
  - He calls it the most expensive piece of equipment in the world.
  - Nvidia manufactures about 8 million chips this year (his wording: "call it 8 million").
- Economics: each gigawatt of AI factory is about $50 billion. He says one such factory generates $300-400 billion in intelligence, so the return on investment is "extremely fast".

chunks.heading: The five-layer cake: where to invest in AI
chunks.text:
Jensen offers this as the industrial map for investing.

1. **Energy.** He calls it the greatest opportunity in generations for energy industries and the first time in roughly 100 years that grids in many countries can be invested in. Any form that produces energy will get funded: nuclear, wind, solar, hydrogen. He cites Siemens, Mitsubishi and GE Vernova as doing well.
2. **Chips, computers and networking.** This includes switches and silicon photonics.
3. **Infrastructure.** Land, power, shell, money and data center operations, all in scarce supply today.
4. **Models.** OpenAI and Anthropic are the two names people hear, but he says not to overlook everything else.
5. **Applications.** These are startups in financial services, legal, accounting, transportation and logistics. About $100 billion of venture capital went into this layer last year, which he calls the largest VC year in history.

Scale claims:
- About $1 trillion goes into the whole stack this year.
- He guesses the AI ecosystem could reach about $20 trillion a year. He frames this as a guess.
- He says it was zero two years ago.

chunks.heading: Models beyond language: anything with structure can be learned
chunks.text:
- Jensen says the model layer is more than the two language-model companies. AI can learn the meaning of anything with predictable structure.
- Examples: proteins, genes, cells, physics, 3D worlds and human anatomy. He asks what a gene or cell means, not only how to sequence or edit it.
- Learning the meaning of a cell is analogous to learning the meaning of a word. Combining two words creates a new meaning, and combining two cells does something similar.
- To the computer it is all tokens. Computer scientists must work out how to represent each domain's information so the machine can understand it, reason, plan and act. He calls this the "intelligence loop".
- Unpredictable things are hard to learn. He gives a quantum-like example: if people floated, had body parts in 17 places and could be seen through, there would be nothing to learn.
- He puts the physical-world industries at about $80 trillion and calls them the most important frontier, and one not much discussed.

chunks.heading: Jobs, task versus purpose, and the radiology example
chunks.text:
- Jensen's advice on fear: "You may or may not lose a job to an AI. But you will absolutely lose a job to someone who uses AI." He says he is certain of that for himself, so the first step is to make sure he uses AI.
- He calls the Terminator, singularity and "20% chance of ending humanity" narratives "complete nonsense". His argument that builders understand the technology is that it improves every year: "If you don't know how something works, how do you make it better?"
- He says the scare narrative can serve people who want to benefit from it themselves.
- Safety evidence he gives: hallucination has dropped to almost nothing compared with two years ago. Models now research, reflect on and question their own answers. He compares it to cars being both better and safer than 100 years ago.
- His two responsibilities:
  - The technology industry must build AI safely.
  - Everyone else must engage with AI and tell family, employers and countries to do the same.
- Task versus purpose:
  - A job is related to its tasks but not the same thing. His own CEO job involves typing and talking, which AI does at superhuman level, and he is busier than ever.
  - Radiology: a leading computer scientist warned about 10 years ago that it would be wiped out, and advised against entering the field. Computer vision did permeate every radiology stack, yet demand and headcount for radiologists rose.
  - The reason is that the purpose of a radiologist is to work with doctors to diagnose disease. Automation made departments more productive and profitable, so hospitals admitted more patients and hired more radiologists.
  - He says careless predictions did harm, because fewer people trained as radiologists.
  - Software engineering: he is hiring more engineers than ever. "Typing is not the job of a software engineer. Coding is not their job. Solving problems is their job."
- Elevating crafts: a plumber could become a designer, a carpenter a home designer, and a furniture salesperson an interior designer.
- Jobs created: he says the trillion-dollar buildout is creating more jobs than ever at every layer.

chunks.heading: Closing the technology divide
chunks.text:
- Jensen has spent about 40-odd years in computer design, during which computers grew more complex and the share of people who could program them shrank.
- He estimates that about 2% of society knows C++. Now anyone can program a computer in human language.
- He calls AI "the greatest force for eliminating the technology divide in my entire career" and says "We got to bring everybody with us."
- He says a country or company that does not invest in AI misses both the jobs boom and the elevation of its people.
- He tailored the talk to a global, mostly non-technical audience. The goal was to give them enough intuition to reason about their next investment, such as recognising when something that looks like a $100 billion market is actually far bigger.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jensen tells how NVIDIA's founding technology was wrong, how a Sega contract and three textbooks saved it, and why accelerating algorithm domains beat building chips. He covers first-principles curiosity, fitting the company to the founder, systems thinking, agents, physical AI, and resilience: get through today.

chunks.heading: NVIDIA started with the wrong technology and survived by learning
chunks.text:
- Jensen says the technology NVIDIA was founded on in 1993 was "absolutely wrong". The idea was to turn every PC into a game console by fitting a new 3D graphics algorithm, normally needing large supercomputers, into the PC.
- In 1995 he realised the algorithm did not work. By then some 35-40 other companies were building 3D graphics for PCs, so it was almost too late.
- He told the team the company would not exist unless it confronted the fact that this didn't work. Nobody on the team knew the right way to do it either.
- He spent a couple hundred dollars at Fry's on three OpenGL textbooks and gave them to the engineers. NVIDIA went on to become the world leader in modern computer graphics, "we learned it from a textbook".
- His lesson: technology changes all the time, so as long as you can confront reality and learn, the specific technology doesn't matter.

chunks.heading: The Sega contract that kept NVIDIA alive
chunks.text:
- Sega had contracted NVIDIA to build the console after Saturn, which became Dreamcast. The contract was worth $12 million.
