- Jensen flew to Japan and told Sega's CEO the technology was flawed and NVIDIA could not deliver. He advised Sega to choose someone else, then asked to keep the money anyway because NVIDIA still needed it.
- He says he was polite and humble, and the CEO recognised his honesty. Jensen's reading: "You don't invest in companies, you invest in people."
- That $5 million kept NVIDIA alive and bought time to find the right approach.
- Sega sold its NVIDIA stake when NVIDIA went public in 1999 at a $300 million valuation.

chunks.heading: What makes a great company: a unique perspective, and algorithms over chips
chunks.text:
- Jensen believes great companies come from "a unique perspective about the world that you deeply believe in", more than from technology or market alone. Right technology, right market and right time help, but the vision comes first.
- The best combination is a high-level vision of an important future, unique and deeply held, and ideally hard to pursue.
- NVIDIA's perspective: CPUs are useful, but accelerators can solve problems otherwise too hard to solve. Examples he names include 3D graphics, molecular dynamics, image processing, inverse physics, particle physics, fluid dynamics and deep learning.
- "It's not about building a great chip, it's about accelerating an algorithm domain." His lens is always to look for an algorithm (e.g. OpenGL, SQL, deep learning) and a problem NVIDIA can help solve.

chunks.heading: Seeing deep learning early, and first-principles reasoning
chunks.text:
- When AlexNet appeared, Jensen asked what the algorithm was, why it worked so well, what else it could do and what it could solve at scale.
- His insight was that AlexNet was not just AlexNet. Deep learning is a universal function approximator that can learn almost any function, and most interesting problems are imprecise anyway.
- About 15 years ago he started asking what this does to the whole computing stack: processor, middleware, algorithms and applications (the "five layer cake"). NVIDIA began work on computer vision, robotics and self-driving cars almost immediately.
- His method is first principles: "if this then what? If this can get better then so what?"
- Planning horizon: a system takes about three years to build, a couple more to ramp, and customers want to use it for 10 years. So NVIDIA has to "live in the future 5 to 10 years".
- Example: seeing early chain-of-thought work from Stanford led him to reason that self-driving might need less data. This led to Alpamayo, which he calls the world's first thinking self-driving car, good with only a million or a couple million miles of data because it uses prior knowledge like a human driver.

chunks.heading: Leading as a founder: curiosity, staying in the weeds, fitting the company to you
chunks.text:
- His starting point is curiosity. He seeks answers to his own questions, then learns the domain well enough to be of service to the company and share it. He calls this "a personality technique", not a management technique.
- Staying close to the technology matters because it changes fast. He compares it to surfing: you have to read the waves, the wind and timing, and you can't without actually doing it.
- Founders don't need to change their personality when they become CEO.
- His F1 metaphor: you are building a race car you can drive. "You should adapt the car to you." Asked what happens when he leaves, he says the next CEO can reshape the company to suit them.
- He is constantly tweaking the company and reshaping business processes so he can be more effective.
- On tools, NVIDIA lets "a thousand flowers bloom": people use Claude Code, Codex, Cursor or Cognition, and the company learns from all of it. Claude Code runs autonomously in sandboxes across NVIDIA.

chunks.heading: Agents, systems thinking and open source
chunks.text:
- Systems thinking is the skill he expects to matter most. Low-level work (chip synthesis, most software) gets automated by agents, so designers become systems designers. Questions: what is the problem, what are the constraints, where are input and output, what is the data rate, is the bottleneck processor, memory or networking.
- Agents already show a form of recursive self-improvement by updating markdown files and long-term memory. The biggest breakthrough needed is controllability: fine-grained control, e.g. changing one word in a plan file and getting a specific delta (one pixel, one CAD component, one via). Agents need not be 100% accurate; 80% or 99% with human help is usable.
- On OpenClaw he said "we just designed the modern computer", a "Linux moment". He told its creator Peter that all of NVIDIA's engineers were his engineers. NVIDIA also released a sandboxing toolkit around agent harnesses, and supports Hermes.
- He encourages everyone to use ChatGPT and Claude, and companies to build their own domain-specific AI with Hermes, OpenClaw, LangChain or Deep Agents. This is relatively easy because "the software is smart".
- He argues open source made modern AI possible (Linux, Kubernetes, PyTorch, TensorFlow, Caffe, Theano). He made his first X post in 2026 in support of open models.

chunks.heading: Jobs, physical AI and what to learn
chunks.text:
- AI automates tasks, not whole jobs. A job has a purpose made of many tasks. He argues "AI destroying jobs is exactly backwards".
- Examples he cites: software engineer jobs up 10% year over year despite automated coding; radiology jobs up some 20% in several years despite AI reading scans, because patient backlogs are huge; paralegal jobs growing, because lawsuit backlogs are high. Productivity drives growth, and growth drives employment.
- Physical AI: generating video of a hand picking up a glass made him see robot articulation as near. He says the "ChatGPT moment" of robots happened a couple of years ago.
- Robotics needs three things: real-to-sim environments, simulators (Isaac Sim, Cosmos) that mix physics-grounded and generative simulation, and sim-to-real via reinforcement learning grounded in physics.
- Self-driving was chosen first for its large market, standardised technology and real economic value. He open-sourced Alpamo because agriculture, mail delivery and warehouse robots each are too small alone to justify a stack. NVIDIA's physical AI business is about $10 billion and he calls it the "next hundred billion dollar business", taking more than 2-3 years but less than 10.
- Advice to students: simple work, including coding, gets automated. Hard problems stay: physics, chemistry, biology, computer science and engineering, systems thinking, the intersection of technology and social issues, and market gaps. Chip design went from about a thousand transistors to trillion-transistor chips because ambition scaled. "Stay in school."

chunks.heading: Advice to founders: "how hard can it be?" and resilience
chunks.text:
- Starting out, Jensen felt there was far too much to know and was scared to raise money because he couldn't answer investors' questions. He bought a 500-page book on starting a company and did not read it. He says "none of that stuff matters", and he still barely knows the answers today.
- He calls now the greatest time in 60 years to start a company, because the computer has been completely reset.
- His mindset: "This is important. I've got to go learn it... how hard can it be?" It will be "way harder than you think", so don't imagine all the difficulty at once and let it turn into anxiety. "Let the suffering come to you a little bit at a time."
- "Learning is the single greatest superpower." Believe that if anybody can do it, you can.
- On resilience: "You don't have to overcome life in one day. You just have to overcome that morning." He calls resilience probably the single most important thing and urges founders not to let fear, anxiety or lack of confidence stop them.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jensen breaks the AI capex question down from first principles, showing buildout doesn't hinge on two labs. He argues safety must accelerate with capability, and that Nvidia's moat grows through fungible, durable full-stack infrastructure. He also describes new software-licensing and revenue-share growth vectors.

chunks.heading: Why agents multiply compute demand: reasoning, harnesses and tool use
chunks.text:
- Jensen explains the "billion times more" compute claim with how thinking works. Early chatbots mostly regurgitated knowledge encoded in the model, then added a quick search to ground it. Real problem solving means reasoning step by step, generating several options, rolling them out, reflecting, pruning and repeating.
- He compares this to human strategy: "great strategists love strategic optionality." You don't prune too fast, but you still optimise resources. AIs now do the same, which costs far more compute.
- Demand compounds twice: each task uses more compute, and because AI does the job well, people hire it for more jobs.
- Last year's unlock was the harness, the "exoskeleton" around the language model. It has two parts:
  - **Memory:** working memory, short and long term, and offline knowledge-graph building, much like humans compact and consolidate memories when they sleep.
  - **Tool use:** agents learn the tools humans already built (SPICE, Verilog, simulators, design compilers, Photoshop, AutoCAD, Synopsys, Cadence, Siemens tools) rather than rebuilding them.
- Coding was the first on-ramp. Next come design, creative and marketing work, and science. He cites OpenAI's Astra turning a photo into CAD that engineers can then fine-tune.
- Open challenge: deploying agents safely and securely into enterprises.

chunks.heading: Falling cost of intelligence, Navier-Stokes and why demand is insatiable
chunks.text:
- Jensen notes the Navier-Stokes result did not come from nothing. It built on decades of mathematicians' foundational work, plus exhaustive AI search of a huge search space. Other fields are on similar precipices and need massive compute to get over.
- He expects the cost of intelligence to fall quickly: more compute comes online and smarter models are more efficient. The host's figure was about $4 million of compute for the Navier-Stokes instance, expected to drop 5-10x.
- Analogy to Moore's law: three decades of compute cost halving every year. He wants intelligence cost to fall 2x or 20x a year, because consumption "more than make[s] up for it."
- GPT-1 example: roughly $10-20 million to train then, about $100 now (his estimates, over about 10 years). Ambition rose just as fast: models are now 3, 10 and 30 trillion parameters, and use is up roughly a million times in 10 years.
- On Keynes's prediction of a 15-hour work week: he argues Keynes "got wrong... the human spirit." Work and discovery are purpose. Each thing you learn opens a new door with more opportunity and problems, so AI will create more ambition, not more leisure. He is working harder and having more fun than ever.

chunks.heading: Physical AI and the three-computer model
chunks.text:
- Jensen says NVIDIA did $10 billion in physical AI in the first six months of this year. Last year's first $10 billion year followed about $5 billion the year before. He says his earlier "$100 billion market" estimate was probably understated and calls NVIDIA the world's largest physical AI company.
- Physical AI covers the whole electromagnetic spectrum: CT machines, ultrasound, imaging radar, 5G sensing networks, satellites and 3D reconstruction, plus robotics, self-driving, warehouse and surgical robots. AI has three parts: perception, reasoning, and planning/actuation.
- His thesis is that industries that were mechanical or electrical become technology industries. Examples: Tesla remade cars into computing; FedEx, Walmart and every car company become AI/technology companies; telecoms (AT&T, Verizon) become technology industries again.
- Building a physical AI platform takes three computers:
  1. A training computer to create the brain.
  2. A digital twin, built on Omniverse, where the robot learns. Labs will also need a digital twin of the internet so agents don't learn on the live one.
  3. The computer inside the robot, car or surgical instrument.
- NVIDIA builds a full stack for each. Customers can take one, two or three: "We don't care." He thinks NVIDIA may eventually not be categorised as a chip company.

chunks.heading: Safety as engineering: containment, out-of-band monitoring, and winning
chunks.text:
- Jensen frames safety as something you build ("an engineering word") and says if it can't be built safely, it shouldn't be built.
- Perfect alignment is a "forever problem" because even "be successful in life" has endless interpretations. Waiting for it means never shipping. His approach mirrors raising children or hiring employees:
  - **Zero trust and containment:** start with minimum rights and tools, and expand access as you test and gain confidence.
  - **Out-of-band monitoring:** a system watched in-band behaves differently, like staff when the boss is in the room. The monitor must detect policy violations and be able to escalate or shut down.
  - He points to NVIDIA's recently announced OpenShell, with over 100 companies joining.
- Safety is part of AI technology, not separate, like airbags, ABS and radar in a car. "Accelerate" means accelerating safety and security too. Without them, "the functionality will never get a chance to speak."
- On the White House meeting, he says every lab leader was constructive and committed to being fast and safe. He says the industry has not been through a transition like this before, so it must prove usefulness first (reached about six months ago) and now deploy safely.
- He redefines "America winning" as every industry, state, county, company, school and citizen winning (Lilly, Walmart, FedEx, Boeing, the military), not only tech.
- On the three-legged security framework (frontier model review, the accord, the SI force): "argue about what is perfect versus what's first" and you never get there. Take action quickly, make it tangible with real teeth, and keep it dynamic. His advice to critics is to learn the problem and the existing solution, then be constructive.
- He is "99.99%" confident the outcome will be good. Smart people are doing smart things without him: "Smart people do smart things. They do more impactful things when you organize" them. Concern is good, but predicting the end of the world underestimates human capacity.

chunks.heading: Compute buildout bottlenecks and NVIDIA's resilience
chunks.text:
- Jensen agrees demand is there "and more." The binding constraint is land, power and shell (permitting, power generation, skilled trades, moratoriums). Moving from digital to physical creates many obstacles, and he expects land, power and shell to be hard next year.
- His mitigations:
  - NVIDIA serves every CSP, neocloud, enterprise (via Dell, HP, Lenovo) and industry across the full AI lifecycle, so if one site stalls, he re-allocates supply. Demand exceeds supply.
  - Global reach: Europe, Africa, Central Asia, Southeast Asia, Latin America and the Middle East. Two gigawatts were announced in Australia, about $80 billion to NVIDIA. He says he doesn't love that the US can't keep up.
- If power is scarce, buyers shift to the most productive compute (most tokens per watt), because CEOs must hit revenue targets. NVIDIA's share is rising even at its size.
- Content per gigawatt has risen from roughly $18 billion, to $20-something billion, to $40+ billion, as NVIDIA moved from GPUs to networking, CPUs, storage, knowledge infrastructure and security (OpenShell). He says it was $5 billion per gigawatt in the general-purpose era and about $50 billion for Vera Rubin.
- Share of capex: single digits six years ago; about 40% with CSPs now; about 80% outside CSPs (on-prem, neoclouds). Both halves of the business are doubling yearly.
- Remaining supply constraints include substrates (larger packages, warpage, thermal coefficients), silicon photonics and more. He told the market 18 months of work lay ahead, and says new orders arrive almost daily.
- Space data centres: he says only NVIDIA compute makes sense there, since high value per watt makes launch cost a small share. Work with Elon's team is on a new server architecture for space and Earth.

chunks.heading: Does AI revenue justify the capex? His three-segment answer
chunks.text:
- Jensen says NVIDIA is about 80% of AI infrastructure revenue share. He breaks the business into three roughly equal segments:
  1. **Classical computing, about a third:** data processing, simulation, XGBoost fraud detection, recommenders. Growing about 30-40% a year with no AI labs at all.
  2. **Frontier labs, about a quarter to 30%:** more than two, including Meta, Grok, Gemini and Anthropic (which started this year).
  3. **Next-generation startups and clouds, about a third:** thousands renting NVIDIA compute, "AWS for the future" (physical, biological and materials AI, Prometheus and others).
- His conclusion: "putting way too pressure on two labs." Don't extrapolate OpenAI or Anthropic revenue into multiple trillions. They will be hugely successful without it.
- Macro argument: infrastructure of $3-4 trillion a year by decade end (closer to four), of which about $1.5 trillion is compute. It was about half a trillion before AI. Moore's law is over, so twice the capacity now costs twice as much. He would not be surprised by roughly $10 trillion in annual capacity building and refresh.
- He advocates open models: about 80% of startups use them. They are not competing with frontier labs but customising models (including Nemotron) into domain "super intelligence" on proprietary data. Closed labs provide general intelligence; vertical companies go deep.

chunks.heading: Moat, fungibility and new business models
chunks.text:
- Jensen says the moat is increasing. The "$100 billion cheque" test: placing an order sight unseen for Vera Rubin Ultra, who else can you trust? Systems costing $50 billion cannot be benchmarked before purchase, and each generation is trusted because the last one (Grace Blackwell) delivered.
- Parallel with TSMC: NVIDIA gives it 100% of that business because he can plan five years out and trust the next process node, its capacity, its agility through his shifts and its scale.
- NVIDIA is infrastructure, so the pitch is risk reduction: CUDA runs pre-training, post-training, agentic inference and every new architecture (flash attention, sharding across NVLink 72, SSM hybrids). Fungibility across workloads, models, customers and geographies lowers risk.
- "Specialization is the enemy of fungibility" and of durability. His chain: fungibility and durability give rentability, then financeability, then lowest TCO. Software updates continue for GPUs sold eight years ago.
- Two new growth vectors beyond hardware sales:
  - **Software licensing for enterprises:** roughly a couple of thousand dollars per GPU per year (his simple math), with about 20 million GPUs shipped a year, half going to enterprises, who need NVIDIA to maintain, secure and support under an SLA.
  - **Revenue share with clouds** that rely on NVIDIA's offtake, ecosystem and financing help, in return for an investment and ongoing economics.
- Capital allocation: buybacks were over 50% of free cash flow, "60 some odd" last quarter. Ecosystem investments will shrink as a share of cash flow because "OpenAI and Anthropic isn't going to come around again," and because cash generation is growing fast.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jensen frames AI as a reinvention of the computing stack and a new industry that turns energy into digital intelligence. He shares leadership lessons: confidence without certainty, strength with vulnerability, reasoning in public, and serving others' success. He also covers robotics and universities.

chunks.heading: AI as a new industry that manufactures intelligence
chunks.text:
- Jensen says computer science has been reinvented: software used to be hand-coded (he started with Fortran, then Pascal, C and C++) and ran on CPUs. Now machines observe data, learn the patterns and relationships, and generate neural networks that run on GPUs.
- He breaks problem solving into three steps: perception, reasoning and planning. A self-driving car is a "digital chauffeur" and an AI reading a CT scan is a "digital radiologist".
- Many digital agents consuming a data center make it look like it is producing "tokens", meaning digital intelligence.
- His analogy is the AC generator. General Electric and Westinghouse built the generator and also invented its consumption (light bulbs, toasters). Copilot and ChatGPT are the light bulbs and toasters of AI, connected to a digital intelligence factory.
- He frames this as a new industry that takes energy in and puts digital intelligence out. It never existed before, just as AC power generation did not before it.
- He describes generative AI as a "universal translator": text to image, protein to text, text to chemicals. Being able to understand the meaning of difficult data helps a digital biologist find a needle in a haystack, a chip designer, or someone searching for new materials.

chunks.heading: Scaling laws and the million-times drop in the cost of computing
chunks.text:
- Moore's law rested on VLSI scaling (Carver Mead and Conway) and Dennard scaling. Doubling every 1.5 years gives about 10x every 5 years and 100x every 10 years.
- The AI scaling law is empirical: the bigger the neural network and the more data it is trained on, the more intelligent it seems. He says it appears to be continuing.
- He names three phases where more computation gives better answers:
  - **Pre-training:** learning from all the data. He compares it to graduating from college, a milestone that is "not enough".
  - **Post-training:** going deep into one domain, using reinforcement learning from human or AI feedback, synthetic data generation and multi-path learning. It is like choosing a career.
  - **Thinking (test-time scaling):** breaking a problem into first-principles steps, iterating and simulating outcomes. The longer it thinks, the higher the quality may be.
- He wants AI answers people "largely trust" rather than having to judge whether they are hallucinated. He says that is several years away, so computation must keep increasing.
- His view of NVIDIA's biggest contribution: over 10 years it cut the marginal cost of computing by a million times. When the cost of something falls that far, habits change. Researchers no longer think twice about having a machine learn exhaustively from enormous data, and that is why machine learning took off.

chunks.heading: Leading for decades: learning, confidence, vulnerability and serving others
chunks.text:
- He started NVIDIA without ever taking a business course and says he has never written a business plan.
- He treats NVIDIA as his "life's work", not a job. He says this mindset matters whether you are a carpenter, an artist or a neurosurgeon.
- A CEO must reinvent themselves constantly. What you know today will be useful but "not even nearly enough". He learns every day, for example by using an AI as a tutor. He asks it why it gave an answer, for step-by-step explanations and for analogies, and says "I torture my AI to teach me."
- **Confidence is not certainty.** A leader can be fully confident in a direction and still leave room for uncertainty, which lets them keep learning. "Uncertainty is your friend not your enemy."
- **Strength is not the absence of vulnerability.** People feed off a leader's strength, but a leader who needs help should ask for it. He says he asks for help constantly.
- **Decide for others, not yourself.** Leaders are trusted when every decision serves the mission and other people's success: colleagues, partners, the ecosystem and the supply chain. When asked what to do in a discussion with a key partner, he asks what is in the partner's best interest and decides from there.

chunks.heading: Flat organisation: 60 direct reports and reasoning in the open
chunks.text:
- He has about 60 direct reports, and he corrected Harry's figure of 50.
- He reasons through strategy in front of everyone, so the whole team hears the same thing at the same time. It is not "I went into a forest and came back out with an answer."
- He usually speaks last, to state the direction and priorities and remove any ambiguity.
- Once aligned, he counts on everyone being an adult. They should say when they don't know something and ask for help. "Nobody loses alone, nobody fails alone."
- When the CEO shows it is fine to be vulnerable, uncertain or wrong, everyone else can do the same. He calls his staff the best in the world, people who "don't need my help" beyond that.

chunks.heading: AI for science, emulation and building a medical school
chunks.text:
- He introduced AI at the supercomputing conference in 2018 and met great skepticism because AI was a black box. He says it is more explainable now: you can probe an AI the way a professor probes a student, asking it to reason step by step.
- AI emulates the physics from observed data and does not solve from first principles. He argues emulation is invaluable, because we know equations like Schrödinger's and Maxwell's but cannot simulate large systems with them.
- Human biology spans nanometers to years, and first-principles solvers cannot handle that. His hope is a digital twin of human biology, so digital biologists and climate scientists can understand large multiscale systems for the first time.
- For HKUST's new medical school he sees a rare chance. Most hospitals started as hospitals and then tried to insert technology, which met skepticism and distrust. HKUST can build from the ground up with technology and AI as the founding expertise, by people who understand its limits and potential.

chunks.heading: Universities need shared AI supercomputers
chunks.text:
- He says AI supercomputers are the instruments of science today, like radio telescopes or particle accelerators. Advancing science at scale is impossible without machine learning, and that needs machines.
- The structural problem is that each principal investigator raises their own funding and then won't share it. Machine learning needs a gigantic machine for a short time, and nobody needs all of it forever.
- Computer science researchers at Stanford or Harvard can raise a lot. Researchers in climate or ocean science struggle.
- His fix is to pool funding and build infrastructure for the whole school. Researchers also intern at companies like NVIDIA, Google and Microsoft to use their infrastructure, and professors do part-time visiting research.
- His advice: universities have to rethink how they do funding.

chunks.heading: Energy use: the goal of AI is inference
chunks.text:
- He argues that if the world uses more energy to power AI factories, "we are a better world when that happens."
- Three points:
  - The goal of AI is to use the model (inference), not to train it. Inference is very efficient and could discover ways to store carbon dioxide, new wind turbine designs, and better materials for energy storage and solar panels.
  - AI doesn't care where it goes to school. Supercomputers can sit slightly off the grid and use sustainable energy, away from where people live.
  - AI can make a heavily over-provisioned power grid smarter and cut waste. He hopes it saves 20-30%.
- His conclusion: using energy for intelligence is the best use of energy.

chunks.heading: Robotics, physical AI and the Greater Bay Area
chunks.text:
- Today's language models understand cognitive knowledge but not physical intelligence, such as a cup not passing through a table. AI must be taught the physical world.
- His reasoning: if generative AI can produce a video of him picking up a coffee cup from a prompt, it can generate the tokens that make a robot arm do it. He says the leap to general robotics is "very very close".
- Robots scale only with a technology flywheel: high volume funds high R&D, which brings breakthroughs and better products, which raises volume further.
- He says only three robot types can reach high volume, because they can be deployed into the world as it is today (brownfield deployment): cars, drones and humanoid robots. Humanoids will be the highest volume, because we built the world for ourselves.
- The Greater Bay Area is the only region where mechatronics and AI technology reside together. Japan and Germany are strong in mechatronics but "quite far behind on AI". He urges the region to lean in.

chunks.heading: Advice for students and founders
chunks.text:
- He started NVIDIA after promising his future wife Lori that he would be a CEO by 30, which he calls his pickup line, and he says he had no idea what he was talking about at the time. He tells students that dating won't hurt their studies.
- Keep learning constantly, and treat your work as your life's work.
- Be confident without needing certainty, and be strong without hiding vulnerability.
- Ask for help early, and make decisions in the interest of the mission and other people's success.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jensen explains why NVIDIA reinvented the whole computer stack for deep learning, why AI is an iPhone moment and a new industrial revolution of producing intelligence, and how company character, forged by 15 years of adversity, drives lasting success. He closes with advice to think from first principles.

chunks.heading: Building the first AI supercomputer (DGX) from first principles
chunks.text:
- In 2016 Nvidia was getting into AI itself and working on autonomous vehicles. Jensen says the team asked what kind of computer is needed for "this new way of doing software".
- AlexNet was the trigger. It was built for computer vision, shattered records set by decades of computer science, and needed Nvidia GPUs to produce.
- Nvidia reasoned about the implications for everything, from chips to systems, operating systems, data centers, networking, algorithms and applications. It concluded a new type of computer had to be created.
- The result was DGX, a deep learning system and "AI supercomputer". Jensen announced it as something built for Nvidia itself, expecting only some interest. He then delivered the first one outside the company to OpenAI in 2016.
- The rethink went chip by chip:
  - The CPU was no longer the ideal processor, so the GPU evolved into an AI processor. A graphics chip built to simulate the virtual world turned out to be a near-perfect starting point for understanding the world.
  - The PC architecture suits personal computing, not giant AI systems that learn from data. The IO and networking had to change.
  - Nvidia bought Mellanox to change how computers connect, so that millions of GPU cores work together instead of a handful of CPU cores.
- Why it is hard: a phone or PC application fits in a few gigabytes. GPT-3 has 175 billion parameters, fits on no phone or single PC, needs a giant data center to train, and many computers to run. Training takes weeks, so shaving off half the time is measured in weeks.
- One of his illustrations of the scale of chip R&D: the R&D budget for one of Nvidia's chip generations is probably around $5 billion, which he says is more than building a rocket.

chunks.heading: Why AI is an "iPhone moment" and the next industrial revolution
chunks.text:
- Jensen's pattern from about 40 years in computing: a platform grows slowly and linearly, then phase-shifts abruptly, like water turning to ice. Examples:
  - The PC existed about 10 years before Windows 95 changed everything.
  - The internet was used by researchers for 5-8 years before Mosaic and Yahoo.
  - Cloud and the iPhone followed the same pattern.
- Each transition makes computers easier to program. Mainframe applications are few, while iPhone applications number over five million.
- AI is the first computer anyone can program with human language, with no Python, C or Java needed. He says the number of people who can program went from tens of millions to several billion, closing the technology divide.
- Industrial revolution framing: the last one produced steam and electricity, and mass-produced physical goods. This one produces information and intelligence. "The production of intelligence is going to be what all companies do in the future."
- Nvidia runs AI factories. Data goes in, improved software comes out every day, and the software helps design chips, run self-driving cars, do computer-vision quality inspection and build better software.
- Companies hold deep domain knowledge, and AI puts that knowledge in every employee's hands.
- On timing and innovation: he says the insight behind ChatGPT was seeing that the technology was close to useful. The jump from GPT-2 to GPT-3 turned a marginally useful product into an incredibly useful one. The iPhone, PC, internet and Google search followed the same pattern: "the innovators are the ones that realize the timing is now" and industrialize it.
- He calls ChatGPT "unquestionably the single best software product the world's ever made". His reasons are that it does surprisingly amazing things, is the easiest product on the planet to use, has no manual, and had been used by over 100 million people.

chunks.heading: Productivity gains: chips, climate and software engineering
chunks.text:
- **Chip design:** Nvidia's chips are the largest and most complex in the world, now impossible to build without AI. He compares it to organising a city 1,000 times bigger than New York, placing every building and routing traffic and infrastructure. The chips are a couple of inches per side, about two-thirds the area of a coaster.
- **Weather and climate:** AI that simulates weather multi-physics is already 10,000 to 50,000 times faster than numerical methods. His point is that you can't act well on a problem you can't simulate, and a simulator helps decide where to put resources. It also helps with infrastructure, flooding and dams, insurance, agriculture and regional impact, and it uses less energy.
- **Software engineering:** software engineers are Nvidia's single greatest expense. Microsoft estimated that some 40-50% of code on GitHub is produced by AI (Copilot-style program completion). Jensen says Nvidia's estimate is that it will improve its engineers' productivity by a factor of 10.
- He declines to put a number on society-wide productivity gains.
- He sees a particular opportunity for countries without many computer scientists, and names India, Southeast Asia and Africa. Developed countries gain from lower cost and acceleration.
- On jobs: "it's less likely that in the near term that AI is going to displace our jobs, it's more likely that someone uses AI is going to displace our jobs." Some jobs change, some are created (such as AI data scientists), and some are displaced. Society should understand and adopt the technology fast.

chunks.heading: Where AI goes next: digital biology, world models and assistants
chunks.text:
- **Digital biology and drug discovery:**
  - Having learned the language of humans, AI has now learned the language of proteins and chemicals.
  - A protein's 3D shape determines its function, as a plier differs from a hammer.
  - From a desired function, AI can synthesize candidate proteins with better solubility, or proteins that capture energy from light or break down plastics and oil spills.
  - Drug discovery is expensive, slow and low in success rate, and this improves the odds.
- **Intelligence as perception, reasoning and planning:**
  - Progress on perception is strong. The goal is a model of the world, both static and dynamic ("if I did this, what would happen to that").
  - There are many worlds at different scales (human, molecular, atomic, galactic), sometimes needing different physics.
  - Reasoning must achieve objectives within core values and principles, keep people safe, and be explainable, interpretable and transparent.
  - Planning must be efficient and cost-effective.
  - AI is progressing along all three, with robotics and autonomous vehicles as examples.
- **Multimodality:** GPT-4 learns from language and images together. His example is that if you know horses and are told a zebra is a horse with black and white stripes, you can imagine a zebra you've never seen.
- **Digital assistants:** he expects personal assistants and group or company assistants for HR, IT and programming. Assistants could also model a company's business or the effectiveness of a new product.

chunks.heading: Regulation, openness and the societal view
chunks.text:
- Jensen says AI is powerful and can be used for harm, so regulation is necessary: "We regulate salmon for God's sake, we should regulate AI." He says governments have no choice but to step in, as with food, drugs, transportation, chemicals, electricity and broadcasting.
- Regulators should engage with the technology and put guardrails in place so it advances helpfully. He says there were none in place at the time.
- He notes that regulating free expression is hard, but what generative AI produces can be regulated, since there are things it should not generate.
- He wants the technology democratized as best as possible, and says it is less good if it lands in the hands of one company.
- Whether OpenAI stays open is "a company choice", and he says they have the right to do that. He adds that plenty of large language models are open, so access is not what holds anyone back. What matters is "the willpower" and the insight on timing.
- He sees fake news as a real harm, since AI can generate it and also detect it.
- He is cautious on geopolitics and says it is hard to say how AI will change US-China relations.

chunks.heading: Building a company that lasts: character, resilience and "how hard can it be"
chunks.text:
- Nvidia was started in 1993 when Jensen was 30. He says nobody in the company knew how to build a company, he didn't know how to be a CEO, and he had never used a PC.
- Skills like raising money, organising the company and recruiting were learned along the way. He says skills are learnable.
- The entrepreneur's attitude is "how hard can it be?" He applied it to learning the PC, building a company, hiring, and later to AI, scientific computing and autonomous vehicles. "It turns out all of those things were super hard", but he says you want to go in with that attitude. He pairs it with reasoning from first principles and learning as fast as possible.
- What made Nvidia successful, in his view:
  - A perspective on the future that spans a long arc and is directionally right. He says Nvidia's was.
  - Above all, the character of the company: how resilient it is, how it handles adversity and new assumptions, and how agile it is when the world changes.
- Culture is people: "It's not made of the document that describes the culture", nor the core values inscribed on the building. It is how people overcame existential crises, through their agility, cleverness, ingenuity and will.
- The values of learning and agility are installed by talking about them, teaching them and living them.
- Nvidia suffered greatly in its first 15 years, with one adversity after another. Five, six or seven times it was existential. He credits that suffering for the company's strong chance of long-term success.
- He describes corporate character as "the utter incredible ability to suffer", doing something even in extraordinary pain.
- On his own persistence, he quotes his 2003 Stanford line: "my will to survive exceeds almost everybody else's will to kill me". He says that once he believes in something he keeps doing it until the company is great at it, and he is hard to discourage or distract.

chunks.heading: Jensen's work habits and advice to young people
chunks.text:
- **Work habits:**
  - He describes himself as focused, curious and a perfectionist.
  - He distinguishes hard work from "insanely hard work", and puts himself in the second category.
  - He wakes at 5am and starts working immediately, works every day, and is asleep by around 9:30pm. He values sleep.
  - He relaxes through work (solving problems and achieving things), reading and family time.
  - He recently read *Chip War* and skims many AI papers, trying to understand all of them.
- **Advice to young people:**
  - Be a learner.
  - Above all, "think from first principles". He says most advice he received over the years was irrelevant because it was an opinion, a perspective of the time, or based on wrong assumptions.
  - He is sceptical of "find something you love". He says he loved every job he had (dishwasher, busboy, paper delivery, waiter), and every day at Nvidia.
  - His alternative is to fall in love with what you're doing. Once you desperately want to do a good job at it, doing it well and doing it hard comes more easily.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jensen explains how he reasons from first principles, runs about 60 direct reports, refuses to fill a chair with the wrong person, and builds corporate character through shared pain. He also covers ignorance as a superpower, CEO vulnerability, and why AI makes problems look smaller and people busier.

chunks.heading: Inventing technology, products, strategies and markets (NVIDIA's founding approach)
chunks.text:
- Jensen says NVIDIA is built to invent technology, then products to carry it to market, then strategies, then ecosystems and markets. He notes many inventors never had product inventors alongside them.
- In 1993 NVIDIA wanted to reinvent computing. The view was unpopular and controversial for a long time, in the era of CPUs, Moore's law and the PC revolution. Early customers were PC chipset startups such as Cirrus Logic, S3, Western Digital and Trident.
- He says it took 33 years to happen, and for the world it "happened very suddenly", with a change in November 2023.
- "In order to create the future you have to live in the future long before it happens."
- The "CUDA everywhere" strategy: he took CUDA to universities, startups, established companies, researchers, labs and conferences, sometimes to an audience of three people, pulling out his laptop to present. "You tell the story long enough, you kind of feel like it's happened."
- He says NVIDIA is the smallest GPU company by volume, even though it invented the GPU. So volume is not what makes it work.

chunks.heading: First-principles reasoning and spotting phase changes
chunks.text:
- Belief should not rest on anecdote ("somebody said something"). Break reasoning down into sound first principles, anchored in physics or ground truth, and check them regularly. If they change, re-evaluate and move on.
- "If you believe in something, you owe it to yourself to do something about it."
- He constantly re-reasons through the past: which assumptions were right, which were wrong, how the company readjusted. He says this teaches you how to reason forward.
- Phase-change idea: make something a thousand times faster, larger or smaller and a phase change happens, with a surprising result.
- Why the company pivoted behind deep learning: AlexNet couldn't be the end of it, the architecture scales, and data is abundant. The expected obstacle was needing human labels, because humans would be the bottleneck. When self-supervised learning arrived, "I knew we were off to the races", and the scaling laws were unleashed.
- He says the first-principles foundations are fundamental computer science, not hunches or taste, so what is happening now is "in a lot of ways inevitable".
- Computers are learning the languages of proteins, cells and quantum systems, and representations such as 3D Gaussian splats. He compares it to the movie Arrival.

chunks.heading: Staying an "employee", the empty chair and 60 direct reports
chunks.text:
- Jensen's line to Jodi Shelton in the 1990s: NVIDIA is "neither a church nor a prison". You don't have to come and you don't have to stay.
- He says the CEO reports to the board and can be let go, so it is an employment in an institution. He feels like an employee of the company, which keeps him grounded and humble. "I don't love my job every day, but I do it to my mightiest every day." He has to earn being the best person for the job every day.
- He was "raised by the company". On day one he couldn't form a company strategy, talk to shareholders, or build a culture.
- He has almost 60 direct reports, whom he describes as potential world-class CEOs elsewhere. He reasons in front of them about every decision, including successes, setbacks and adversity, so "NVIDIA has 61 CEOs".
- Hiring: "An empty chair is better than a chair filled with the wrong person." He is never in a hurry because the company keeps moving and people swarm the mission. Worst case he does it himself.
- On Colette Kress, the CFO (the host says he interviewed 22 CFOs; he doesn't give a number): in her first week she asked how long he wanted her as CFO and he answered "for as long as we shall live". The end date is only when she decides NVIDIA is no longer right for her.
- He doesn't have a formula for a great employee or leader. Everyone is smart and competent. What makes the difference is chemistry and corporate character.

chunks.heading: Character, pain and suffering, and a safe place to drop passes
chunks.text:
- Getting Grace Blackwell into production "almost broke our company's back, but we wouldn't let it." He calls that 100% character, not intelligence or hard work, and says character can't be interviewed into existence.
- He believes you can bring almost anyone in and NVIDIA will instill character. The company "tortured greatness out of us" and forged character into everyone, and none of the 60 are the same people as when they started.
- Most companies lose someone after a hard stretch through blame or firing. NVIDIA keeps the team together.
- "It's always somebody's fault": the team loses together but everyone knows who dropped the pass. Nobody is fired for dropping passes, and he says he has dropped plenty. The culture is tolerance, forgiveness and learning from mistakes, as long as teammates gave everything.
- What he looks for: not a jerk, not self-serving, can answer simple questions, wants to be on the team, is transparent, vulnerable and willing to learn. "They don't have to know it all, they just have to learn it all."
- Pain and suffering is described half-jokingly as NVIDIA's "secret sauce". Fear and anxiety are real when you hold the lives of tens of thousands of people. A leader who feels none of it is a bad leader.
- His pet peeve is someone who won't answer the question asked in a hard moment, when the team needs facts fast.

chunks.heading: Wisdom, ignorance and having no endgame
chunks.text:
- On whether you must sacrifice your 20s: he thinks it is a mistake to assume so, citing Morris Chang working into his 80s. In his 20s he thought faster and concentrated harder. Now he is slower but reaches right answers faster because of wisdom, patterns and strategic thinking. He will "go toe-to-toe with a 20-year-old all day long".
- Wisdom and grit about pain can be partly learned through imitation (reading, watching), but the emotional toll can't be learned without going through it.
- "Ignorance is a superpower." If he had known everything he knows now, he would never have built NVIDIA. His attitude was "how hard can it be?" He says it is impossible to build NVIDIA, but no one convinced him because he didn't know better.
- He worries about a generation made cynical by seeing too much. People need to build an internal reserve of optimism and goodness.
- NVIDIA has no endgame: "Staying in business is our plan." He has future dreams of the world but no life goals beyond staying employed and doing good work with amazing people.

chunks.heading: Childhood lessons on expectations and will
chunks.text:
- His mother kept telling him he was incredibly smart, which put a burden on him to live up to it. He thinks setting expectations "beyond reason" on people or a company can make them rise to it.
- His mother, who did not speak English, taught the children English every day with a Webster's dictionary, writing each word and its Chinese translation on folded paper. His lesson: not knowing how shouldn't stop you.
- In 1973 he was the first Chinese kid in Kentucky and the youngest at Oneida Baptist Institute. At age 9 he crossed a hanging bridge with missing planks every day, rougher kids waiting on the other side, and cleaned bathrooms as his school job.
- He describes himself as not an outlier in intelligence, with intensity and care that are hard to hire into.

chunks.heading: How AI changes the next five years
chunks.text:
- Computers will shift from being programmed to programming themselves under guidance: you tell them to go learn Japanese rather than teaching it.
- Faster tools make problems look smaller, like Mach 10 planes shrinking the world. Once all of the internet's data looked "tiny", researchers could feed it to a computer. Problem sizes could be a billion times larger. Many solvable problems are limited by our imagination in formulating them.
- He expects effects across digital biology, physical sciences, material sciences, traffic and smart grids (less over-provisioned energy). Companies will be more productive and profitable. NVIDIA still releases once a year but can try many more design iterations.
- Jobs: "100% of the world's jobs will change" is more likely than half being lost. More solvable problems means more work. Thought experiment: if answers come back in a second, he becomes the critical path and is busier than ever.
- He is surrounded by 60 people better than him in their fields, and uses AIs that are already smarter than him in ways, with no trouble working with either.
- AI closes the technology divide, e.g. vibe coding. He cites Cursor and Lovable, and says Lovable's CEO told him users built small businesses making $23 million a year.
- He hopes for household robots (the Disney robots he brings on stage at GTC) and thinks they could help lonely, aging people. In five years the computer is still a computer and applications are just smarter.

chunks.heading: Leadership as vulnerability, and what "smart" means
chunks.text:
- CEOs are surprisingly vulnerable: "I'm the only person in the company who can't get anything done without other people's help." He often opens conversations with "I need your help" and people have been generous.
- The job is lonely "in our heads": he has talked to himself for thousands of hours through every phase shift and reinvention.
- He wants others to succeed for their own sake, and says that is part of why he gives people undivided attention. He also describes respect for craft, such as watching people cook.
- His definition of smart: technical skill combined with human empathy and the ability to infer the unspoken and see around corners. He calls pure problem-solving intelligence a commodity, noting software programming is the first thing AI is solving.
- Public speaking scares him. He says company meetings and GTC keynotes stress him more than earnings week. He won't regurgitate old talks, so each has to be fresh, genuine and useful. He calls himself a "highly reluctant CEO" but an enthusiastic NVIDIA builder.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jensen explains designing NVIDIA from first principles: attract great people with barely-possible problems, stay small and flat, skip one-on-ones and status reports, plan continuously, and empower people by avoiding commodity work and sharing information openly.

chunks.heading: Staying technically current to lead a technology company
chunks.text:
- Jensen says he is "surrounded by amazing people" who are generous teachers, and he dedicates himself to "being a good student". He loves teaching great students, and he treats learning as an effort he has to make.
- NVIDIA works across many domains, from self-driving cars to climate research to digital biology. Jensen says that breadth is why he has to keep learning.
- In a tech-driven industry, he says leaders must understand the underpinnings of the technology. That gives an intuition for how the industry will change, and for which technology is "a little bit of a left turn" and which is fundamental.
- Example: generative adversarial models, variational autoencoders and diffusion models are "cousins of each other". Seeing the impact of one can lead to a breakthrough in another, as with today's diffusion models.
- Intuition lets you extrapolate and "see down the road". This matters because solutions take several years to build, on top of technology that changes "by a factor of a thousand every few years".

chunks.heading: Designing the company from first principles
chunks.text:
- Jensen starts company design from first principles: what machine are we creating, what is the input and output, what are the conditions, and is the industry fast-moving, bureaucratic or regulated.
- Goal one: a company that naturally attracts amazing people. NVIDIA's mission is to solve computing problems that are "barely possible". If normal computers can solve a problem, NVIDIA doesn't do it.
- Goal two: a company as small as possible, "as large as necessary to do the job well" but no larger.
- To empower people, he makes the organisation as flat as possible so information travels quickly. A pyramid is for command and control, "all the way back to the Roman Empire".
- There are no business units and no divisions. "Everybody works as one." The company is shaped to build accelerated computing fast. He jokes it would struggle with fried chicken, and have "no chance" with Swedish meatballs.

chunks.heading: Flat organisation: many direct reports, no one-on-ones
chunks.text:
- Jensen has no one-on-ones. The host puts it at about 40 direct reports, and he agrees with "something like that".
- Reasoning: the first layer is the most senior people, who need the least management. None of his management team comes for career advice. They are experts who are "fabulously happy" and know what they are doing.
- Strategic direction goes to everyone at once. After strategising, he tells everybody at the same time, takes feedback and refines it. He asks why he would tell one person.
- Flatness, wide access to information and empowered staff make the company agile. He calls the "algorithm" well conceived and the architecture well implemented.
- The practical difficulty is getting all direct reports in one room. The odds of everybody being in the office at once are "approximately 0%".

chunks.heading: Direct communication, reasoning out loud, and ground truth in the room
chunks.text:
- Jensen says he has no leadership style: "It's just me." If he dislikes a direction or has a different opinion, he says so openly. He does not take people aside or do one-on-one coaching. He admits this can be "a little too direct".
- He reasons through decisions in every meeting: why he decided something, and how the ideas compare and contrast. This teaches employees how leaders think through problems, which he sees as empowering.
- His meetings are not limited to vice presidents or directors. New college graduates and people from every organisation sit in.
- He wants the person who is most informed, best skilled or most experienced, the one who "actually made the mess" or confronted the situation. "You want ground truth."

chunks.heading: Top Five Things instead of status reports
chunks.text:
- Jensen reads no status reports. By the time one reaches him it is meta information: distilled, biased and given a perspective, so he is no longer looking at ground truth.
- Instead, anyone can send an email called "Top Five Things": whatever they observed, did or learned. It can include a great restaurant or a new baby.
- Each person sends their own version, from the edge inward. It is not one shared thread. He reads about a hundred every morning.
- He keeps his own top five private. He compares it to IoT: sending his out "from the center" would contaminate the system.
- He uses the emails to check strategy. "Strategy is not words, strategy is action." If people's top five things don't reflect the strategy, they are not executing it, and what they do is the real strategy.
- He doesn't read them all every week. He samples "sporadically and stochastically" to sense whether the company is heading where everyone agreed.

chunks.heading: Continuous planning and changing your mind
chunks.text:
- NVIDIA has no periodic planning system, no five-year plan and no one-year plan. "There's just what we're doing." The world is "a living, breathing thing", so planning is continuous.
- He calls five-year plans "horrible for technology" and "ridiculous".
- Big bets should be reasoned from first principles, starting with the key assumptions behind believing that the computer, chip architecture, software development or data center must change.
- Example: every company will have data centers that are not centers for data but factories that produce intelligence. Data comes in, is refined by the computer, and "intelligence" comes out. He formed this view by working backwards from first principles.
- Then he pursues it with dedication and conviction, even when it is hard. If he is wrong, he says so ("That was goofy") and changes his mind.
- Because the company replans constantly, people may not notice that he "adapted 17 times in the last year" or changed his mind "maybe 35 times". He thinks this makes leadership easier.

chunks.heading: Empowering people to do their life's work
chunks.text:
- Jensen says it is a leader's mission to create the environment for others to do their life's work.
- Most important: don't make people do commodity work. NVIDIA never talks about market share. Market share implies many others doing the same thing, so he asks why he would squander talented people on work already done. He prefers to do things never done before.
- He shows this by walking away from commoditised businesses. NVIDIA has done so many times, by its own initiative or otherwise, and employees see that it won't do commodity work.
- He encourages transparency and says NVIDIA has few secrets, because siloed information disempowers people.
- He says that a sense of hierarchy is not empowering, but anyone, including a new college grad, being able to contribute in a meeting is.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jensen tells three NVIDIA stories: admitting the Sega console architecture was wrong and asking for help, persevering through years of CUDA losses to create accelerated computing, and abandoning the phone market to create robotics. He frames AI as a rebirth of computing and urges graduates to run after their ideas.

chunks.heading: Company purpose: helping great minds do their life's work
chunks.text:
- Jensen opens with a story about Dr Chang at National Taiwan University (NTU). Chang built a homemade supercomputer out of Nvidia GeForce gaming cards in open PC motherboards, on metal shelves, cooled by oscillating fans. He did it after his son in Silicon Valley told him about CUDA.
- Chang told him: "Because of your work I can do my life's work in my lifetime."
- Jensen says this "perfectly capture[s] our company's purpose": to help the "Einstein and da Vinci of our time do their life's work."

chunks.heading: Story 1: Admitting the wrong strategy and asking for help (Sega and Riva 128)
chunks.text:
- Nvidia was founded to create accelerated computing. Its first application was 3D graphics for PC gaming.
- It used an unconventional approach called forward texture mapping and curves, which was substantially lower cost. It won a contract to build Sega's game console. That attracted games to the platform and funded the company.
- After one year of development, Jensen realized the architecture was the wrong strategy:
  - It was technically poor.
  - Microsoft was about to announce Windows 95 Direct 3D, based on inverse texture mapping and triangles.
  - Many companies were already building 3D chips for that standard.
  - Finishing the console would have meant inferior technology, incompatibility with Windows and no way to catch up.
  - Not finishing meant running out of money. Either way, Nvidia would be out of business.
- He told Sega's CEO that the approach was wrong, that Sega should find another partner, and that Nvidia could not complete the contract. He still needed Sega to pay in full or Nvidia would fail. He was embarrassed to ask.
- The Sega CEO agreed. His understanding and generosity gave Nvidia "six months to live."
- With that time Nvidia built Riva 128. It shocked the young 3D market, put Nvidia on the map and saved the company. Demand for the chip took Jensen back to Taiwan to meet Morris Chang at TSMC, starting a partnership that has lasted 25 years.
- Lesson: "confronting our mistake and with humility asking for help saved Nvidia." He says these traits are the hardest for the brightest and most successful people.

chunks.heading: Story 2: Creating a new computing model with CUDA
chunks.text:
- Nvidia announced CUDA, GPU-accelerated computing, in 2007. The aim was a programming model to boost applications from scientific computing and physics simulation to image processing.
- Jensen calls creating a new computing model "incredibly hard and rarely done in history". The CPU model had been the standard for 60 years, since the IBM System/360.
- The chicken-and-egg problem:
  - CUDA needed developers to write applications.
  - Developers needed a large installed base.
  - A large installed base needed customers buying new applications.
- Solution: use GeForce, the gaming GPU with an already large market of gamers, to build the CUDA installed base.
- The cost was very high. Profits took a huge hit for many years. Market cap hovered just above one billion dollars. Shareholders were skeptical and preferred a focus on profitability.
- Nvidia persevered because it believed the time for accelerated computing would come:
  - It created the GTC conference and promoted CUDA "tirelessly" worldwide.
  - It worked with each developer to write their algorithms and achieved large speedups.
  - Applications arrived one science domain at a time: seismic processing, CT reconstruction, molecular dynamics, particle physics, fluid dynamics and image processing.
- In 2012, AI researchers discovered CUDA. AlexNet, trained on GeForce GTX 580, started the "Big Bang of AI."
- Nvidia recognized deep learning as a whole new software approach and "turned every aspect of our company" toward it. Jensen says it "risked everything", and a decade later the AI revolution began.
- He says the journey "forged our corporate character to endure the pain and suffering that is always needed to realize a vision."

chunks.heading: Story 3: Strategic retreat from mobile phones to create robotics
chunks.text:
- In 2010 Google wanted Android to become a mobile computer with excellent graphics. Nvidia's computing and graphics expertise made it a fit. It entered the mobile chip market and was instantly successful, and its business and stock price surged.
- Competition swarmed in. Modem chip makers were learning to build computing chips while Nvidia was learning to build modems. The phone market was huge and Nvidia could have fought for share.
- Jensen instead sacrificed the market. His reasoning: Nvidia's mission is to build computers that solve problems ordinary computers cannot, so it should dedicate itself to its vision and a unique contribution.
- By leaving, Nvidia "opened our minds to invent a new one." It imagined a new type of computer for robotics, with neural network processors and safety architectures. At the time this was a "zero billion dollar market."
- Today Nvidia has billions of dollars of automotive and robotics business and started a new industry.
- Principle: "strategic retreat, sacrifice, deciding what to give up is at the very core of success." Retreat does not come easily to the brightest and most successful people.

chunks.heading: View on AI as a new computing era (2023)
chunks.text:
- Jensen calls AI the start of a major technology era, after PC, internet, mobile and cloud. He says it is "far more fundamental" because every computing layer has been reinvented, from how software is written to how it is processed. He calls it a rebirth of the computer industry.
- Within the next decade, he says, the industry will replace over a trillion dollars of the world's traditional computers with new accelerated AI computers. He calls this a golden opportunity for Taiwanese companies, which he describes as the foundation and bedrock of the computer industry.
- AI automates tasks in the world's multi-trillion dollar industries, including healthcare, financial services, transportation and manufacturing.
- Companies:
  - Agile companies that take advantage of AI will boost their position.
  - Companies that don't "will perish."
- Jobs:
  - AI will create new jobs such as data engineering, prompt engineering, AI factory operations and AI safety engineering.
  - It will obsolete some jobs and change every job.
  - Programmers, designers, artists, marketers and manufacturing planners will be supercharged.
- Advice: learn to work with an AI co-pilot. "Someone who is expert with AI will" take your job, not AI itself.
- He notes that every earlier era produced new industries from new entrepreneurs, and expects AI to do the same.

chunks.heading: Advice to graduates
chunks.text:
- Success is a risk: "today is the most successful day of your life so far," and Jensen says he was also successful until he started Nvidia. There he met big, humiliating, nearly fatal failures, and those failures define the company.
- He argues timing is relative. He graduated in 1984, the year of the IBM PC and Apple Macintosh, and calls it a perfect year. He predicts 2023 will be as well.
- He tells graduates they are at the starting line of AI, where every industry will be "revolutionized, reborn" and ready for new ideas.
- Closing: whatever you create, "run after it like we did. Run, don't walk. Remember, either you're running for food or you are running from being food."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jensen explains why Nvidia keeps a flat structure so information moves at the speed of accelerated computing, why healthy paranoia beats assured survival, and how he reasons from first principles on weak signals. He also covers diversity, redundancy and human oversight in AI safety.

chunks.heading: How generative AI works and why Jensen sees it as a general-purpose tool
chunks.text:
- Jensen says the core of generative AI is software that can learn the representation and meaning of data. This works for English, pixels, 3D objects, proteins and chemicals: "almost any data with structure."
- Once meaning is learned for one modality, it can be linked to another. Example: the pixels of a cat linked to the word "cat."
- That link lets you translate between modalities: English to Chinese, English to pixels (generative AI), pixels to language (captioning), text to text (summarization).
- He says the industry is now mixing these translation and generative methods into many applications. The core excitement is learning representations and moving between modalities.
- Generative AI predicts the next word, pixel or video frame, and these predictions can hallucinate.

chunks.heading: Retrieval augmentation: talking to a company's dormant data
chunks.text:
- One effective way to reduce hallucination is to give the model lots of context and prompts before asking it anything.
- Retrieval augmentation: vectorize (embed) a structured or unstructured database by learning the relationships among its data. The database's meaning can then be searched semantically.
- The retrieved embedding augments the prompt, so the model gets richer background information.
- A large language model connected to a vectorized database lets you "talk to your data." Jensen notes that every company holds a lot of data that is now dormant and hard to use.
- Example: a customer service department's logged interactions. Vectorize them, then ask what people are most upset about, what trends are emerging, and the top two or three things to improve service. "You can talk to your database like you're talking to a person."
- Inside NVIDIA, AI is used to:
  - optimize chip design and transistor placement
  - find which line of code likely caused a bug after a failure

chunks.heading: Staying alert to weak signals and reasoning from first principles
chunks.text:
- Jensen says NVIDIA is full of best-in-field experts (compilers, chip design, processor design, interconnects). Meanwhile the company should be as alert as possible.
- Information should move freely, "without being trapped in silos," especially as the company grows and the industry moves fast.
- He wants people watching for "very weak signals," such as a research paper in digital biology or robotics that generalizes to another field.
- Example: reinforcement learning was developed for animating stick figures, fingers and playing games, yet reinforcement learning from human feedback proved useful for fine-tuning large language models.
- His method:
  1. Start with strong foundational expertise in the company.
  2. Stay alert to weak signals, including from adjacent or unrelated fields.
  3. Distill each observation back to first principles: why is it important, and what are the governing dynamics behind it?
  4. Generalize and extrapolate to useful applications in other domains.

chunks.heading: Flat organisation: why NVIDIA removed layers of management
chunks.text:
- Jensen says the organisation's architecture exists so the company can operate as efficiently as possible.
- Speed of change drives it. He says Moore's Law in the older days gave 10x every five years and 100x every ten. Accelerated computing is moving "somewhere between 1,000 to 100,000 times every 10 years." At that speed, information must flow quickly and the company must stay aligned.
- Complexity drives it too. He says an AI GPU weighs 70 lbs, has 35,000 parts (eight of them from TSMC) and consumes 10,000 amps. It is so heavy that robots manufacture it, and it takes a supercomputer to test another supercomputer.
- NVIDIA designs chips, systems, software, networking and silicon photonics, and helps customers stand up and operate data centers. Information therefore must move "with no barriers and no boundaries."
- He rejects hierarchical information flow. In most organisations a few people sit at the top, and there can be seven to ten layers of management before reaching someone who deals with ground truth.
- His fix: make the top of the company as flat as possible. He says this removed roughly three or four layers of management.

chunks.heading: Perpetual peril: why NVIDIA's culture feels existential
chunks.text:
- Asked whether he deliberately instills paranoia, Jensen says you don't have to: "If you don't think you're in peril, it's probably because you have your head in the sand."
- He says no company is assured of survival. NVIDIA nearly went out of business a handful of times, so the feeling is real and not staged.
- He says "the company's always in peril and we feel it." The company doesn't need assurance of success to do its best work.
- He wants the company between aspiration and desperation, which he considers better than always optimistic or always pessimistic.
- His stance: a guarded optimism plus a realistic sense that the company could be in peril at any time, so it must stay focused, alert and "constantly earn the right to be in business."

chunks.heading: Human in the loop, diversity and redundancy
chunks.text:
- Jensen says human in the loop is important. Levels of autonomy should rise only with many "nines" of safety.
- Self-driving example: for a car to carry a sleeping family autonomously, the sensors, computing and vehicle control need diversity and redundancy. That means cameras plus radar plus lidar, and redundant steering and braking.
- Air traffic control is his analogy: two pilots, redundant autopilots, air traffic control, and pilots watching each other. The human can sit outside the system and still monitor it.
- He applies the same idea to companies. Diversity and redundancy make a company resilient: sales augmented by marketing, and the same problem analyzed from different perspectives.
- For generative AI he says:
  - We must invent safety technologies and apply safety engineering and validation methods.
  - For a long time there will "surely" be humans in the loop. Before a model trained on a new batch of data is released, humans should validate, test and red-team it, instead of letting it learn and update continuously on its own.

chunks.heading: Operating under export restrictions and quantum computing
chunks.text:
- On China export limits, Jensen says the restriction is on capability (GPU performance level), not an absolute ban, and similar limits on CPUs and computers go back a long way.
- His sequence:
  1. Understand exactly what the regulation limits and comply, noting the rules are inspired by national security.
  2. Offer products that customers may still find attractive.
  3. See whether customers buy. He says "there's no guarantee," since local competitors in China are numerous and moving quickly.
- On quantum computing, he says building the next fastest computer requires the fastest computer to design, simulate and create algorithms for it, and that is NVIDIA's accelerated computing systems.
- NVIDIA doesn't build quantum computers but works with nearly everyone in the quantum ecosystem, from basic designers to algorithm developers and architects.
- He expects industrial-scale quantum computing in probably "another decade and maybe two." When it arrives, he expects it to be an accelerator attached to accelerated computing systems, with classical computers doing pre- and post-processing.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jensen explains why he would not start Nvidia again knowing the pain, then walks through NV1's failure, the Sega deal, the emulator bet, and carrying CUDA on GeForce for years. He also covers first-principles reasoning, leadership by values, and why AI fear harms young people.

chunks.heading: Why Jensen says he would not build Nvidia again
chunks.text:
- Asked if he would do it again, he says "absolutely not", and thinks most people who say yes are being dishonest.
- His reasoning: the question is not whether he loves the outcome (the contribution to the world, the joy for employees, the benefits). It is whether he would start if he knew how hard it was and did not know the result.
- What he would be signing up for: how hard it is to build Nvidia and CUDA, how long it takes to get the world to use CUDA, plus the pain, suffering, embarrassment, humiliation and setbacks.
- His warning to his 30-year-old self: it will take much longer than you think, you will deliver horrific financial news, activists will come after the company, you may have to lay people off, and you may go out of business.
- His conclusion: "the pain and suffering necessary, the endurance necessary to do something great" are routinely forgotten.
- On the 2007-era CUDA spending while the stock was down, he calls it "embarrassing" and "humiliating". He describes being "the only face that everybody hates", with employees probably embarrassed for him.

chunks.heading: Forgetting yesterday: how he handles pain and long timelines
chunks.text:
- He spends "all of my life trying to forget yesterday". Revisiting past setbacks triggers anxiety, which is why he dislikes talking about his past.
- He compares it to athletes: "Forget the last point."
- He frames high tech as a "marathon sprint": full out every day, and Nvidia has taken 34 years and is still at it.
- His method: look forward with promise, enthusiasm and deep belief. Learn from the setbacks, codify the learning, make sure it goes into "every fiber in your body", then let go of the pain.
- He calls this healthy but says it takes a lot of discipline.
- On conviction: he was never worried CUDA would fail. "It would have been harder to give up." The idea was already fully real in his head, so the only questions were when it would succeed and which application would come first.

chunks.heading: Founding Nvidia and the near-death of NV1 (1993-1997)
chunks.text:
- Chris and Curtis kept asking him to join their startup. He had a good job at LSI Logic, two kids, a wife at home and "$30,000 in the bank".
- The seed idea: the PC was the first general-purpose computer. Bring Silicon Graphics-style 3D graphics (like Jurassic Park) to a personal computer at an affordable price. A Jurassic Park-class machine cost about $1 million; the target was about $300.
- The NV1 sold 250,000 units, but the algorithm (forward texture mapping) was wrong. The right one was inverse texture mapping, which DirectX in Windows 95 used. All 250,000 came back. He calls it a technology disaster.
- Sega had contracted Nvidia for $12 million (1994-95) to build the NV2 and NV3 for its console. Continuing meant two more years on a flawed architecture, while 30 competitors did it the right way.
- What he did:
  - Flew to Japan and told Sega's CEO the architecture would not serve them, and recommended Sega find another partner.
  - Asked him to convert the remaining contract money into an investment, saying his first job as CEO was to keep the company alive. Sega turned the remaining $5 million into equity.
  - Cut the company from about 250 people, laying off two-thirds.
- At 32, he had around six months of cash and could not iterate on silicon. He bought a leftover emulator from a failed company (IKOS) for about half the company's remaining money, so the chip could be verified in software before tape-out. It worked well enough to save the company (the Riva 128).
- On the team: it was existential, and everyone was "super calm, super focused", reasoning step by step that this was the only chance.

chunks.heading: Disruption, focus and software-first strategy
chunks.text:
- Clayton Christensen's *The Innovator's Dilemma* shaped him. His takeaway: the moment technology becomes "good enough" and overserves the market, it is ready for disruption.
- He says Nvidia was the disruptor at every step. Riva 128 and the first HPC GPU were imperfect but good enough, and initially looked "toyish".
- Nvidia was the first graphics company built to focus fully on one application industry: video games.
- From the start he treated applications as what creates industries, so the company worried about software and downstream developers, not only the chip.
- His stance on markets: he does not want Nvidia fighting for a point of share in someone else's market. He wants something really hard that makes sense to him first, in a direction nobody has gone.

chunks.heading: CUDA: carrying a platform on GeForce for years
chunks.text:
- Origin: he wanted physics (fluids, particles, explosions) in virtual worlds, which pushed the GPU toward general-purpose parallel programming. He was constantly looking for algorithms that only ran on supercomputers and could reach many more people on a PC.
- Early uses (seismic processing, CT reconstruction at Mass General, molecular dynamics) came from universities and did not pay the bills. Only gaming did.
- CUDA launched in late 2006. From roughly 2006 to 2012 the stock was weak, and he describes the period as years of pain.
- His reasoning: "We believed on first principles this should be quite useful." The problem was chicken-and-egg:
  - A new architecture needs a large installed base to attract developers.
  - Developers are needed for the killer app.
  - The killer app is needed to sell the hardware.
