- His answer: put CUDA on GeForce so it reached every PC, at the cost of gross margins going "from bad to horrible". CUDA was given away free. GeForce has carried it for 25 years.
- Tactics:
  - A "CUDA everywhere" initiative.
  - Evangelising to universities, researchers and companies, with him pitching personally.
  - Technology demos, and asking developers (for example imaging software) to port to CUDA.
- He admits he thought about being too early and running out of money "all the time", and says there were "900 other smart strategies" to keep the company alive.
- Researchers such as Ian Buck and later the Toronto deep-learning group bought GeForce cards from retail.
- When AlexNet won ImageNet, the leap over prior algorithms caught his eye. He asked what it was, why it worked, where it could go and what it meant for chips and computers.

chunks.heading: Becoming an AI company: first principles and bringing people along
chunks.text:
- He says his method is to break things down to first principles, then ask what the foundations are, how far it can go and what it means for the industry. He calls himself good at connecting dots and systems thinking.
- Before sending the 2013-era email declaring the company an AI company, he had already held tens of engagements with groups across the company. By the time the email went out, "everybody's already been brought along". He then sets the direction.
- On people: he deeply believes in the idea, helps others believe it, and the company follows.

chunks.heading: Leadership style, resilience and luck
chunks.text:
- On being tough: "I don't think people care about style." They care about values and what you care about. Be tough on the same things every time, and once the moment is over, it is over. People must know they are safe, that you love them and want them to succeed.
- He says he works harder than ever because he wants everything he has to reach his people and partners. Being "pure and high integrity" and fully there for them lets him be quite challenging while they know he is on their side.
- Decisions: he has taken "several hundred forks in the road", mostly the right one, through judgment, values, friends, informed decisions, critical thinking and some luck.
- The company built a system for self-reflection: don't take yourselves too seriously, don't be so hard on bad decisions, adjust quickly and never let a bad decision be fatal.
- The people who help with the next fork will likely differ from those who helped with the last, so you must find them.
- He felt safe taking risks because of Lori, the kids and the employees behind him. His summary: "It's always personal."
- Humility and being grounded help: "Not doing this job from a yacht is helpful."
- Supply chain: build resilience through diversity and redundancy where possible, and do your best where you cannot.

chunks.heading: AI fears, jobs and advice for students
chunks.text:
- He did not sign the 2023 extinction-risk letter. He is worried about safety but wants worry channelled into building safer technology, as the auto and airline industries do, rather than repeating doom narratives.
- He argues for speeding up AI innovation, because innovation makes it safer. Today's AI hallucinates and lies less.
- His greatest fear: the US scares people out of using AI. He says Western sentiment is "really out of control" and that China is not buying the doom narrative.
- Radiology example: a decade ago experts predicted radiology would vanish. AI now does scans faster and more accurately, yet demand for radiologists has gone up because scans are cheaper and hospitals see more patients. His point: "a job has a purpose and a task". The task is reading scans, the purpose is diagnosing disease. The harm was young people avoiding the field.
- He says the opportunity for a new graduate in computer science, software or chip design today is far greater than when he graduated, with tools "a billion times more capable".
- On Nvidia headcount, he says AI makes little difference to the number of employees. Each will have hundreds or thousands of AI assistants, and expectations rise: "Things that takes 10 years, I think it'll take one year."
- On Taiwan, he is less worried about hot conflict than most. He urges balanced, nuanced policy and not pushing adversaries to the wall.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: At a fireside chat in Kazakhstan, Jensen argues that ambition is the one quality that decides whether AI lifts you. He makes the case for sovereign AI built from national data, for physical AI as the next wave, and for investing in people. His advice to an 18-year-old: become the world's best programmer of AI.

chunks.heading: AI as a new industry: factories, electricity, data and offtake
chunks.text:
- Jensen frames AI as a general purpose technology driving an industrial revolution that affects every person, company and country.
- He also calls it a new industry in itself, because "AI is manufacturing." It has to be generated in real time for every use and cannot be pre-computed, so it needs a new type of factory.
- NVIDIA builds the computing systems that power these AI factories.
- AI factories consume natural resources: electricity, data, and offtake.
- Offtake comes from leadership inspiring young people, students, university scientists and industries to engage the AI economy.
- He endorses the "five-layer cake" as a framework for a national AI strategy, and says Kazakhstan has the assets to build all of it.
- Advice to a resource-rich country: instead of only exporting energy, "transform the energy into intelligence and export intelligence."
- He notes a planned 1 gigawatt data center valley in Kazakhstan. With telecom interconnection, he sees it as a compute and AI factory hub for Europe.

chunks.heading: Sovereign AI: a country's data is its natural resource
chunks.text:
- Jensen argues a country's data encodes its culture, history, humanity and values. That data belongs to the country, "just as your natural resources belong to you."
- He calls building national AI capability "a national security concern," not just a good idea.
- His reasoning:
  - Intelligence is foundational and general purpose, and it touches every citizen, company and industry.
  - You cannot export something as fundamental as your culture and values in order to import intelligence from someone else.
  - Countries should control their data and the delivery of intelligence to their people.
- Analogy: countries have their own electric grid, internet and telecommunications. In future they will also have their own "intelligence grid."
- Foreign companies and countries can supplement it, but it cannot be delivered completely from abroad.
- On how to build it: inventing the core technology is hard, but adapting it is "not so difficult" (though not easy). A country with strong mathematicians, scientists and programmers can take open-source models and apply them to its own language and culture, then run its own intelligence infrastructure.
- He praised Kazakhstan's Kazakh LLM as an example of turning national data into national intelligence.

chunks.heading: Physical AI as the next wave and the largest industry
chunks.text:
- Jensen calls physical AI the next wave and "the largest industry of all," because most of the world involves interacting with and understanding the physical world.
- AI starts with cognitive ("soft") intelligence and extends all the way to physical AI.
- Physical AI is broader than robotics. He lists seismic understanding, mapping mines and wells, geography and geology (where and how best to mine), material science, and chemical processing.
- For a country with mining, natural resources and agriculture, every stage from extraction to turning minerals into new materials can benefit.
- He says everyone is at the beginning of this journey, which makes it a chance to help shape the industry.
- Prediction: just as there will be artificial general intelligence for cognition, there will be "artificial general robotics." He extends this to artificial general farmers, miners, scientists and engineers in every field.
- He says NVIDIA is already working with robotics companies in Kazakhstan.

chunks.heading: Ambition is what decides who AI lifts
chunks.text:
- Asked about jobs, Jensen says "The only thing that matters is do you have ambition?"
- Examples of ambition plus AI:
  - A farmer uses robots to farm, then expands the operation, horizon and business.
  - A scientist's AI assistant expands the universe they can explore.
  - An engineer's AI engineer helps explore better designs.
- The same logic applies to children: if a child wants to learn more, AI helps them learn more. If the child wants to do less, AI can help them do less.
- He says it is the job of parents to instill "hope, ambition, aspiration" and help children dream bigger.
- It applies equally to adults, companies and nations.
- He says leaders, whether country leaders, CEOs or parents, should instill ambition in their people, families, companies and nations. He cites Kazakhstan's president declaring the country an AI nation as an example.

chunks.heading: How NVIDIA decides to invest: people, not companies
chunks.text:
- On NVIDIA's investment in Higgsfield AI, Jensen says: "you invest in people, not companies." He calls this "the first thing and the last thing."
- Why the Higgsfield founders stood out:
  - They are visionary and had a hard idea to execute.
  - They compete globally against well-funded, formidable rivals, many in San Francisco.
  - Their team of about 600 people in Kazakhstan has an average age of 25, and many are deep tech engineers and computer scientists.
  - They bridge the culture and expertise of two nations, with offices in Kazakhstan and the United States.
- His rule: when you invest in a company, you are really investing in people, so you have to select the best people.
- He joked that he starts work at 5 a.m., and that day he started at 4 a.m.

chunks.heading: Building and deploying AI responsibly
chunks.text:
- Jensen says the world can only enjoy AI's benefits if it is developed, advanced and deployed responsibly. Safety must be built in from the very beginning, as with self-driving cars and mining.
- He says creators like NVIDIA and Higgsfield carry that responsibility.
- Safety technology is foundational and has to be invented and engineered.
- NVIDIA created OpenShell. He describes AI agents as "essentially self-driving cars or robots inside a computer." If given access to files and tools, they will freely use them to do their job.
- OpenShell's approach:
  - Contain agents so access is exactly what is wanted.
  - Limit privileges to what the agent needs for its job.
  - Monitor it at all times.
- He advises everybody to use it.
- On whether his view of AI changed in the past year: no. He is more enthusiastic than a year ago. Agentic systems made AI useful, and he cites generated video going from short clips to long, temporally and physically consistent stories, which he says is not possible without agentic reasoning systems. He also names software coding, robotics and drug discovery as fields where it has become very useful.

chunks.heading: Advice to an 18-year-old: become the world's best programmer of AI
chunks.text:
- Jensen says he envies being 18 today, because technology has caused a complete reset.
- His own generation was defined by the creation of the personal computer. In his 43 years of work, all of that effort led to AI, "a complete reset of everything that we've done."
- Shift: "Instead of programming the computer, you have to learn how to program AI."
- Because AI is new for everybody, he says he would "dedicate myself to be the world's best programmer of AI."
- AI can automate, partner with and assist people, but as with working with a human assistant, you have to learn how to interact and "program each other."
- He says you need both technical understanding and the human skill of interacting. The best programmer of AI understands how AI works: its fundamental principles, strengths, weaknesses, how it is developing and where it is going.
- Analogies: "The best user of a machine is someone who understands how the machine works. The best driver of a race car is someone who understands how the car works."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jensen explains AI from first principles as a platform shift that reinvents the computing stack. He describes it as a five-layer industrial cake and the largest infrastructure buildout in history. He argues AI creates jobs when you separate a job's purpose from its tasks, and urges every country to build its own AI.

chunks.heading: AI as a platform shift and why it is different from earlier software
chunks.text:
- Jensen reasons from first principles about what changed in the computing stack. He calls AI a platform shift, like the PC, the internet and mobile cloud. In each shift the stack was reinvented and new applications were built on top.
- ChatGPT is itself an application, but new applications will be built on top of ChatGPT and on top of Anthropic's Claude.
- Old software was "pre-recorded". Humans typed the algorithm or recipe, and it worked on structured information (names, addresses, account numbers) retrieved with SQL. He calls SQL "the single most important database engine the world's ever known".
- AI is the first computer that understands unstructured information (images, text, sound). It processes context in real time, reasons about the user's intent, and performs the task. Prompts are how intent is described.
- Because AI is software you teach rather than write, he says "You don't write AI, you teach AI."

chunks.heading: The five-layer cake of AI and the infrastructure buildout
chunks.text:
- Jensen describes AI industrially as a five-layer cake, from the bottom up:
  1. Energy, because intelligence is generated in real time.
  2. Chips and computing infrastructure (the layer he lives in).
  3. Cloud infrastructure and services.
  4. AI models, where most people think AI is.
  5. Applications (financial services, healthcare, manufacturing), where the economic benefit ultimately happens.
- Models improved enough last year that the application layer is now taking off. He cites 2025 as one of the largest VC years ever, with most funding going to AI-native companies in healthcare, robotics, manufacturing and financial services. He gives "over a hundred billion dollars" worldwide.
- He calls this "the largest infrastructure buildout in human history", with "a few hundred billion dollars" spent so far and "trillions of dollars" still to build.
- Examples he gives of the buildout across layers:
  - TSMC announced 20 new chip plants.
  - Foxconn, Wistron and Quanta are building 30 new computer plants with Nvidia.
  - Micron has started investing $200 billion in the US. SK Hynix and Samsung are also doing very well.
- He describes three kinds of factory being built: chip factories, computer factories and AI factories.

chunks.heading: Three breakthroughs in AI models last year
chunks.text:
- **Agentic AI.** Models hallucinated less and became better grounded. They can research, reason about situations they were not trained on, break problems into steps, make a plan and perform tasks.
- **Open models.** DeepSeek, the first open reasoning model, was a huge event for industries around the world. Open reasoning models let companies, researchers, educators, universities and startups build domain-specific or specialized systems.
- **Physical AI.** AI that understands nature: proteins, chemicals, fluid dynamics, particle physics and quantum physics. He treats proteins as essentially a language. His example is the Lilly partnership, where AI can understand protein and chemical structures well enough to "talk to the proteins like we talked to ChatGPT".

chunks.heading: Jobs: purpose versus task framework
chunks.text:
- Jensen argues AI is creating jobs, and expects labor shortages rather than mass displacement.
- The buildout creates trade jobs: plumbers, electricians, construction and steel workers, network technicians and equipment installers. He says salaries in the US have nearly doubled, to six figures for people building chip, computer and AI factories. "You don't need to have a PhD in computer science" to make a great living.
- His test for AI's impact on a job is to separate the **purpose** of the job from its **tasks**. Watching him and the host on camera, you would think they are typists, but typing is a task, not their purpose.
- Radiology example:
  - Ten years ago it was predicted to be wiped out, because computer vision was the first superhuman AI.
  - AI now permeates radiology completely, yet the number of radiologists has gone up.
  - The purpose of the job is diagnosing disease. Faster scan reading frees time for patients and clinicians, so the hospital sees more patients, revenue rises and it hires more radiologists.
- Nursing example:
  - The US is 5 million nurses short.
  - Nurses spend half their time charting. AI charting and transcription (he names Abridge, a partner) frees them to see patients.
  - Hospitals then do better and hire more nurses.

chunks.heading: Advice for developing countries and individuals
chunks.text:
- AI is infrastructure, like electricity and roads, and every country should have it. Countries can import AI, but he urges them to build their own.
- Training is "not so incredibly hard" now, and open models plus local expertise let countries build models for themselves. Language and culture are a country's fundamental natural resource, so countries should develop AI on them and make national intelligence part of their ecosystem.
- AI is "the easiest software to use in history", which is why it is the fastest adopted, nearing a billion people in two to three years. He expects it to close the technology divide.
- Everyone should learn to direct, prompt, manage, guardrail and evaluate an AI. He says these skills "are no different than leading people". In future companies will manage digital, silicon AIs as part of the workforce alongside carbon-based ones.
- Anyone can be a programmer now. If you do not know how to use AI, ask the AI how to use it. If you want a website, it asks questions about what you want and writes the code.
- He praises Claude, which Nvidia uses across the company for coding and reasoning, and says any software company should get involved. He calls ChatGPT probably the most successful consumer AI in history.

chunks.heading: Advice for Europe
chunks.text:
- Nvidia works with every AI company in the world because it sits low in the infrastructure layer.
- Europe's strong industrial and manufacturing base lets it "leap past the era of software", which the US led. He says to fuse industrial capability with AI and move into physical AI and robotics, "a once in a generation opportunity".
- Europe's deep sciences can use AI to accelerate discovery.
- Europe must get serious about increasing its energy supply to invest in the infrastructure layer and have a rich AI ecosystem.
- Europe's skilled trades workforce is an advantage that the US lost over the last 20 to 30 years.

chunks.heading: Why he says this is not an AI bubble
chunks.text:
- His test is GPU rental demand. Nvidia has millions of GPUs in every cloud, and renting one is "so incredibly hard".
- Spot prices for GPU rentals are going up, including for GPUs two generations old.
- Demand comes from the growing number of AI companies and from companies shifting R&D budgets. Lilly's R&D, which was once all wet labs, is moving toward AI, including a big AI supercomputer and AI lab.
- Investment is large because every layer above has to be built.
- He urges investing in energy, "land, power and shell" and trade workers.
- He argues pension funds and ordinary savers should take part in the infrastructure investment so they are not "watching it from the sidelines".

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jensen explains the OpenAI partnership, the three scaling laws, and why general-purpose computing is giving way to accelerated computing and AI. He covers extreme co-design as Nvidia's moat, how to build a market as a startup, sovereign AI, China, immigration, and why AI augments jobs.

chunks.heading: Three scaling laws and why inference is going up by a billion times
chunks.text:
- Jensen says AI now has three scaling laws, not one: pre-training, post-training and inference ("thinking").
- Post-training is "AI practicing" a skill until it gets it right. It needs inference, so training and inference are now integrated in reinforcement learning.
- Old inference was one shot. New inference is thinking before answering: doing research, checking ground truth, learning, thinking more, then generating. The longer it thinks, the better the answer.
- A year earlier he argued inference would go up by a billion times, not 100x or 1,000x. He says he is more confident now and "underestimated."
- Reason for the confidence: AI is no longer a single language model. It is a system of models running concurrently, using tools, doing research and working across modalities (including video).
- He says over 40% of Nvidia's revenue is already inference.
- Two compounding exponentials drive compute demand:
  - Usage: more customers, because the AI keeps getting better. He cites OpenAI at roughly 800 million weekly active users, less than two years after ChatGPT.
  - Compute per use: each query now thinks before it answers.

chunks.heading: The size of the market: $5 trillion of AI capex, and why a glut is unlikely
chunks.text:
- He gives three points for why Nvidia's opportunity is larger than Wall Street consensus (he says analysts model flat growth from 2027, and Nvidia is comfortable beating them).
- Point 1 (laws of physics): general-purpose computing is over and Moore's law is dead. Trillions of dollars of installed computing must be refreshed, and it will be refreshed as accelerated computing and AI.
- Point 2: hyperscale infrastructure is moving from CPUs to GPUs. Recommenders, search, shopping, TikTok, YouTube Shorts and personalised content all depend on AI now. This is "hundreds of billions of dollars" before any new application is considered.
- Point 3 (new applications): AI factories generate tokens that augment human intelligence, which he sizes at roughly 55-65% of world GDP, or about $50 trillion.
- Worked example:
  - Take a $100,000 employee and add a $10,000 AI that makes them 2-3x more productive. "Heartbeat," he would do it.
  - He does this across every software engineer and chip designer at Nvidia (100% coverage). Nvidia is hiring more people, building more chips, with higher revenue and profitability.
  - Assume the $50 trillion is augmented by about $10 trillion of tokens, at 50% gross margin. That implies about $5 trillion of AI infrastructure capex a year.
- He puts today's annual market at about $400 billion, so the TAM is a 4-5x increase.
- He says Nvidia's revenue is almost correlated to power. Alibaba's CEO said data centre power will rise 10x by the end of the decade, and the market is power-limited.
- On a glut: he says the chance is extremely low until all general-purpose computing, recommenders, content generation, shopping and e-commerce have moved to accelerated computing and AI, which will take a few years.
- Other points on demand:
  - Nvidia sits at the end of the supply chain, so it responds to demand. Customers' forecasts have all been too low, which leaves Nvidia "in scramble mode."
  - Nvidia has geared up the supply chain (wafer starts, CoWoS, HBM) and says "if we need to double we'll double."
  - Accelerated data processing (SQL, Databricks, Snowflake, Oracle) is a huge CPU-run market that has yet to move to accelerated computing. A big initiative is coming.
- He says the world's GDP growth must accelerate because AI adds "billions of co-workers."
- His prediction: Nvidia will likely be the first $10 trillion company. People said a decade ago there could never be a trillion-dollar company, and now there are 10.

chunks.heading: The OpenAI partnership and "circular revenue" criticism
chunks.text:
- He says OpenAI is likely the next multi-trillion-dollar hyperscale company, with both consumer and enterprise services.
- Nvidia works with OpenAI on four tracks:
  - Microsoft Azure buildout, with several years and hundreds of billions of dollars of work to go.
  - OCI buildout, with roughly 5-7 gigawatts (with Oracle and SoftBank), already contracted.
  - CoreWeave.
  - A new track: helping OpenAI build its own AI infrastructure for the first time, working directly at the chip, software, systems and AI-factory levels. It is additive to everything else.
- He says OpenAI wants a direct working and purchasing relationship, as Meta, Google, Microsoft and xAI already have with Nvidia.
- His figures: 10 gigawatts is roughly $400 billion. The announced investment is up to $100 billion.
- Reply to the circular-revenue critics:
  - The $400 billion must be funded by OpenAI's offtake (revenue), equity and debt. The size of the equity and debt depends on investors' and lenders' confidence in that revenue.
  - The investment side "is not tied to anything." It is an opportunity to invest in a company he expects to be hugely valuable.
  - Nvidia is not required to invest and OpenAI is not required to use Nvidia chips. If Vera Rubin isn't good, they can buy other chips.
  - Underlying demand is real: consumers paying for ChatGPT, a billion and a half monthly users, enterprises and sovereigns.
- His only regret is that Nvidia was "so poor" when OpenAI first invited it to invest that it didn't invest enough. He also names early investments in xAI and CoreWeave.

chunks.heading: Extreme co-design and the annual release cycle
chunks.text:
- Why Nvidia moved to an annual cadence: token generation and usage are both growing exponentially, but Moore's law is dead, so transistors cost about the same each year and power is about the same. Performance has to come from somewhere else. A discount of a few percent cannot make up for two exponentials.
- Performance gains he cites:
  - Kepler to Hopper: about 100,000x over 10 years.
  - Hopper to Blackwell: 30x in one year, thanks to NVLink 72.
  - Rubin and Feynman: further X-factors.
- Extreme co-design means optimizing the model, algorithm, system and chip at the same time, "innovating outside the box" when the chip alone can't get faster.
  - He changes the CPU, GPU, networking chip, NVLink scale-up and Spectrum-X scale-out together, plus the whole software stack. Scale-across links multiple AI factories.
  - Spectrum-X is "not just Ethernet." He says it is the fastest-growing Ethernet business in the world.
  - Nvidia builds six or seven chips a year and optimizes across all of them.
- Nvidia invented CUDA and GPUs, and "invented the idea of co-design at a very large scale." He says it checks in more open-source software than almost anyone, which makes deep co-design possible.
- Without AI inside Nvidia, this velocity and scale would not be possible.
- Releases and products he names: Hopper, Grace Blackwell, Vera Rubin (second half of 2026), Rubin Ultra (2027), Feynman (2028), Rubin CPX (context processing and video generation), Dynamo (open-source disaggregated inference orchestration) and NVLink Fusion.

chunks.heading: Moat, ASICs and pricing competitors at zero
chunks.text:
- He says competition is greater than ever but winning is harder, for these reasons:
  - Wafer costs keep rising, so without extreme co-design nobody can deliver X-factor gains.
  - It is not about building an ASIC. It is about building an AI factory with many co-designed chips.
  - Scale: a gigawatt is about 400,000-500,000 GPUs working together, "a miracle." Few customers would place a $50 billion purchase order on an unproven architecture, and few suppliers would start hundreds of billions of dollars of wafers and DRAM for a chip that has just taped out. Nvidia's proven architecture and delivery record allow it.
- On ASICs:
  - Google's advantage was foresight. It started TPU 1 before the market existed, which is how a startup should operate.
  - His startup rule: "You're supposed to take 100% of a tiny industry," not a few percent of a large one. He calls "just take a few percent of a big market" a fallacy.
  - He describes three chip categories: architectural (x86, ARM, Nvidia GPUs, with rich ecosystems), ASICs and customer-owned tooling (COT).
  - He worked at LSI Logic, which invented the ASIC and is no longer around. ASICs suit small markets, where a contractor charges 50-60 points of margin. When volume is large, customers move to COT (Apple's smartphone chips are the example), and he expects TPUs to follow.
  - ASICs fit narrow workloads (video transcoders, smart NICs). AI workloads keep changing (low latency, high throughput, chat, thinking, video), and CUDA's programmability lets labs experiment with attention variants and disaggregation.
- Why competitors can price at zero and Nvidia still wins:
  - Customers are power-limited. If tokens per watt are twice as high, the customer earns twice the revenue from the same gigawatts.
  - The gap between Nvidia's roughly 75-point gross margin and others' 50-65 points is small next to a 30x performance gap.
  - Land, power and shell alone cost about $15 billion, so the opportunity cost of weaker performance is "insanely high."
- He sells any way customers like: full rack, a single chip, networking only, CPU only. His only ask is "just buy a little something from us."
- He describes Nvidia as "an AI infrastructure company," not a chip company.
- Partnership over rivalry: NVLink Fusion links Intel (which he says tried for most of its life to put Nvidia out of business) and ARM into the Nvidia ecosystem. His logic: "bring it on," and the future is big enough that "it could be us and them."

chunks.heading: Sovereign AI, China, and talent
chunks.text:
- Sovereign AI: "Nobody needs atomic bombs. Everybody needs AI." Every country needs AI infrastructure as it needs energy and communications infrastructure.
  - Countries should use OpenAI, Gemini, Anthropic, Grok and open models. They should also build sovereign capability to encode their history, culture and values, and to build industrial, manufacturing and national-security models.
- He calls AI the "greatest equalizer": people no longer need C++ or Python, they "just have to learn human." If you don't know how to program an AI, you ask the AI.
- China:
  - He says Nvidia had about 95% market share there and now guides with no China included.
  - He argues that forcing Nvidia out gave Huawei monopoly profits and a path to compete globally, and that the policy backfired.
  - He describes Chinese competitors as "formidable, innovative, hungry, fast-moving, under-regulated." China has strong STEM schools and many AI engineers ("996" culture: 9am-9pm, 6 days a week), and he calls claims that they are "years behind" absurd: "nanoseconds."
  - His position is that selling in China serves both countries, and "those two truths can coexist." He stays patient and believes wisdom will prevail.
  - On the skeptic who says he only wants to sell chips: "Just because I want America in ecosystem and economy to grow doesn't make me wrong."
  - He argues against decoupling and for maximizing exports so the world builds on American technology.
- Talent and the "American dream":
  - He calls the $100,000 H-1B fee "a great start" that "sets the bar a little too high" but cuts abuse. He hopes it is not the end, and notes it may push investment overseas.
  - His principle: "Start somewhere, move towards the right answer." Don't wait for the perfect answer.
  - He treats smart people's desire to come to and stay in America as KPIs, "early indicators of future success." He is concerned about falling numbers of Chinese students staying.
  - He says to compete with China, "but be careful not to be tough on Chinese," and calls damaging the pipeline "not patriotic."
  - His own story: his parents had no money, and he bussed tables, washed dishes and cleaned toilets.

chunks.heading: Jobs, AI adoption and getting on the train
chunks.text:
- Jobs: AI changes tasks, not whole jobs. Some tasks are eliminated and many are created. Nvidia hires more engineers because it has more ideas and more productivity. The "mass job destruction" claim "starts with the premise that we have no more ideas."
- "Intelligence is not a zero-sum game": more intelligent people around him means more ideas, more problems to solve, more work and more jobs.
- He says reindustrializing America (skilled trades and manufacturing) brings people along, and he loves "people who make things with their hands." He supports the Invest America accounts for children, with $1,000 invested in American companies at birth.
- Near-term predictions: AI fused with robotics ("our own R2-D2"), a personal AI model for each person (8 billion GPUs), and digital twins for health care.
- Advice on exponential change: "If you have a train that's about to get faster and faster... the only thing that you really need to do is get on it." Don't try to predict where it will be, "just get on it while it's going kind of slowly" and figure out the rest as you go.
- On Elon Musk as a builder: AI supercomputers are "the most complex systems problem humanity has ever endeavored." Musk has an advantage because all the interdependencies (technology, financing, land, power) sit in one head, along with a sense of urgency.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jensen explains why Nvidia's moat is a full-stack, flywheel-wide system rather than a chip, why it makes markets instead of taking share, and how he reasons about AI demand from first principles. He also covers AI-augmented flat organisations, safety, and staying relevant by learning.

chunks.heading: Nvidia's moat is the full stack and the learning flywheel, not the chip
chunks.text:
- Jensen calls the "flips and flops and bits and bytes" chip-comparison view "old thinking". It dates from when software was static, pre-compiled and shrink-wrapped, and only faster chips improved the system.
- Machine learning is not just software. The thing to design for is the whole data-to-model flywheel: AI curates data, synthetic data is generated, data is processed, then training, post-training and inference.
- He applies Amdahl's law: if a step is 30% of the time and you speed it up 3x, you have not sped up the process much. So Nvidia accelerates every step, because only then does cycle time (the rate of learning) fall materially.
- Nvidia's accelerated-computing work is driven by domain-specific libraries below PyTorch: cuDNN, Optix, cuQuantum, RAPIDS. He says "nobody talks about cuDNN" yet it made deep learning work.
- Parallel computing is hard because every algorithm must be refactored for the architecture. There is no compiler that targets multiple ISAs, so the architecture company must write its own "OpenGL" for each domain.
- He says a company's view of what it is really doing "manifests itself into the product". Nvidia's view is the flywheel, so the products accelerate all of it.
- He argues the moat is greater today than three to four years ago, because the advantage compounds across the stack.

chunks.heading: Parallel vs serial processing and why Nvidia differs from Intel
chunks.text:
- Jensen credits Intel as extraordinary at manufacturing and process engineering, fused with x86 chip design.
- Serial processing needs every transistor to be excellent. Parallel processing needs many transistors to be cost effective. He would rather have 10x more transistors that are 20% slower than 10x fewer that are 20% faster.
- Nvidia's world is "much better going up" (scale and architecture), not about being incrementally better going down.
- Marginal cost of computing fell about 100,000x over 10 years, versus roughly 100x from Moore's law. He credits accelerated computing, new numerical precisions, the tensor core, NVLink, HBM, NVLink and InfiniBand scaling, and work across the whole stack.
- Old model: static software on hardware improving at Moore's law. New model: the whole stack improves at once, so innovations compound.

chunks.heading: Annual cadence, install base and why custom ASICs don't change the mission
chunks.text:
- Jensen treats the data center as the unit of computing: "when I think about a computer I'm not thinking about that chip", the whole system with software and orchestration is the computer.
- Nvidia builds a new one every year. Each year it delivers 2-3x more performance, 2-3x lower cost and 2-3x better energy efficiency. He tells customers not to buy everything at once but to "buy a little every year" and cost-average, since all of it is architecturally compatible.
- The harder part is that Nvidia disaggregates the system and integrates it into GCP, AWS, Azure, X and others, each differently: libraries, frameworks, security and networking. That is about 10 integrations a year. He calls this "the miracle".
- The supply chain works because APIs, methodologies and design rules were propagated backward and forward and hardened over decades.
- Install base matters. Gear used for training yesterday becomes inference capacity today, a "trail of free infrastructure" that is CUDA compatible. Nvidia keeps compatibility and keeps writing new algorithms, so Hopper, Ampere and even Volta improve. Hopper can become 2-4x better than when it was bought.
- A vision-language model built in the cloud runs on a robot at the edge without modification.
- On ASICs (Trainium, TPU, MTIA): Jensen is "situationally aware" of alternatives, sometimes adversarial, but that "doesn't change what the purpose of the company is". The purpose is a platform available everywhere.
- Nvidia is "a market maker, not a share taker". He says no company slide talks about market share. The questions are the next problem in the flywheel and how to cut a one-year loop to a month.
- He shows his roadmap to cloud partners years ahead while they do not show him their ASIC roadmaps, and says it does not offend him. A sole, meaningful purpose lets you be transparent.
- Pitch to a startup: choose CUDA and you can go everywhere and defer other chip decisions. Nvidia is "the onramp to the world of AI".
- Test for any company: is the mission necessary, valuable and impactful?

chunks.heading: First-principles case that demand is durable (not Cisco 2000)
chunks.text:
- His method: "reason about it from first principles". State ground truths, then ask what follows.
- Ground truth 1: computing is reinvented. Applications will be highly machine-learned, and agents will help people use them.
- Step 2: there is about $1 trillion of installed data-center infrastructure to modernize over four or five years. Given $50 billion of capex, spend it on generative AI, since Moore's law has largely ended and the old capex is already in place.
- Step 3: new "AI factories" run digital employees 24/7 in companies, factories and autonomous systems. This layer does not exist today. Size is unknowable, "probably a few trillion dollars". The architecture for modernized data centers and AI factories is the same.
- He jokes that the 25 analysts who forecast about $26B for 2023 when Nvidia did $60B made "the single greatest failure of forecasting the world has ever seen".
- Companies are limited by the size of their fish pond. Share takers can only be so big, market makers can be large. Nvidia had to invent its market from the beginning (the 3D gaming PC market and graphics-card ecosystem), so inventing new markets is comfortable.

chunks.heading: Scaling, inference and the Elon/xAI cluster
chunks.text:
- Scaling now has three vectors: pre-training (model and data size roughly doubling, so compute up about 4x a year), post-training (synthetic data, reward systems, reinforcement learning) and inference.
- "Everything is hard now." People thought inference was easy. One-shot thinking is "ridiculous"; there is fast and slow thinking, reflection, iteration and simulation.
- Inference reasoning can't be done a priori; it needs runtime context. Some answers need a quick reply, others "take a night" or "a week". He imagines telling his AI to think overnight.
- Interactive inference needs time to first token, which needs enormous bandwidth and FLOPs together. Nvidia built Grace Blackwell with NVLink for this, thinking ahead from training work.
- Training a few years ahead pays off: Nvidia invented Megatron (about seven years ago), NCCL and GPU Direct, which enabled large-scale parallel training.
- He expects distributed or federated asynchronous training to be invented, and that millions of GPUs will be needed. Data centers could be gigawatt or 250 MW scale; he expects both.
- On xAI: 100,000 GPUs as one cluster, in 19 days from power-on to first training. Normally about three years to plan plus one year to bring up. He credits Elon as "an N of one", and the hardened Nvidia platform and pre-planning by both engineering teams.
- He says Nvidia uses its own agents: cybersecurity can't run without them, and AI chip designers, software engineers and verification engineers are built in-house. "Hopper wouldn't be possible... Blackwell wouldn't be possible, Rubin don't even think about it" without them.

chunks.heading: Layers of the stack: model vs AI vs company
chunks.text:
- A model is "necessary but not sufficient" for AI. AI for self-driving cars, humanoid robots and chatbots are related but not the same.
- Every layer has opportunities, but not infinite ones. Same logic as GPU vs accelerated computing vs AI infrastructure: each layer needs different skills. Many companies build GPUs, few are accelerated-computing companies.
- Founders should decide where to play, watch what gets commoditized, and tell a feature from a product from a company.
- On OpenAI he calls it one of the most consequential companies of our time, and praises its velocity and singular purpose, and the economic engine that can fund the next frontier.
- Open and closed both matter: closed models are the engine of an economic model that sustains innovation, and open models let every industry build domain-specific AI. Nvidia's Nemotron 340B is meant for synthetic data and reward modeling, "the best critique" for improving other models.
- Synthetic data logic: one AI looping alone is like a super smart person in a padded room for a month. Two or three with different knowledge debating can all come out smarter.

chunks.heading: AI, jobs, productivity and safety
chunks.text:
- Nvidia has 32,000 employees today. Jensen hopes for 50,000 with 100 million AI assistants. AIs will recruit other AIs and sit in Slack channels with humans.
- Productivity gains show up as better earnings or growth, so "the next email from the CEO is likely not a layoff announcement". There are more ideas than can be explored, and people are needed to pick which problems to solve before automating.
- Evidence inside Nvidia: chip and computer complexity rising exponentially while employee count grows "barely linearly". He cautions this could be overfit.
- He has 60 direct reports who are world class and better than him at their jobs, and he has no trouble "prompt engineering" them. He says everyone will become a CEO of AI agents, and the skills are creativity, will, knowledge and breaking problems down.
- How he prompts people and AI is the same: give context, constraints and the mission, be clear on the outcome, and leave ambiguous space for creativity so they can surprise him.
- Intelligence is "the single most valuable commodity the world's ever known", now manufactured at scale.
- Safety: much safe-AI work is under-celebrated (red teaming, model cards, guardrail AIs, AIs monitoring AIs, evals), voluntary and coordinated by builders. Treat AI as a system of engineered systems.
- Regulation: mostly at the application level through existing bodies (FAA, NHTSA, FDA), not one universal "galactic AI council".

chunks.heading: Staying relevant and the job is important, not always fun
chunks.text:
- Jensen says his job is not fun all the time, nor does he expect it to be. It is important all the time. "I don't take myself too seriously. I take the work very seriously."
- Fun is not always there, but love is: like family, "do we always love it? Absolutely."
- The real question is not how long he can do it but how long he can stay relevant, which depends on continuing to learn.
- He uses AI daily as tutor, assistant and brainstorm partner. No research without AI, and even when he knows the answer he double-checks, and the next two or three questions reveal something he didn't know.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jensen Huang explains how Nvidia deliberately moved from fixed-function graphics chips to programmable shaders, CUDA and a full integrated stack. He covers the pain of building for a future market, the ARM bid, his upbringing, and why every company will produce intelligence.

chunks.heading: Why Nvidia built a fully integrated stack, deliberately, over decades
chunks.text:
- Jensen says every step of the path from fixed-function graphics to CUDA to AI "was done on purpose." What the outside view leaves out is "all the mistakes that we made" along the way.
- The sequence: accelerate defined graphics functions, invent the programmable shader, build a programming model (CUDA), then add SDKs, libraries and frameworks on top.
- He describes the company's growth as a repeating move: "You build one thing and you generalize it and you realize it could be used for other things, and then you build that thing derived from the first thing and then you generalize it." GPU led to deep learning, which led to robotics and autonomous driving, which led to medical imaging. "That's how we built the company."
- On why deep learning needed full integration: it "needed a brand new stack," just as graphics once did. That meant a new processor, compiler, engine and framework (PyTorch and TensorFlow at the top). It happened that the best processor for deep learning about ten years earlier was an Nvidia GPU.
- The Tensor Core GPU is "a thousand times better at doing deep learning than our original GPU."
- The four layers he describes are hardware, system software, platform and application frameworks.

chunks.heading: Programmability as a bet against commoditisation
chunks.text:
- Fixed-function chips are super efficient, but there are only so many pixels and so many functions, and transistor counts keep growing. His conclusion: graphics would become good enough for anyone, and "we will be commoditized out of existence" unless Nvidia reinvented itself. Integrated graphics today shows the prediction was right.
- Two motives drove the programmable shader at once:
  - Defensive: avoid being commoditised.
  - Creative: games looked like "OpenGL Flight Simulator" with blurry textures and "no life," and he felt the medium would die if artists could not tell different stories.
- The cost was unexpected. Programmability carries overhead that current applications do not need. Nvidia built for the future, so existing games did not benefit, the chip was too expensive for a competitive market, and gross margins were "under pressure all the time."
- What saved it: the core GPU still ran old applications at the best performance in the world.
- Becoming a processor company forced Nvidia to build everything around it:
  - a compiler team
  - SDKs and libraries
  - developer evangelism
  - helping developers port their applications, even doing the library work itself
  - helping them market their software
  - GTC, the developer conference
- In his words, the day you become a processor company you must internalise that this is a brand-new programming model and create everything associated with a computing platform.

chunks.heading: Install base, backward compatibility and technical bets
chunks.text:
- Rule: "If you want developers, they're going to want install base, and if you want install base, they have to be compatible with each other."
- That forced CUDA into GeForce, Quadro and data center GPUs, so that "in every single chip that we make, it's all CUDA compatible." Every generation stays backward compatible so existing software runs faster on new chips.
- Technical choices he calls good ones:
  - GeForce FX used IEEE-compatible 32-bit floating point, although the DirectX shader spec at the time was 24-bit. Results matched a CPU, which opened GPUs to general-purpose computing.
  - RIVA 128 introduced a floating point setup engine, a texture cache and very wide memory. TNT doubled everything, with dual textures and two pixel pipelines, and started the multi-pixel-pipeline architecture.
- Memory bandwidth mattered from the start. Rendering is a painter's algorithm with read-modify-write and blending, so graphics chews through bandwidth. Machine learning, with its huge data volumes, is "all just memory bandwidth," so Nvidia was comfortable in that territory.
- The GPU needed a latency-tolerant design with heavy threading: up to 10,000 threads in flight, versus two in a typical CPU core.
- Mistakes along the way included Cg ("C for Graphics"), which taught Nvidia that processors need shared on-board memory, and GeForce FX itself.
- He chose not to rename the GPU (GPGPU, XPU and VPU were all considered). His view: buyers are smart enough to work out what it does, and Nvidia explains the benefits.

chunks.heading: Where Nvidia chooses to play: partnerships and not squandering resources
chunks.text:
- Company rule: "not squander the resources of our company to do something that already exists." If an x86 CPU or a cloud service exists, Nvidia uses it or partners.
- If something makes sense for Nvidia but not for others, Nvidia first asks others to do it, and builds it only if they decline. "We try to be very selective about the things that we do."
- On services: any Nvidia service would run on GPUs in everybody's clouds, plus something of its own only if needed.
- Partnerships are long-running. He calls himself probably TSMC's longest-running CEO partner and cites SPIL, Foxconn, Asus and MSI.
- Nvidia nurtures old partners (it keeps expanding its PC vision) but "forks off" into data center acceleration, AI and robotics, and keeps adding new partners. He says the company can "reinvent ourselves at will."
- His pride point: "we're the only AI company in the world that works with every AI company in the world." Nvidia contributes from chips through the AI operating-system layers to algorithms.

chunks.heading: The ARM bid and Grace
chunks.text:
- Jensen gives three reasons for wanting ARM:
  1. It was up for sale.
  2. It is "a singular asset," and "you'll never find another ARM asset again."
  3. Mobile is ARM's strength, but its future ought to be the data center. Servers are far smaller in units than mobile, so ARM's economic motive to focus there is questionable. Under Nvidia's ownership, he could have channelled ARM purposefully toward data centers.
- After the deal failed, he says the two years spent seeing the future together were still helpful. ARM's single-thread performance roadmap has improved tremendously since, and ARM now sees the data center as a real opportunity.
- His stance now: Nvidia stays focused on what is best for Nvidia, and ARM does what is best for ARM, including investing in software. His response to losing the breakup-fee money: "We can always go make more money. It was worth a try."

chunks.heading: Manufacturing intelligence: why every company becomes an AI company
chunks.text:
- Definition: "Intelligence is the ability to recognize patterns, recognize relationships, reason about it and make a prediction or plan an action." He says it has nothing to do with general intelligence; "intelligence is just solving problems."
- Claim: for the first time in history, humans can produce "the single most valuable commodity the world's ever known, which is intelligence."
- Deep neural network capability is doubling every six months, versus Moore's Law at every two years.
- GTC keynote framing: data centers become "AI factories," and companies become intelligence manufacturers. Over a decade, Nvidia-accelerated computing delivered a million-x speed-up in AI, and he talks about "the next million-x."
- He predicts some part of every company will codify and automate the production of its intelligence, so every company will be an AI company. The AI will augment humans, with humans in the loop.
- The first wave of AI was perception and inference (recognising images, speech, recommendations). The next wave is robotics: AI that perceives, plans and acts, via digital robots, avatars and physical robots. Omniverse is meant to be essential for making robotics software, as PyTorch and TensorFlow are for AI software.
- Recommender systems as the example: a trillion things on the internet and one small phone, so an AI filter must predict what you want from content features and your explicit and implicit preferences. He calls it "a miracle." Future predictions he lists: best financial strategy, medical therapy, health regimen, vacation plan.
- Autonomous driving as the robotics case: it needs real-time, isochronous processing of radar, camera, lidar and ultrasonic data with diverse, redundant algorithms, producing perception, localisation, a world map and a drive plan.

chunks.heading: Resilience, hard work and surrounding yourself with great people
chunks.text:
- Childhood: he moved to Kentucky in 1973 at age nine, attending Oneida Baptist Institute, an affordable boarding school. He cleaned bathrooms while his older brother worked on tobacco farms.
- Lesson: "We learned hard work, but it never occurred to us that it was hard work." Expectations are set by surroundings, and "I expect very little and it doesn't matter what the circumstances are, you make the best of it."
- His self-described greatest gift: "surrounding myself with amazing people and giving them the opportunity to do amazing work and helping them achieve more than they thought was possible."
- He credits co-founders Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem: without them Nvidia "wouldn't be here." He says he carried the torch longest "because I'm resilient," and that once on a road he can stay on it a very long time and believe in it.
- On the company he built: no other computing company has Nvidia's depth of talent, from chief scientist to chip and system design. A CEO can start from a blank sheet and build every transistor, line of software and system component from scratch, and "it will be utterly expected to work and it will work and it will be world class."
- He says Nvidia has no mission statement; the aim is an environment where people "could do their life's work."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Huang explains why ChatGPT created a new computing platform, how Nvidia responded with inference products and DGX Cloud, and why it builds full stack but goes to market disaggregated. He also covers resilience through redundancy, not competing where everyone can, and why full-stack beats a slowing Moore's Law.

chunks.heading: ChatGPT as AI's iPhone moment and a new computing platform
chunks.text:
- Jensen says GPT-3, WebGPT and InstructGPT were each impressive, but ChatGPT "woke the whole industry up". He calls it "unquestionably the most easy-to-use application that has ever been created" for tasks that consistently surprise people.
- The ease of use and the capability surprised everyone, from novices to deep computer scientists. The transformer work had been done in plain sight, but ChatGPT put the interface, fine-tuning and results together in one flashpoint.
- Within about sixty days, every cloud and software company asked what it meant for them, hundreds of startups appeared, and VCs began funding generative AI.
- Executives who had enjoyed GTC keynotes without being affected by them now call him and say "Now I understand what you were talking about." He says not one executive he knows has been left unmoved.
- His earlier pitch: large language models first learn human language, but will learn "the language of everything, everything that has structure". The physical world, proteins and chemicals all have structure. Understand the language and you can generate new proteins with new properties and functions.
- Three properties characterise a computing platform: how you program it, what applications you can build, and who can put it to work. ChatGPT created a new computing model on all three.
- Reach by platform: workstations in the hundreds of thousands of people, PCs in hundreds of millions and billions, mobile in billions. App counts grew each time: about 5 million in app stores, 350,000 to 500,000 websites that matter. He expects hundreds of millions of LLM applications "because we're going to write our own".
- He frames it as a phase shift: "We're going to look back and we're going to say 'Hey, guess what, we were there'."

chunks.heading: How Nvidia responded to ChatGPT demand
chunks.text:
- First task: respond to a step-up in demand, in two forms.
  - Training: nearly every major cloud provider was already working on LLMs and now has to reach the next level faster. That means bigger models, more data, and the supporting models for fine-tuning, alignment, guard-railing and augmentation.
  - Inference: generative AI is being wired into Microsoft Office, Google Docs and web browsers, so "inference demand has gone through the roof".
- Inference is the biggest change in how he thinks about the business. The workloads differ, so they need different GPUs:
  - Generative video, such as relighting faces, eye reposing, background enhancement. He cites RunwayML as a favourite.
  - Image and 3D graphics generation.
  - LLMs from more than 175 billion parameters down to 5 to 8 billion, where response time per token matters because users watch long outputs stream.
  - Retrieval models with vector databases, where he says Grace Hopper is ideal.
- The core technology already existed. Turning it into inference products for data centers at scale took about six months.
- Inventory write-downs: he admits "Last year was unquestionably a disappointing year". Nvidia expected a bigger year and, with long cycle times, had built or committed to more supply than it sold. Older Ampere parts have a shelf life as Ada and Hopper take over, and Hopper's transformer engine suits LLMs well.
- What limits supply: a GPU is not a chip. A data center Hopper is eight chips with advanced packaging, NVLink, extreme thermal management and about 35,000 components, and weighs around 70 pounds. An AI supercomputer also needs switches, NICs, cables, PDUs and data center space, all on the critical path.

chunks.heading: Full stack inside, disaggregated at go-to-market, and DGX Cloud
chunks.text:
- His principle: "the data center is the computer". It must be orchestrated as one machine, a single pane of glass, which requires software-defined infrastructure and a separate compute plane and control plane.
- Nvidia builds the whole system vertically integrated, full stack and at data center scale, across domains (quantum, computational lithography, graphics, AI, robotics) and from cloud to edge. When it goes to market, it disaggregates everything and integrates into Dell, Lenovo, Quanta, Foxconn, Azure, GCP, AWS and OCI.
- Doing this depends on telling the ecosystem what Nvidia intends to build, so partners can prepare. That is why GTC is transparent about direction, and he says DGX Cloud was built in plain sight.
- Nvidia is "an extension of Dell" and HP for OEM purchases. DGX Cloud applies the same idea to cloud providers: the same Nvidia stack running natively on any cloud, multi-cloud, hybrid, to the edge.
- He calls DGX Cloud "the largest, most significant business model extension we've ever had". Nvidia sells alongside the cloud providers, "when we win, they win". Customers can use a pre-negotiated provider or take Nvidia's suggestion.
- He did not frame it as a way to get subscription revenue and smooth the cycle. The aim is to engage customers directly, to hosting, and move faster: "Nvidia's in the browser", so a team can start from a browser without building a DGX system.
- OCI was first because of compatibility, not for any other reason. He worked with Oracle's architecture team on the best native integration, not a drop-in system. AWS is not shut out, and the deep AWS partnership continues (SageMaker, recommenders, graph neural networks, robotics). He wants to work with everyone the same way, though time to market differs.
- Nvidia already works directly with end users: about 10,000 AI startups, nearly every game developer, nearly every car company, nearly every drug discovery company, and directly with TSMC on cuLitho and with ASML. Fulfilment historically came through others.

chunks.heading: Who should use DGX Cloud, and picking fights worth having
chunks.text:
- Large teams at AWS, Google and Microsoft still need Nvidia's large team. He says "nobody knows accelerated computing better than we do" and nobody has a richer set of libraries to integrate. SageMaker and Vertex AI work with Nvidia teams to accelerate them.
- Accelerated computing is not like spinning up a CPU. It takes many acceleration libraries and a lot of computer science. His line on Moore's Law: "How do you overcome physics except for cleverness?" and the cleverness is computer science.
- Newcomers to ML should just use a public cloud. SageMaker and Azure ML are "terrific", and Nvidia GPUs are integrated into most AI frameworks. He estimates about 80% of the world should go straight to a cloud partner.
- Best fit for working directly with Nvidia: bespoke domain frameworks (drug discovery, industrial AI), high-end generative video, or a proprietary LLM that must scale, be refined and deployed performantly. "We should not be the world's fifth cloud service provider."
- On commoditisation (PyTorch abstraction, AMD, Intel): "You build a great company by doing things that other people can't do. You don't build a great company by fighting other people... to do things that everybody can do."
  - "We're just not a share company." Nvidia works on problems it should solve, that only it can solve or is singularly best placed to solve.
  - He is happy when partners such as AWS and OpenAI succeed, whether or not they use CUDA. "CUDA has great value to us, whether it has great value to somebody else or not, so what?" If someone else is the best answer, "so be it. We move on."

chunks.heading: Export controls, resilience and supply chain
chunks.text:
- A800 and H800 are the China versions of A100 and H100. They are physically fused to lower floating point performance, interconnect, or both, and cannot be unfused. They are form-fit-function identical, plug into the same sockets and run the same software, slower, yet "still the world's best". "The most important thing is it complies with regulation."
- Slower interconnect still scales but less effectively. For example, scaling to 1,000 processors becomes less linear and plateaus earlier. Faster processors need faster fabrics.
- On TSMC Arizona: "that resilience comes from diversity and redundancy". Fabs in the US and elsewhere are incrementally more expensive, and there is a price for that, which Nvidia accepts.
- He compares this to how Nvidia runs itself: power, storage and security redundancy, and even organisations. Sales and marketing overlap so there is diversity, and engineering does the same. Packaging, assembly and testing already carry built-in redundancy, which costs money.

chunks.heading: Where inference runs, and why full-stack beats Moore's Law
chunks.text:
- "Inference will be the way software is operated in the future", meaning software written by a computer instead of a human. He expects every computer to run it eventually.
- Generative AI is the most energy-conserving way to compute: "Why look up an answer if you already know the answer?" He compares it to a human brain at roughly 25 watts.
- Local inference follows the OpenGL path: from a Reality Engine in a data center, to a $100,000 to $150,000 workstation, to a phone. The largest LLMs today need an A100 HGX costing a couple of hundred thousand dollars. He expects performant smaller versions on phones in "no more than ten years".
- The mix will be inference on phone, PC and cloud, with the cloud as the more capable backup. He expects today's distributed computing model to remain.
- Moore's Law delivered 10x every five years at ISO power and ISO cost. He says that will not happen in the next five years. Meanwhile, AI has advanced "a million times" in ten years, from AlexNet detecting cats to today.
- That came from reinventing every layer: chip, system, interconnect and algorithms. He expects LLMs to improve by another factor of a million over the next ten years, and says "It just has to be full stack."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: In a Computex 2025 interview, Huang explains why AI is a full-stack platform whose install base and developer flywheel decide who leads. He frames AI as a new industry built on factories, argues for competing everywhere, and shows how Nvidia is integrated yet disaggregated to serve customers however they buy.

chunks.heading: AI is a new industry powered by "AI factories"
chunks.text:
- Jensen says Nvidia has reinvented itself into a data-center-scale company. Its technology is "wholly integrated to work together, but disintegrated so that the whole ecosystem could work with it."
- He argues Nvidia is now building computers "not just for the technology industry" but for a new industry called AI. AI is partly technology and partly labor, because it augments labor, and robotics will make that clearer.
- This industry will be powered by factories. What people call data centers are really "AI factories," and he expects the computing they need to be "quite large."
- On Microsoft's reported token count, he says actual token generation is far higher. Microsoft's figure covers only what it generated for third parties, and excludes its own consumption and OpenAI.
- Nvidia's goal is to "reinvent Nvidia" so it is "ahead of the puck," where the industry will go, and to solve hard problems.

chunks.heading: Moving from the IT budget to a roughly $50 trillion market
chunks.text:
- For 60 years the IT industry sold technology and tools used by people. Jensen says Nvidia is about to leave the IT budget and move into the manufacturing (CapEx) and OpEx budgets.
- Manufacturing budget: robots, and robotic systems used to build products. OpEx budget: digital workers.
- He puts world OpEx plus CapEx at about $50 trillion, against an IT industry of about a trillion. AI brings the industry into that larger pool.
- His reasoning on jobs: some jobs will be lost and many created. Labor is short (unemployment at lows, restaurants and factories struggling to staff), so robots and agents are likely to expand world GDP over the next 5-10 years.
- He would hire a $100,000-a-year AI agent "in a heartbeat." If it amplifies someone paid $500,000 a year, it is a bargain.
- Foresight: he says what he shows in keynotes today he spoke about five years ago, with less precise vocabulary. He has talked about robotics for about three years and expects it to happen in a couple of years.
- Nvidia's original TAM estimate when it started was $300 million.

chunks.heading: Why AI leadership means the full stack, and why chip controls backfire
chunks.text:
- Jensen calls the AI diffusion rule "exactly wrong" for America. If the goal is American leadership, the rule as written would cause the US to lose its lead.
- AI is a full stack: chips, factories, infrastructure, models and applications. America must lead at every layer, and "you can't just... protect one layer at the expense of everything else."
- The goal should be "accelerating the adoption of American technology everywhere before it's too late," not limiting other countries' access.
- Platform flywheel: a larger, more capable platform gets a bigger install base. More developers build on it, so applications improve. That sells more, which grows the install base further. He says this positive feedback is "the reason why Nvidia is successful today."
- China holds about 50% of the world's AI developers. Staying out of that market makes no sense architecturally.
- If American companies don't compete in China, a Chinese ecosystem will build new, non-American platforms. As AI diffuses worldwide, China's technology would diffuse with it.
- He says not competing in China is "about 90%" of the problem, versus about 10% for the Gulf deals.
- On China's capability: 50% of AI researchers are Chinese and "you're not going to hold them back." DeepSeek is "deeply excellent work." Huawei is a formidable, world-class company. He says restrictions spur competitors, but he expected China to be there every step of the way.
- Cost of the H20 ban: Nvidia wrote off $5.5 billion of inventory ("no company in history has ever written off that much"), walked away from $15 billion of sales, and lost roughly $3 billion in taxes. He says the China market is about $50 billion a year, "like Boeing, not the plane, the whole company."
- Long-run risk: leaving China means losing profits, scale and ecosystem building, and lets China build an alternative to CUDA. Anyone who thinks banning H20s cuts off China's AI is "deeply uninformed."
- On competing: "We want America to win. Every company should want their country to win." He says he doesn't begrudge anyone who aspires to be great, and argues "we ought to go faster." Nvidia got where it is with "absolutely zero support from anybody," so he says to "just let us keep running hard."

chunks.heading: Building policy presence late, and the Gulf partnerships
chunks.text:
- Jensen says he never had to deal with government for most of Nvidia's life. The focus was building technology, the company, the industry, the supply chain and the ecosystem, and competing "every single day."
- Nvidia built a presence in Washington DC over the last several years. It has a handful of people where companies its size have hundreds. They explain how chips and AI ecosystems work and the unintended consequences of policy.
- He says he supports the President's vision and senses a desire to compete while looking for opportunities to cooperate.
- Why the Gulf: Saudi Arabia and Abu Dhabi leaders asked him to attend. He says they have abundant energy and a shortage of labor, so AI converts energy into digital and robotic labor (agents, robots).
- Nvidia helped launch HUMAIN in Saudi Arabia, which aims to build AI factories and host international companies such as OpenAI.

chunks.heading: Data-center economics: throughput per watt and the Pareto frontier
chunks.text:
- A data center is limited by energy: "100 megawatts is 100 megawatts." The factory's job is to maximize throughput per watt in tokens.
- Token quality varies, from free-to-use tokens to premium ones that might be worth $1,000 or $10,000 a month. A chip designed for only one end is underutilized, and an overly fragmented architecture makes it hard to move workload around.
- Systems tuned for a high token rate have low overall throughput, and the reverse. "It's easy to hug the X-axis, it's easy to hug the Y-axis, it's hard to fill out that area."
- Filling the curve is the Blackwell invention. It combines FP4, NVLink 72, the balance of HBM memory capacity and bandwidth against floating point, and the Dynamo software.
- Perf-per-watt matters even where power is plentiful, because a factory is always a fixed size.
- Worked example for 1 GW: about $30 billion for shell, power, land and operations, plus about $50 billion for compute, networking and storage. An architecture with half the perf-per-watt means doubling the $30 billion to $60 billion. His conclusion: "even free is not cheap enough" if the architecture is poor enough.
- Speed outlook: Grace Blackwell is 40 times faster, and another 40x step is plausible. He sees agentic models 100,000 times faster within five years, so reasoning models become the baseline and "even slow thinking is fast."

chunks.heading: Dynamo: the operating system of an AI factory
chunks.text:
- Inference has different stages. Dynamo disaggregates the large language model's processing and spreads it across the data center, metering workload and processor load.
- Pre-fill is context processing (memory, reading PDFs) and is floating-point intensive.
- Decode generates the reasoning and predicts the next token. It needs a lot of bandwidth, and chain-of-thought feeds more tokens back into context.
- Needs vary with the user, model and context. A one-shot query with a strong KV cache needs little floating point, while loading context needs a lot.
- He calls Dynamo "super important" and "essentially the operating system of an AI factory."

chunks.heading: Integrated but disaggregated: serving customers however they want to buy
chunks.text:
- Nvidia builds fully integrated systems because software must be integrated with hardware, but "with enough discipline" that software can be separated from hardware, and system parts can be swapped.
- Grace Blackwell is stood up in many clouds, each slightly different, all on Nvidia standards, and Nvidia fits into each.
- He calls this "the real challenge of Nvidia's business model," and it goes with being a computing platform company.
- On compute and networking stacks, he says adoption of either is "terrific" and both is "incredible." He feels as strongly about networking as about compute. NVLink Fusion lets customers integrate NVLink with their own ASICs.
- He still believes Nvidia builds the better overall system. With 36-38,000 people united on one job, it would be "quite painful to internalize" a 14-person team doing better, so Nvidia strives to do better.
- Principle: "Serving a customer is just smart." He has preferences, but wants "to serve every customer however they'd like to be served."

chunks.heading: GeForce, drivers and abstraction layers
chunks.text:
- Jensen says RTX PRO, Omniverse, robotics and Newton "wouldn't be possible without GeForce." GTC is not the audience for GeForce launches, since Nvidia has a separate game developer conference.
- Nvidia renders only 1 out of 10 pixels in games, and AI generates the rest.
- Drivers: the driver abstraction, which Microsoft helped pioneer, lets an API stay stable while hardware changes significantly. Nvidia's driver is open source, but few outside contribute because each new GPU makes earlier driver work obsolete.
- He says the isolation layer, whether CUDA or DirectX, is what lets people build on top. He adds "I love GeForce actually."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Post-GTC 2026 interview with Ben Thompson. Huang explains why Nvidia is an accelerated computing company, not a chip or GPU company. He covers building vertically then opening horizontally, the Groq deal, CPUs for agents, and why he opposes doomerism and bundling the AI stack.

chunks.heading: Accelerated computing is a full-stack problem, not a chip problem
chunks.text:
- Jensen starts from "What do we need to be?", not "What am I not?". He does not worry about being squeezed into a "chip company" box.
- Early on Nvidia realized accelerated computing is a full-stack problem. To accelerate an application you must:
  - understand the application
  - build the developer ecosystem
  - have deep algorithm expertise, because algorithms written for CPUs do not work well on GPUs and must be rewritten or refactored
- The payoff justifies the work: "50 times speed up, 100 times speed up, 10 times speed up, and so it's totally worth it."
- Nvidia is "an accelerated computing company, not a GPU company". It is "not obsessed about where computing is done"; it wants to accelerate the application.
- Accelerated computing is not parallel computing. About 30 years ago there were roughly 10 to 30 parallel computing companies and only Nvidia survived, because it recognized the goal was never to get rid of the CPU but to accelerate the application.

chunks.heading: Why AI agents mean accelerating all the world's software
chunks.text:
- AI will use tools built for humans (Excel, Photoshop, Synopsys and Cadence logic synthesis tools, databases). Because AIs are fast, those tools must be "super-accelerated".
- Example: SQL is "the ground truth of businesses". Soon agents, not just people, will hammer SQL databases, so the first job is to accelerate SQL.
- His stated priority: get all the world's software accelerated "as fast as possible", then put it in front of AI so it can use it agentically. Data processing is the first big example, which is why the GTC 2026 keynote opened with an IBM partnership.
- He used the first hour of the keynote to retell the CUDA story, partly for Nvidia's own employees, to remind them what is important.
- Tool use comes in two types:
  - Structured (CLIs, APIs): explicit commands and arguments. Mostly SQL and database work in data centers.
  - Unstructured: apps never designed for CLIs or APIs. AI must learn multi-modal use, such as browsing sites and recognizing buttons and menus. This will run on PCs.

chunks.heading: Building AI factories: help customers de-risk, and co-design the whole system
chunks.text:
- A gigawatt AI factory costs roughly $50-60 billion. About $15-17 billion of that is land, power and shell; the rest is compute, networking and storage.
- At that scale, "unless you're helping customers achieve the level of confidence that they're going to succeed in building it, you just have no hope, nobody's going to risk $50 billion."
- Nvidia's progression: help customers build chips, then systems, then AI factories. Factories contain a lot of software (cooling management, electricals, redundancies), not all of it Nvidia's.
- Over-design is the cost of siloed teams: "When you have a lot of people who don't talk to each other... you have to, by definition, over-design your part of it." Working as one team lets you push limits and get more throughput from the same power or save money.
- Biggest wish on supply: land, power and shell stood up faster.
- On supply chain: Nvidia plans upstream and downstream, has a couple of hundred partners with long-term partnerships, and "prepared everyone for growth". He does not think there is twice as much of anything (power, chips) as needed.

chunks.heading: CPUs, Amdahl's Law and the Vera CPU
chunks.text:
- Moore's law is over, and the idea of general-purpose computing that just keeps adding transistors is "so dead". But Nvidia was "never against CPUs" and does not want to violate Amdahl's Law.
- Nvidia buys the best, most expensive CPUs for its systems, because a weak CPU "holds back millions of dollars of chips". GPU time must never sit idle. That is why it built Grace: the highest-performance single-threaded CPU, moving data faster.
- Vera is designed for agentic tool use, unlike the last decade of CPUs built for hyperscale cloud:
  - Cloud monetizes by rentable core, so those CPUs maximize core count (a couple of hundred to 300-400 cores) with performance secondary.
  - For agents, with a GPU waiting on a tool call, the priority is the fastest single-threaded performance plus very strong I/O and memory bandwidth.
  - Vera's bandwidth per CPU core is three times higher than any CPU ever designed, so it never throttles the GPUs.
- x86 remains important: some of the world is happy with Arm, but enterprises have stacks they won't move. Nvidia's own PCs and workstations are still x86, which is why the Intel partnership matters.

chunks.heading: Groq: extending the inference frontier, and building for a pain you feel yourself
chunks.text:
